title: Immigration reporting measure fuels debate over Colorado's role with ICE
description:
A 2021 law blocks employees from providing personally identifiable information to immigration enforcement without a warrant or as part of a criminal investigation.
Walsh called Proposition 81 a “recipe for abuse,” saying it would inevitably lead to racial profiling and the detainment of citizens and legal residents.
Burton Brown disagreed, noting that nothing in Proposition 81 allows profiling or gives ICE agents any authority they don’t have in Colorado.
“Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement,” he said.
“If Proposition 81 passes, we would no longer be able to do that.” Larimer and Jackson County District Attorney Gordon McLaughlin also attended the rally.
text:
A coalition of advocacy groups and several district attorneys rallied outside the Colorado Capitol on Thursday to oppose a ballot measure that, if approved by voters in November, would require state and local law enforcement to cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

Backed by Advance Colorado, Proposition 81 would require local law enforcement agencies to notify Immigration and Customs Enforcement when they charge a person who is in the country illegally with a violent crime or when the individual has previously been charged with a felony. This also applies when the person’s legal status cannot be determined.

Kristi Burton Brown, executive vice president of Advance Colorado, told Colorado Politics that the group is pursuing the measure because state law now bars law enforcement from proactively reporting violent offenders or repeat felons to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

She said that, under a recent state law, an officer faces a fine of up to $50,000 for choosing to report a violent offender to federal authorities. She also noted that other “sanctuary” states, including California and New York, include exceptions in these situations that Colorado does not.

While many have characterized Colorado as a “sanctuary state,” Gov. Jared Polis has pushed back on the label, saying the state “fully cooperates with federal authorities in identifying, apprehending and prosecuting criminals – regardless of immigration status.”

Over the years, Colorado has adopted several laws whose provisions fall under the broad outlines of what constitutes a “sanctuary” state.

Notably, a 2019 law prohibits a law enforcement officer from arresting or detaining an individual solely based on a civil immigration detainer and bars a probation officer or probation department employee from providing an individual’s personal information to federal immigration authorities.

A 2021 law blocks employees from providing personally identifiable information to immigration enforcement without a warrant or as part of a criminal investigation. In 2025, Colorado’s legislators imposed the same restrictions on local government employees as well as judicial and legislative employees.

Some local governments, such as Denver, have also adopted “sanctuary” policies.

Speaking from the Capitol steps Thursday, ACLU Colorado director Olivia Mendoza said approving Proposition 81 would make communities less safe, particularly under the current administration.

“We have seen that since the beginning of the Trump administration’s second term, our communities have been gripped by the fear of ICE’s brutal immigration enforcement, from warrantless arrests to physical brutality to deplorable detention conditions,” she said. “ICE has no place in our state, and Amendment 81 invites them to take a strong foothold in Colorado.”

Mendoza argued that Proposition 81 violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits the government from taking away an individual’s life, liberty or property without fair legal proceedings.

Burton Brown countered that the allegations that the measure violates due process are unfounded because law enforcement would be allowed to report to ICE only after obtaining enough evidence to charge someone with a crime.

If the measure passed, it would require law enforcement to contact ICE every time they charge someone who has a prior criminal record, unless that person happened to have proof of citizenship with them in the form of a birth certificate or passport, according to Denver District Attorney John Walsh.

Walsh called Proposition 81 a “recipe for abuse,” saying it would inevitably lead to racial profiling and the detainment of citizens and legal residents.

“To make things much worse, this obligation triggers on charging a person with a crime, not on a conviction,” he added.

Burton Brown disagreed, noting that nothing in Proposition 81 allows profiling or gives ICE agents any authority they don’t have in Colorado.

She added, “Instead, this gives Colorado law enforcement the ability to report violent criminals or repeat felons if they are here illegally without facing a $50,000 fine from the state.”

Walsh insisted that Proposition 81 would further erode the already strained relationship between immigrant communities and law enforcement.

“Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement,” he said. “If Proposition 81 passes, we would no longer be able to do that.”

Larimer and Jackson County District Attorney Gordon McLaughlin also attended the rally.

Earlier this week, in a victory for DOJ, a federal judge in Kansas ruled that state’s tuition law unconstitutional.

text:
The U.S. Department of Justice sued Utah, the District of Columbia and two more states this week for granting in-state college tuition and scholarships to immigrants without permanent legal status. The cases are the latest in a push by the Trump administration to end the practice across the country.

The department’s attorneys argue the policies discriminate against U.S. citizens from out of state. The new cases, filed Thursday, bring the total to 25 lawsuits over allowing resident tuition for unauthorized immigrants in states where they live, the department said in a news release.

Earlier this week, in a victory for DOJ, a federal judge in Kansas ruled that state’s tuition law unconstitutional.

“No more placing illegal aliens over American citizens on this Department of Justice’s watch,” said Stanley Woodward Jr., associate U.S. attorney general, in a prepared statement.

The lawsuits follow President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive order directing the DOJ and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to take action against states’ enforcement of policies granting resident tuition to immigrants without legal authorization.

Utah allows in-state tuition for students who graduated in Utah after attending high school in the state for at least three years. Proponents of such policies say they don’t change any academic requirements and allow students to pay the same rate as the classmates they grew up with.

A legislative proposal seeking to end the benefit in Utah passed the House by a narrow margin but did not get a vote or sponsor in the Senate this year after opponents raised concerns it could make college unaffordable for students who have lived much of their lives in Utah.

State lawmakers are likely to continue the debate into next year. Top Republican legislators focused Thursday on the question of who taxpayer money should serve.

“Utah taxpayers should not be footing the bill for benefits extended to individuals who are here illegally. Our taxpayer dollars should prioritize Utah citizens,” House Speaker Mike Schultz said Friday in a statement to Utah News Dispatch. Schultz, R-Hooper, voted in favor of the 2026 measure.

“The Legislature has a responsibility to protect Utah taxpayers and make sure state resources are being used as intended,” Schultz said in the statement. “I look forward to addressing this issue and making the necessary changes during the 2027 General Session.”

Senate President Stuart Adams said Friday that he and his colleagues in the Senate were still reviewing the lawsuit. Adams seemed to reference tenets of Utah’s moderate 2010 immigration compact as he reflected on the state’s next steps, though he didn’t signal what they may look like.

“Utah has long valued those who come to this country legally, strengthen our communities and contribute to our economy. But taxpayer-funded benefits should prioritize those they are intended to serve,” Adams said in a prepared statement.

He said the Senate “is committed to protecting Utah taxpayers, respecting those who follow the legal immigration process and ensuring Utah law is fair, lawful and consistent with federal requirements.”

As of 2023, the state was home to an estimated 140,000 unauthorized immigrants, according to the Pew Research Center, though it wasn’t clear how many were of college age. Utah’s total population at the time was roughly 3.4 million.

DOJ’s lawsuit filed in federal court in Utah names the state, the Utah System of Higher Education and its commissioner, Geoffrey Landward, as defendants.

In an unsigned statement to Utah News Dispatch, the Utah System of Higher Education said “we support students who meet the eligibility requirements established in state law and defer to the Utah Legislature’s authority to set tuition policy for our public colleges and universities. We will continue to administer that in accordance with legislative direction.”

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown declined through a spokesperson to speak about the pending litigation that advocates condemned as shameful.

“This coordinated attack on the rights of young immigrants is unprecedented and unwarranted,” said Thomas Saenz, president of the Los Angeles-based Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, in a Friday statement. “No administration of either party has ever previously challenged these state tuition-equity laws.”

In-state tuition and fees at the flagship University of Utah is $10,480 for the current academic year, while non-resident tuition is $32,932, according to the university’s estimates. The exact cost varies based on a student’s specific program and coursework.

title: Body camera footage of '25 ICE raid to be used in lawsuit - The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
authors: VALERIE GONZALEZand MARK VANCLEAVE The Associated Press
description:
The sprawling snack-food factory in upstate New York appeared to be closed when a small army of immigration officers arrived after 9 a.m.
A male officer peered through a locked stall door, and his body cam video revealed a woman sitting on the toilet.
Not all officers wore body cameras, but those who did often indicated to other officers that they were recording before they initiated a conversation.
Law enforcement agencies have come under criticism for not using body cameras and for refusing to release footage when they do.
The Trump administration has repeatedly promised to equip ICE field agents with body cameras, as required by Congress.
text:
Body camera footage from September 2025 shows a raid at the Nutrition Bar Confectioners plant in Cato, N.Y., a town of 2,500 people east of Syracuse, and offers a rare glimpse inside a workplace immigration sweep. The Associated Press analyzed the video, which was part of a lawsuit filed Thursday that accuses authorities of overstepping their search warrants.

The sprawling snack-food factory in upstate New York appeared to be closed when a small army of immigration officers arrived after 9 a.m. Following a brief discussion of whether to force their way inside, a manager opened the front door.

Over the next several hours, body cameras were running as federal authorities from several agencies made 57 arrests, debated which files to seize and when to release employees who were U.S. citizens. They also searched for anyone in hiding.

The officers ordered a manager to announce their presence over loudspeakers while they entered the building and caught employees on the production line, in the warehouse and a few in the bathroom. Officers covered all exits while others swept the interior, including homing in on locked doors.

Male officers encountered a locked bathroom and began shouting instructions in broken Spanish at female employees through the door, demanding that they come out. After about 10 seconds, officers broke through the door.

One woman was outside of a stall and another in the stall. A male officer peered through a locked stall door, and his body cam video revealed a woman sitting on the toilet.

"Miss, pull up your pants. Come out of the bathroom," he told her.

"You have to wait. I can't come out like this, naked!" she replied.

Investigators interviewed the general manager and said they were looking into hiring practices and potential fraudulent documents. Inside and outside the building, officers checked every office, storage room and hallway for anyone who was hiding.

Employees were lined up and separated into groups of U.S. citizens and potential noncitizens. Officers asked for their immigration status, requested documents and posed questions about their entry into the U.S. Some employees were pregnant.

Some were parents and expressed concern for their children at home. Others said they would not answer questions without first speaking to their attorneys, and officers told them they would be arrested.

One employee refused to answer questions. "Will you let me talk to my attorney?" she asked the officer. He raised his voice and continued asking about her immigration status.

U.S. citizens were asked for personal information, including their phone numbers and addresses before they were allowed to leave.

A Border Patrol agent who spoke to another official wearing a camera used disparaging language about children from other countries when recounting his experience working at a South Texas immigrant detention center. He said former President Joe Biden's administration allowed millions of people to enter the United States from countries where children are treated "differently" than they are by American parents.

"In other countries, kids are more of a commodity or it's more of like, I'm going to put it in those terms. It's more like an animal, right? It's not prized the way that we do it," he said.

"There's countries like Brazil and other places where they're literal street rats at a very young age who commit crimes, and then they come here. I don't know if you have kids, but they'll eat our kids for breakfast."

The Homeland Security Department said Friday that it executed a criminal search warrant at the plant as part of an investigation that is still open. Its statement did not address the contents of the video or the merits of the lawsuit.

Not all officers wore body cameras, but those who did often indicated to other officers that they were recording before they initiated a conversation.

ICE's Homeland Security Investigations unit is responsible for workplace raids, which have been relatively few and low-key compared to ICE's removal unit, which arrests people in the street, at homes and in public and also manages detention centers. The Trump administration's largest workplace raid was last year at a Hyundai electric vehicle plant in Georgia. It resulted in nearly 500 arrests and fueled diplomatic tension with South Korea.

The lawsuit against Homeland Security claims federal officers exceeded the authority of their warrants and violated workers' constitutional rights against unlawful search and seizure.

"There were no arrest warrants," said Perry Grossman, a supervising attorney at the New York Civil Liberties Union, which filed the lawsuit with the Worker Justice Center of New York.

"There was no suspicion that individual workers had committed crimes. And they seized easily 100 people for nonconsensual questioning. They arrested 57. Out of those 57 people, criminal charges were brought against only five. And the most serious charge was unlawful reentry."

Grossman said one employee got her charges dismissed after contending in a lawsuit that her Fourth Amendment rights were violated. He said he was not aware of any charges or indictments against the employers.

Officers detained about 60 people and deported some employees, including two plaintiffs who are part of Thursday's lawsuit. One plaintiff has since been allowed to reenter the country. Attorneys for the second deported plaintiff are seeking his return.

Law enforcement agencies have come under criticism for not using body cameras and for refusing to release footage when they do. ICE, in particular, has been scrutinized after a $75 billion infusion from Congress and an expanding street presence that has led to three fatal shootings this year.

ICE's own rules on releasing video are unclear. Its policy calls for expedited release of footage after a serious injury or death in custody when doing so is determined to be in the "best interests of the agency."

The Trump administration has repeatedly promised to equip ICE field agents with body cameras, as required by Congress. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last week that the agency was "on track" to do so by the end of September.

title: Immigration activity taking toll on children's health, doctors say | Fulton Sun
description:
Clinicians like Jayawardena say immigration arrests and detentions are taking a particularly acute toll on children's health as families isolate at home.
Along with missing health milestones and getting needed health care, kids are grappling with the long-term trauma of losing a parent.
Preventive care, such as vaccinations, as well as chronic disease management and mental health care were the most affected, health care workers reported.
Elsewhere, one of KIND's clients in California, a preteen sexual assault victim, has gone weeks without mental health care.
Fernandez said KIND has been offering Uber and Lyft rides to field offices because clients are afraid to drive to appointments to receive health care.
text:
In Minnesota, an elementary school child has gone without surgery to treat a rare, life-threatening neck infection that isn't responding to antibiotics.

Another young child can't use their hearing aids because the family ran out of batteries and hasn't come to get replacements.

Yet another child's cochlear implant surgery was delayed by several months.

These patients' families, all immigrants, have been afraid of showing up to the hospital after immigration officers flooded their communities in recent months, said their doctor, pediatric otolaryngologist Asitha Jayawardena, a head and neck surgeon at Children's Minnesota.

Clinicians like Jayawardena say immigration arrests and detentions are taking a particularly acute toll on children's health as families isolate at home. He's seen some cases -- such as the child with the neck infection -- worsen because fearful parents aren't coming in.

"Without a doubt, it oscillates between being infuriating and absolutely disheartening," Jayawardena said about the chilling effect.

As the Trump administration's immigration enforcement leads to sweeping arrests, healthcare workers say those actions have hit children hard -- including children who are U.S. citizens and those in families without arrests.

Many health care providers report that since January 2025, they've seen a surge in missed pediatric appointments, delayed preventive care, and sick or injured kids going without treatment. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests have continued to climb -- with a record 51,000 arrests in July -- and experts predict continued unhealthy outcomes among children, causing collateral damage that could extend for years.

Health care workers told Stateline that in addition to the physical healthcare fallout, they've also seen a significant increase in depression, anxiety and post-trauma symptoms among their pediatric patients.

Delayed health care has critical consequences for young kids. For example, hearing loss, such as that experienced by Jayawardena's patients, can hinder crucial development including speech, language and social skills. Along with missing health milestones and getting needed health care, kids are grappling with the long-term trauma of losing a parent.

"Community-wide trauma that is being inflicted is having a really important impact on families and children in particular. There are children that are losing their guardians. There are families that are losing their breadwinners," said Amy Liebman, chief program officer of the Migrant Clinicians Network, a nationwide organization of health care workers serving migrant families.

"That certainly is going to ultimately impact their health and then their ability to access care," she said.

The Trump administration also has introduced rules that allow federal agencies to take into account a family's use of public benefits when reviewing applications for lawful immigration status. Dr. Gabriela Maradiaga Panayotti, a pediatrician in Durham, North Carolina, pointed to studies showing that such policies lead to a decrease in health care use, including among U.S. citizen children.

One of her patients, a U.S. citizen on Medicaid, had stopped a medication for ADHD that had helped him achieve better grades at school. His parents feared being targeted through Medicaid paperwork, so they didn't refill his prescription. The child's grades began to drop again.

"They didn't want to be labeled as utilizing resources," Maradiaga Panayotti said. "I hurt for him, especially because he's at this tender preteen age where self-confidence and performance at school can really either build on and set a good foundation for success in high school, or can drop."

Millions of children

Researchers at the Brookings Institution, a public policy research nonprofit, estimate that since Jan. 20 of last year, the day President Donald Trump was sworn in, and through early April of this year, more than 146,000 U.S. citizen children have had a parent detained.

But many more are living with that fear.

The Pew Research Center estimates 4.6 million U.S.-born children lived with an unauthorized immigrant parent in 2023, and roughly 2.5 million children could face the detention of both household parents, according to a Brookings analysis.

But the trend cuts across immigration status -- including those born to refugees, DACA recipients, asylees and people with temporary protected status. Across the nation, about a fourth of children are born to immigrant families, according to the Migrant Policy Institute.

Increased ICE activity has included arrests at hospitals, and the agency has also made unprecedented efforts to obtain private health data, including Medicaid patient records, to extract addresses and immigration statuses -- another major source of fear for families.

Jayawardena and his colleagues published a study in the American Academy of Pediatrics medical journal in August measuring whether pediatric outpatient care visits were disrupted during and after the large-scale immigration raids of Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, when the Trump administration deployed 3,000 agents, heavily targeting Somali and South Asian communities.

The research team found that the rate of missed appointments among Hispanic or Latino children increased by more than 50 percent during Metro Surge compared to the same time period -- the first week of December to second week of February -- in the prior two years.

Missed appointments increased by 80 percent among Spanish-speaking families and 53 percent among families needing language interpretation services.

"The barrier is not necessarily lack of access, but more the fear and the isolation, and so the enforcement is having this chilling effect on immigrant families who, even though they may need these critical services, may be avoiding the hospital, the counseling, the victim services, and other essential care," said Jasiel Fernandez, vice president of psychosocial supports at the global pro bono nonprofit KIND, or Kids in Need of Defense. "We see that happening over and over."

The Migrant Clinicians Network, along with Physicians For Human Rights, surveyed nearly 700 health care workers across 30 states between March and August of last year, amid spikes in immigration activity. Most of the surveyed professionals -- 84 percent -- reported significant or moderate drops in pediatric patient visits since Trump's January 2025 executive orders on immigration.

Kids also were spending less time outdoors, which affects overall health, and saw delayed diagnoses of their conditions. About 27 percent of clinicians said patients feared enrolling in benefits for their children, and couldn't afford doctor visits. Preventive care, such as vaccinations, as well as chronic disease management and mental health care were the most affected, health care workers reported.

And in both the survey and through interviews with Stateline, clinicians have reported seeing kids show up to emergency departments alone.

In Missouri, one pediatric emergency medicine physician, who spoke with Stateline on the condition of anonymity because he feared retaliation against his hospital, recalled an 11-year-old child who had been attacked by a dog, his legs riddled in bites. He came to the hospital with only his teenage sister.

"He told us that (his parents) were scared to come in because ICE might be at the hospital," the physician recalled.

Others aren't showing up to care at all. "Kids like these are so vulnerable that they kind of could fall through the cracks," he added. "We see the downstream effects of policy changes, and we try to address all these needs. But when kids are coming in, they're super sick."

Missed care, advanced illness

Some clinicians told Stateline that by the time some children reach their clinics, their health conditions have advanced to a more difficult stage.

One North Carolina pediatrician has seen kids with asthma miss inhaler prescriptions, leading to more asthma attacks. In another case, a large family of refugee children came in covered in splotchy, itchy rashes -- scabies. The family had been sharing two bedrooms. Afraid, they had postponed care for four weeks.

"All of these children, totally ridden throughout their bodies, and it's so uncomfortable. You can't sleep because it's horribly itchy," said the pediatrician, who spoke to Stateline on the condition of anonymity, fearing retaliation since her clinic receives federal funding.

"We're creating tremendous problems for our community that will probably come back to bite us, because now these kids are going around with untreated medical conditions that are only going to get worse," she said. "It's a time when they need even more support than before, and our administration just isn't really allowing that."

She and others said they're also noticing worsening depression among their patients.

"They're spiraling out, and they're not getting any support because they can't come in and get care," said the North Carolina pediatrician. She recalled one teenager telling her that they couldn't sleep at night. "'I'm sobbing and crying, terrified that my parents will be taken away,'" she recalled the teen telling her.

Elsewhere, one of KIND's clients in California, a preteen sexual assault victim, has gone weeks without mental health care.

"The child's sponsor, who is undocumented, is very afraid to take the young person to mental health appointments or any other kind of follow-up service," Fernandez said. "Choosing basically to forgo that for the time being."

In Texas, which has the most immigrant detainees of any state, a 14-year-old's primary caregiver was detained. The teen has been suffering suicidal ideation.

"That young person is unable to access services," Fernandez said. "Even if we think that a teenager has a certain level of agency to do certain things, when the caregiver is removed abruptly ... the sponsor is not able to support, is not able to meet significant needs and monitoring for that young person."

Fernandez said KIND has been offering Uber and Lyft rides to field offices because clients are afraid to drive to appointments to receive health care.

In southeast Florida's Indian River County, Heather Miranda is CEO of Treasure Coast Community Health, which runs multiple clinics serving nearby communities of agricultural workers. Clinic staff in the northern area of the county, where Miranda said most immigration enforcement activity has been concentrated, told her they've seen a significant decrease of kids coming in -- nearly 500 pediatric no-shows since February, 16 percent of all appointments.

"They've seen kids not coming in for sick visits," Miranda said. "Not coming in for their well-child or their vaccines. ... It's just been, overall, a decrease in preventative care, which is really, really important."

Back in Minneapolis, Jayawardena said that even months after Operation Metro Surge, fear among his patient families remains "a persistent problem."

"I want to help take care of these children, and the families want to get taken care of, as does my entire hospital system -- and we cannot get them just physically into the hospital for things that are necessary," he said. "It's just very disheartening knowing that there's something I can do, but I am prohibited from doing it because families don't feel safe."

Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassaneinstateline.org.

title: Federal judge rules Trump administration plan for 50% FEMA staffing cuts was unlawful
description:
A federal judge has ruled that a plan by the Trump administration to slash staffing at the federal agency tasked with responding to disasters by 50% was unlawful.
The issue of the FEMA staffing was part of a much larger lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees and other labor groups, contesting efforts by the Trump administration to slash the federal workforce.
“Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” wrote Illston.

text:
A federal judge has ruled that a plan by the Trump administration to slash staffing at the federal agency tasked with responding to disasters by 50% was unlawful.

The opinion issued late Friday marked a victory for labor groups who had sued the agency. The labor organizations had argued that plans by the Department of Homeland Security, which was then led by Secretary Kristi Noem, violated congressional protections that were designed to safeguard the independence of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

The issue of the FEMA staffing was part of a much larger lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees and other labor groups, contesting efforts by the Trump administration to slash the federal workforce.

U.S. District Judge Susan Illston wrote in her opinion that top Homeland Security officials late last year directed FEMA’s leadership to submit a staffing plan that included a 50% staffing cut even though the agency’s own supervisors objected.

“Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” wrote Illston.

FEMA responded in a statement late Saturday saying that while it does not comment on personnel matters and ongoing litigation, “DHS and FEMA are ready for the 2026 hurricane season.”

“We’re ensuring workforce stability and a strong, deployable force for upcoming national events and potential disasters; making the agency leaner, faster and laser-focused on supporting state, local, tribal and territorial partners before, during and after disasters,” the statement said. “FEMA continues to maintain a roster of experienced leadership and support staff across headquarters and regional offices.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In the opinion, Illston wrote that it was clear that the government violated rules established after 2005’s Hurricane Katrina that put decisions on staffing levels squarely in the hands of FEMA, not the Department of Homeland Security, and that prevented Homeland Security from “substantially” reducing the “functions” of FEMA.

Illston didn’t order a specific remedy to carry out her opinion but directed the two sides to meet and decide on a course of relief.

Although FEMA has experienced terminations, the 50% staffing cuts ultimately were not carried out. In recent months, after top leadership changes at FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security, the agency has rehired some staffers who were let go.

FEMA was one of the agencies targeted for staff reductions in the federal government as part of a broad Trump administration plan to reduce the size of government. The embattled agency has been buffeted by mass staff departures, disruptions of grant programs and delays of disaster aid.

In May, a Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council submitted a final report recommending sweeping changes to how the agency supports states, tribes and territories in disaster.

The final version backed away from the recommendation to cut the FEMA workforce by 50%, which was included in a December 2025 draft reviewed by the Associated Press.

The council instead recommended the agency conduct a “strategic review” to determine “appropriate staffing levels.”

In an August report, the Government Accountability Office said it found that the departures of thousands of staff in 2025 resulted in a “loss of institutional knowledge and experienced personnel” and “exacerbated longstanding workforce challenges.”

More than 4,300 employees, or about 17% of FEMA’s workforce, separated from the agency in the 2025 budget year, with over 1,500 through voluntary reductions. The agency also made about 2,900 new hires.

The GAO recently recommended to Congress that it “consider requiring” FEMA to base “significant workforce decisions” on a more strategic planning process.

Without it, the GAO found, “FEMA cannot be assured that the agency is positioned to effectively meet its mission needs.”

text:
A federal judge has ordered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to halt construction on a planned detention facility in Gilroy after attorneys for the state of California and Santa Clara County sued to block it on environmental grounds.

Judge Eumi K. Lee of the U.S. District Court Northern District of California, who was nominated for the post by former President Joe Biden, sided with the county and state Attorney General’s office Friday by issuing a preliminary injunction against the planned detention center. The order pauses work on the project until the lawsuit is resolved.

In her ruling, Lee wrote that the federal agency failed to study potential environmental pollution at the planned detention center, which, if built, would occupy property that used to be an agricultural resource center. That research “resulted in known hazardous waste violations,” Lee wrote.

ICE had offered no proof that a “meaningful environmental analysis” was conducted before starting construction, the judge wrote. Evidence submitted to the court suggests that construction and demolition work on-site “increases the risk of releasing hazardous materials into the environment,” Lee wrote.

“We’re hopeful the court’s ruling sends a clear message that this is the wrong process and the wrong place for this facility,” Santa Clara County Counsel Tony LoPresti said in a statement Friday. “The federal government’s legal violations concealed fundamental flaws with this project — you can’t plop a facility like this onto sensitive land that lacks basic infrastructure to support the detention of individuals.”

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat who has filed lawsuits relentlessly against the Republican Trump administration, celebrated the ruling in a statement on Friday.

“The Trump Administration tried to rush construction of this facility in secret, ignoring environmental safeguards and shutting out the communities that would bear the consequences,” he said.

A spokesperson for ICE did not immediately comment.

The state and county have sought a court order permanently shutting down the project. If built, the Gilroy Holding Facility would allow for the detention of at least 120 people per day, ICE wrote in court filings. However, Lee said the actual capacity of the center could be larger than the agency’s estimates.

The parcel of land occupies 25 acres, just east of Highway 101 and Gilroy city limits and just north of Highway 152.

Lawyers for the county had argued that construction could release hazardous materials, and that the facility’s operations would overload its septic system — posing risk to nearby communities and wildlife.

From 1993 to 2023, the site housed several agricultural research companies, which had received permits from Santa Clara County to operate as “hazardous waste generator facilities” because of their use of pesticides as well as solvents, acids, alkaline cleaners and other chemicals, Lee wrote. County inspections had found “multiple” violations of actual or possible releases of chemicals.

Federal attorneys disputed those claims, arguing that the county already knew hazardous materials might be present at the site and that the expected increase in occupancy was not significant.

An Afghan woman accused of supporting the ISIL (ISIS) armed group has been deported from the United States in the first case brought before an obscure and long-dormant court created 30 years ago to remove people classified by the government as “alien terrorists”.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) announced on Friday that Nazira Haji Zada was deported to Afghanistan after being brought before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.

The 47-year-old lawful permanent resident, who had been living in Fort Worth, Texas, was arrested in 2024. US Attorney General Todd Blanche filed the papers for her removal on July 15 this year. She waived her rights to challenge her detention and was subsequently deported to Afghanistan.

The DOJ accused Haji Zada of helping conceal an ISIL-inspired plot for a mass shooting in the US state of Oklahoma on election day in 2024. She was never charged with a crime, but her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, pleaded guilty to related charges.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created by Congress in 1996 as part of a broader effort to combat international terrorism. It is a specialised US federal court made up of five judges serving staggered five-year terms. It allows the US government to submit classified information in cases where disclosure could threaten national security, while requiring an unclassified summary that the court determines is sufficient for the accused to prepare a defence. The government must prove with strong evidence that the person is an “alien terrorist”.

The defence said that bringing lawful permanent residents before a court while withholding the evidence against them violated due process and predicted the court would eventually be found unconstitutional.

DOJ officials described the deportation as a national security victory.

“Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said, adding that the case showed the department would use “every tool at its disposal” to protect the country.

Haji Zada’s attorneys said her decision to consent to removal “should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy.”

“Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process,” the defence lawyers said in a statement. “We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue.”

It is unclear whether the DOJ would pursue additional cases through the previously unused court.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC: The Trump administration had taken a major immigration detention dispute to the Supreme Court and secured an October argument date.

But the case has now disappeared from the Court's docket after New York Gov Kathy Hochul pardoned one of the two noncitizens at its center.

The administration and the respondent jointly moved to dismiss Genalo v Black after the pardon eliminated the criminal conviction that had made Keisy GM subject to mandatory immigration detention.

The Supreme Court case concerned whether noncitizens detained for lengthy periods must receive bond hearings under the Fifth Amendment.

A major case reached the Court

The Supreme Court agreed in June to hear the Trump administration's challenge to a 2024 Second Circuit ruling involving two lawful permanent residents, Carol Williams Black and Keisy GM.

The appeals court held that noncitizens held under a federal mandatory-detention law may be entitled to an individualized bond hearing when their detention becomes unreasonably prolonged.

It also ruled that the government must justify continued detention by clear and convincing evidence in such circumstances.

The Trump administration challenged that ruling, arguing that the Supreme Court should address when prolonged detention triggers a constitutional right to a hearing.

The case had been scheduled for oral arguments on October 13.

Kathy Hochul's pardon changed the case

On August 28, Hochul granted Keisy GM a full and unconditional pardon for the offense that formed the basis for his mandatory detention under federal immigration law.

A filing submitted to the Supreme Court after the pardon argued that the move eliminated the prospect that he could again be detained under that provision, leaving no live controversy for the Court to decide.

The Justice Department subsequently agreed that the case had become moot.

The administration and immigration advocates then filed a joint stipulation seeking dismissal, ending the case before the scheduled argument.

The Second Circuit ruling remains in effect

The dismissal means the Supreme Court will not decide the broader constitutional questions presented in Genalo v Black.

The Second Circuit's 2024 decision found that mandatory detention without a bond hearing could violate due process once the detention becomes unreasonably prolonged.

Black had been detained for seven months, while Keisy GM had spent approximately 21 months in detention without such a hearing.

The ruling remains significant within the Second Circuit, which covers New York, Connecticut and Vermont.

The Supreme Court had also asked the parties to specifically address whether Keisy GM's case was moot before Hochul issued the pardon.

Administration plans to keep fighting

The dismissal does not end the Trump administration's broader challenge to prolonged-detention bond hearings.

According to the government's position in the case, the administration intends to seek another case through which the Supreme Court can address the issue.

The dispute could therefore return to the justices with a different detainee at its center.

For Americans, the case could affect how long certain noncitizens facing deportation can be held without a bond hearing.

For now, that question remains unanswered by the Supreme Court after a New York pardon brought this particular challenge to an end.

text:
Residents on Chicago’s Northwest Side say they were outraged to learn federal immigration agents used police-run parking lots this month to stage and transfer detainees, in violation of an executive order barring federal immigration enforcement on city-owned property.

Videos reviewed by the Sun-Times show federal immigration agents moving detainees from one vehicle to another last week at a parking lot run by the Chicago Police Department’s Albany Park District.

Denise Poloyac, a member of Indivisible Chicago, said she saw masked agents staged at the parking lot on Wednesday.

“I saw what was obviously a federal agent get out of a car. He had a black mask on, and he was all dressed in black,” Poloyac, 66, told the Sun-Times. “State and local law enforcement in Illinois is not to, in any way, cooperate with federal immigration agents doing immigration enforcement, and that’s clearly what their intent was — to use this as a meeting spot to then go out and detain people.”

Last year, Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order barring city-owned property from being used as staging grounds for raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. The order followed a 2021 revision to Chicago’s Welcoming City ordinance under former Mayor Lori Lightfoot that prohibits Chicago police officers from cooperating with ICE under any circumstances.

At an Albany Park District council meeting on Saturday, residents called on the Chicago Police Department to “end the collaboration” between the department and federal immigration agents.

District Councilor Elizabeth Rochford told the Sun-Times she heard about federal immigration agents allegedly using the lot to stage and transfer detainees Wednesday after learning about similar rumors in other areas. She immediately reached out to Cmdr. Jesse Alvarez, who has since ignored her requests for a response.

“[Resident concerns] seem to be falling on deaf ears unfortunately,” Rochford said. “It’s very frustrating. … I feel like we wanted there to be more respect for their positions, and more of a give and take, and that doesn’t feel like it has come to pass.”

Paddy Lindley, a resident of Albany Park, said Alvarez has shown a pattern of ignoring residents’ concerns and allowing federal agents to stage in the precinct is just the latest example.

“What we have seen from this district commander is a pattern of stalling, of lying to us, and of not prioritizing the activities that keep us safe,” Lindley said. “Instead, what we continue to see are instances of ICE terrorizing our neighbors, harassment of youth, of immigrant populations, of our homeless neighbors in encampments. These are the populations that need the most protection.”

The Chicago Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office said the mayor and CPD were aware of the incident and were “actively monitoring and responding” to the violation of Johnson’s executive order.

“Following recent reports, senior members of the Johnson administration and CPD met with district commanders to verify full compliance with the Welcoming City ordinance was upheld and reiterate that when violations occur, CPD personnel must take action to direct federal immigration personnel to leave City property and comply with local law,” the mayor’s office said in a statement.

At a press conference before the district council meeting, residents and local officials demanded answers from police and accountability for their actions.

“Illinois has made a commitment that our state and local resources would not be used to facilitate federal civil immigration enforcement,” said state Sen. Graciela Guzman (20th).

“That commitment has to mean something, and it especially has to mean something when our communities are under attack,” she said. “We deserve the facts. We deserve transparency.”

text:
SANTA CLARA COUNTY, CALIF. — California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the County of Santa Clara late yesterday secured a preliminary injunction blocking the illegal construction of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in the unincorporated area of Santa Clara County near Gilroy, California.

In June 2026, Attorney General Bonta and County Counsel LoPresti filed a lawsuit challenging the construction of this facility, which the federal government pursued without required environmental review or consultation with state and local governments. ICE subsequently agreed to pause construction until September 9, 2026. Yesterday’s order by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California continues to halt construction and asks the parties to meet and confer and submit a proposed order by September 30, 2026 on the scope of the injunction.

"No one is above the law — not even the federal government," said Attorney General Rob Bonta. "The Trump Administration tried to rush construction of this facility in secret, ignoring environmental safeguards and shutting out the communities that would bear the consequences. This ruling sends a clear message: California will hold the federal government accountable and protect our communities, our environment, and the rule of law.”

“We’re hopeful the court’s ruling sends a clear message that this is the wrong process and the wrong place for this facility,” said County Counsel Tony LoPresti. “The federal government’s legal violations concealed fundamental flaws with this project—you can’t plop a facility like this onto sensitive land that lacks basic infrastructure to support the detention of individuals. We’re proud to stand with Attorney General Bonta in fighting this battle, and we’re honored to support an immigrant community that has been under constant assault by an Administration that is all too willing to proceed without regard for the law.”

Background

In January 2025, the federal government leased a 24.5-acre parcel of incorporated land near Gilroy, California from a private developer for use by ICE as a likely Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) holding facility. From there, the federal government moved to build out the site rapidly and without transparency — bypassing required environmental reviews and failing to consult with state or local governments at any point. The construction of the facility threatens to cause the release of hazardous materials and disrupt the ecosystem, habitat, and agricultural value of land that the county and the state have protected for exclusively agricultural uses since the 1960s. The project is also likely to have severe impacts on vital infrastructure, overwhelming a septic system designed for much smaller use.

Attorney General Bonta and the County of Santa Clara filed a lawsuit and a motion for a preliminary injunction in June 2026, arguing that the development of this facility violates the National Environmental Policy Act, the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Intergovernmental Cooperation Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and California’s Williamson Act. Yesterday's decision on the motion for a preliminary injunction finds Attorney General Bonta and the County of Santa Clara are likely to succeed in the litigation and halts construction of the facility pending further instruction by the court.

text:
(NewsNation) — As backlash against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement continues to mount, border czar Tom Homan says the agency is simply enforcing laws passed by Congress.

Homan discussed the state of ICE during an exclusive interview with “NewsNation Prime,” arguing that officers and agents have no personal incentive when making arrests.

“Members of Congress want to call ICE white nationalists, racists, secret police and Nazis,” Homan said. “Well, if they’re Nazis for enforcing immigration law, what’s that make Congress? They wrote the law.”

“ICE is simply enforcing the laws enacted by Congress and signed by a president. If Congress doesn’t like what they’re doing, then change the law.”

ICE operating at schools and hospitals is a lie: Homan

ICE has faced criticism over some enforcement actions, including allegations by Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., that agents arrested parents at bus stops in Connecticut last month.

Homan disputed that characterization, saying the arrest occurred after the child had already left the area and arguing that having children does not exempt migrants from immigration law.

“That is a stone-cold lie,” he said regarding claims that ICE is operating in hospitals, churches and schools. “The people who say that, I have challenged them.”

In May, an ICE-related incident outside a Brooklyn hospital sparked protests and several arrests. According to the Department of Homeland Security, the man involved was an undocumented immigrant from Nigeria who had been taken to the hospital by federal agents after being detained. Officials said he refused commands to exit his vehicle, prompting agents to use what they described as the “minimum amount of force” necessary to make the arrest.

“It hasn’t happened. Now, we could. We have the authority. If there’s a significant national security threat, there’s no sanctuary. If we find them, we’re going to arrest them,” Homan said. “But ICE has simply not done that. The men and women of ICE are professionals. They try to do things in the safest possible way.”

ICE detention standards are among the highest, Homan says

Homan also pushed back on criticism of conditions inside ICE detention facilities.

A Marshall Project report found that more than 500 babies and toddlers have spent time in ICE detention facilities since the beginning of last year.

“There are a lot of lies about ICE detention, about what ICE is doing every day, about numbers, about arrest numbers, because people are simply going to use it as a political tool,” Homan said.

One facility that has drawn significant attention is Delaney Hall in New Jersey. Homan argued that claims about poor conditions and inadequate food are inaccurate.

“We have the highest detention standards in the industry,” he said. “ICE has higher detention standards than any federal facility, any state facility or any county facility.”

“I went up there unannounced on a Saturday. I sat in the cafeteria with detainees and ate the same meal they ate. And it wasn’t bad at all.”

FBI, DOJ ‘all over’ probe into Alex Pretti’s death: Homan

Asked about the status of the Alex Pretti investigation, Homan said the FBI and Justice Department continue examining the Jan. 24 shooting death of the U.S. citizen by federal immigration authorities in Minneapolis.

“It takes a while. I get frustrated, too, but I can tell you that … DOJ and FBI are all over it,” Homan told NewsNation.

Thousands of officers were sent to the Minneapolis and St. Paul area by the Department of Homeland Security in what was its largest immigration enforcement operation ever. The shooting deaths Pretti and Renee Good by federal officers drew condemnation and raised questions over officers’ conduct.

text:
A recent incursion by masked federal agents on Tohono O’odham land didn’t just anger that tribe, which has been trying to block border wall construction along the remote stretch it controls in Arizona. It also infuriated Native Americans around the country who had higher hopes for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the former Oklahoma senator who is only the second Indigenous presidential Cabinet member ever.

“This is especially disappointing when the DHS is headed by (…) a member of the Cherokee Nation,” said Angelique EagleWoman, director of the Native American Law and Sovereignty Institute at Mitchell Hamline School of Law in Minnesota.

Masked agents from Customs and Border Protection and the Bureau of Indian Affairs entered the Tohono O’odham Nation Reservation at 4 a.m. Tuesday, Aug. 25, to prevent tribal authorities from blocking border wall contractors, according to a statement issued that day by the tribe.

Jason Nichols, like Mullin a member of the Cherokee Nation, called the incursion by agents a “step backward” in federal-tribal relations — and surprising, given Mullin’s “knowledge on the importance of tribal sovereignty.”

A former mayor of Tahlequah, Nichols was Mullin’s Democratic opponent in 2018 when Mullin won reelection to his U.S. House seat. Nichols was dubious about Mullin’s preparation for the Homeland Security post, he said, but had been relatively impressed with his performance on border policy until the Aug. 25 incident.

“What I’m hoping for is that they take a deep breath, you know, take one step back,” Nichols said, referring to Mullin’s department. He called for “substantive consultation with the tribe, because I do think the tribes have proven to be willing and even eager partners.”

This story was reported by Gaylord News, a reporting project of the Gaylord College of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Oklahoma, and Cronkite News, a reporting project of the Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication at Arizona State University.

Indeed, the Tohono O’odham have long cooperated with the federal government on border security, though the nation has also strongly opposed wall construction. One all-Native American unit of Immigration and Customs Enforcement called the Shadow Wolves patrols the Sonoran Desert from its base in the nation.

The Tohono O’odham has members and communities on both sides of the border, which spans 62 miles west of Nogales, a city that also straddles the U.S.-Mexico divide.

In April, a DHS contractor partly destroyed a sacred archaeological site. The Tohono O’odham filed a lawsuit in June to block further construction, and in early August it posted “no trespassing” signs. But on Aug. 14, a federal judge in Washington rejected the nation’s request for a temporary pause, despite pleas that construction threatens many other sacred sites.

DHS defended the ongoing construction, though officials deflected questions about the use of force to keep tribal authorities at bay.

“The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border: remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity,” CBP commissioner Rodney Scott said in a statement his office provided to Cronkite News. “Congress funded this work, a federal court has affirmed it and CBP is carrying it out under the legal authorities that apply.”

According to the Tohono O’odham Nation, contractors engaged in “pre-construction activities” with drilling equipment at three locations. CBP and Bureau of Indian Affairs agents and a SWAT team used a vehicle blockade to prevent contractors’ removal by tribal police, who could only monitor the activity from a distance, according to the tribe.

EagleWoman, the Minnesota professor, said “the trespassing and covert-style operations” likely violated internal DHS protocols.

“If this was someone else’s backyard — in Paradise Valley, at the White House — this would be handled differently,” she said.

text:
A Cary pastor who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in July has been released, according to the pastor's daughter.

The family of 55-year-old Gabriel Johnson, in a statement posted on Instagram on Friday, said he has been released from ICE custody and will be moving to a 24-hour rehabilitation hospital for medical treatment.

Other WRAL Top Stories

"My father's release does not erase what has happened or the challenges our family continues to face," his daughter, Gabri Johnson, said in the Instagram post. "But it allows him to focus on healing and begin the rehabilitation he so desperately needs."

According to Gabri Johnson, ICE took her father into custody in mid-July in what the family was told was a "misunderstanding around a missed immigration appointment." The family was later told officials were pursuing Gabriel’s removal under a broader change in federal immigration policy, she said.

Gabri Johnson told WRAL News that her father was born in Liberia but had lived in the United States with legal status since he was 15 years old. He never became a citizen.

While in ICE custody, Gabri Johnson said her father had been treated poorly, which resulted in him suffering a stroke that paralyzed the left side of his body. She said ICE was blocking her father from entering the rehabilitation care he needed to relearn how to walk.

ICE sent WRAL News the following statement in August when we asked about Gabri Johnson's claims:

"ICE categorically rejects the allegation that Johnson is being denied medical care. Johnson was transported to the Texas Health Harris Hospital on July 30 after exhibiting stroke-like symptoms and remains under the care of licensed medical professionals.

Any suggestion that ICE is preventing Johnson from receiving necessary treatment is false. ICE does not make clinical decisions, direct treatment, or interfere with the medical judgement of doctors, nurses or hospital staff. Johnson is being treated in a civilian hospital by medical professionals who are responsible for his care. Claims that he is not receiving appropriate treatment disregard the work of the physicians, nurses, and other medical personnel providing care in accordance with their professional judgement."

Gabri Johnson said her father's release was an "enormous victory," but said it was shadowed by "the grief we share with families who still live afraid that someone they love could be abruptly taken from them and never make it home."

"We pray that they, too, will see the day when their loved ones can come home," Gabri Johnson said. "Thank you, from the bottom of our hearts."

text:

text:
Irma Chavez has no doubts about the impact of nationwide enhanced immigration enforcement on Northwest Arkansas businesses.

"I know five businesses that have lost one of their heads of the house," said Chavez, the founder and executive director of the Arkansas Hispanic Chamber of Commerce. "They go to immigration court to have a hearing for their green card. If there's even a little mistake where maybe that they didn't do something or their lawyer didn't do something, it gets attention and puts them in a bad position.

"I know a very successful business that moved here from California. They prepare meals, freeze them and sell them. The father went to an immigration appointment. He was sent to a camp where he stayed in a tent and then got deported to Guatemala. They were in the middle of building their house and of growing their business."

Arkansas United, a nonprofit immigration rights group based in Fayetteville, works with area employers to help them comply with immigration law, but those regulations are ever changing and the data on the immigration crackdown's economic impact have not been gathered, according to Mireya Reith, the immigrant rights group's executive director.

"One of the things that we're hoping to inspire, working with our universities, is higher education institutions getting some dedicated energy to look into this," she said.

The construction trades and other outdoor enterprises such as tree services appear to be suffering shortages of workers, said Randy Zook, president of the Arkansas State Chamber of Commerce and the Associated Industries of Arkansas. At the other end of the spectrum, he said, the trucking industry is pleased to see unqualified or minimally qualified drivers being removed from the roads, mostly from smaller trucking businesses cutting corners. The poultry industry, which keeps close track of workers' immigration status, seems largely unaffected, Zook said.

Springdale Mayor Doug Sprouse recently said his city experienced a 3% downturn in sales tax revenue during the first six months of the year.

The mayor thinks rumors about ICE activity could've forced a portion of the city's economy underground, he added.

"Hopefully that will all straighten out as the rumors subside, and I have no scientific evidence, but the timing was such that it would make sense because our sales tax has been off 2% or 3% for a few months, and I could see where if people are afraid to get out and spend their money, then I could see how that could have some impact," he said.

While bigger businesses can protect themselves from the immigration enforcement campaign's impact, small and family-owned businesses cannot, Chavez said.

"Who's going to protect a business that makes $50,000 a year?" she said.

Yet the total effect on small businesses taken together must be severe, she said.

"I mean, they're running on a shoestring anyway, and then they take a vital member of the business out," Chavez said. "One was a jewelry business and the husband was the one who repaired the jewelry, who even made jewelry. This state needs people with skills like his."

Undocumented workers are likely to work as self-employed or at small family start-ups because bigger businesses will not hire them, she said.

The crackdown's effect on businesses' customers also must be considered, Chavez said.

"Our people right now, recently, with all that's happening, when they first started, it was like, 'Oh, I'll be OK. I can go out. I can go hang out. I will be fine,'" Chavez said. "But now it's like people just go grocery shopping or not even that. They just go to work, go back home and order food and order your supplies for your house from the delivery. They don't want to drive. They don't want to be on the streets. Don't want to go out. Festivals and other such businesses are hardly surviving right now because there is a lot of people who's not showing up."

"People won't even go to a yard sale," she said.

Many customers of immigrant-owned businesses are sending money back to their countries of origin because they may soon have to return, Chavez said.

The legal and regulatory environment for business is chaotic, Chavez said. Whom businesses can employ is constantly changing, she said. Deferred action with childhood arrivals, or DACA, people who have lived here for years under temporary protective status and even legal permanent residents can no longer count on their status and neither can their employers, she said.

"The rules are changing every day for everybody. For everybody," she said. "So, we cannot even keep up with the rules. Then there is another issue: You don't know what to believe anymore. Because of all the things that's going on, what is the source? Who is saying that right? Who is the person that you can trust, you know?"

The news organizations maintain full editorial control over this story and all other coverage.

text:
(NewsNation) — As backlash against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement continues to mount, border czar Tom Homan says the agency is simply enforcing laws passed by Congress.

Homan discussed the state of ICE during an exclusive interview with "NewsNation Prime," arguing that officers and agents have no personal incentive when making arrests.

"Members of Congress want to call ICE white nationalists, racists, secret police and Nazis," Homan said. "Well, if they're Nazis for enforcing immigration law, what's that make Congress? They wrote the law."

DHS launches tip line for reporting 'CDL fraud' amid crackdown

"ICE is simply enforcing the laws enacted by Congress and signed by a president. If Congress doesn't like what they're doing, then change the law."

ICE operating at schools and hospitals is a lie: Homan

ICE has faced criticism over some enforcement actions, including allegations by Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., that agents arrested parents at bus stops in Connecticut last month.

Homan disputed that characterization, saying the arrest occurred after the child had already left the area and arguing that having children does not exempt migrants from immigration law.

"That is a stone-cold lie," he said regarding claims that ICE is operating in hospitals, churches and schools. "The people who say that, I have challenged them."

Body camera video offers a rare look inside an immigration raid at a NY factory

In May, an ICE-related incident outside a Brooklyn hospital sparked protests and several arrests. According to the Department of Homeland Security, the man involved was an undocumented immigrant from Nigeria who had been taken to the hospital by federal agents after being detained. Officials said he refused commands to exit his vehicle, prompting agents to use what they described as the "minimum amount of force" necessary to make the arrest.

"It hasn't happened. Now, we could. We have the authority. If there's a significant national security threat, there's no sanctuary. If we find them, we're going to arrest them," Homan said. "But ICE has simply not done that. The men and women of ICE are professionals. They try to do things in the safest possible way."

ICE detention standards are among the highest, Homan says

Homan also pushed back on criticism of conditions inside ICE detention facilities.

A Marshall Project report found that more than 500 babies and toddlers have spent time in ICE detention facilities since the beginning of last year.

ICE to spend $2M on robot dogs for immigration crackdown

"There are a lot of lies about ICE detention, about what ICE is doing every day, about numbers, about arrest numbers, because people are simply going to use it as a political tool," Homan said.

One facility that has drawn significant attention is Delaney Hall in New Jersey. Homan argued that claims about poor conditions and inadequate food are inaccurate.

"We have the highest detention standards in the industry," he said. "ICE has higher detention standards than any federal facility, any state facility or any county facility."

"I went up there unannounced on a Saturday. I sat in the cafeteria with detainees and ate the same meal they ate. And it wasn't bad at all."

FBI, DOJ 'all over' probe into Alex Pretti's death: Homan

Asked about the status of the Alex Pretti investigation, Homan said the FBI and Justice Department continue examining the Jan. 24 shooting death of the U.S. citizen by federal immigration authorities in Minneapolis.

"It takes a while. I get frustrated, too, but I can tell you that … DOJ and FBI are all over it," Homan told NewsNation.

Thousands of officers were sent to the Minneapolis and St. Paul area by the Department of Homeland Security in what was its largest immigration enforcement operation ever. The shooting deaths Pretti and Renee Good by federal officers drew condemnation and raised questions over officers' conduct.

Armendariz has been against the proposed detention facility since day one.

According to court records, if built, the facility on the 24-acre parcel near Gilroy could hold as many as 120 people a day.

The state and Santa Clara County joined forces in a legal battle to block construction of the detention center based on environmental concerns, including possible hazardous materials and an inadequate septic system.

The judge’s ruling means all construction must now stop.

Last week, before a federal hearing on the center in San Jose, some 200 people spoke out against the proposed facility.

"I think that the county and the state are on very strong footing, and so my belief is that there will be a permanent injunction put in place, and we hope it will permanently shut down this project,” Kalra said.

title: Federal judge rules Trump DHS plan for 50% FEMA staffing cuts was unlawful - AP News
authors: Rebecca Santana, immigration policy, ICE operations, employment-based immigration, apnews.com, rebecca-santana
description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge has ruled that a plan by the Trump administration to slash staffing at the federal agency tasked with responding to disasters by 50% was unlawful.
U.S. District Judge Susan Illston wrote in her opinion that top Homeland Security officials late last year directed FEMA’s leadership to submit a staffing plan that included a 50% staffing cut even though the agency’s own supervisors objected.
“Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” wrote Illston.
The Department of Homeland Security and FEMA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Although FEMA has experienced terminations, the 50% staffing cuts ultimately were not carried out.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge has ruled that a plan by the Trump administration to slash staffing at the federal agency tasked with responding to disasters by 50% was unlawful.

The opinion issued late Friday marked a victory for labor groups who had sued the agency. The labor organization had argued that plans by the Department of Homeland Security violated congressional protections that were designed to safeguard the independence of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

The issue of the FEMA staffing was part of a much larger lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees and other labor groups, pushing back on efforts by the Trump administration to slash the federal workforce.

U.S. District Judge Susan Illston wrote in her opinion that top Homeland Security officials late last year directed FEMA’s leadership to submit a staffing plan that included a 50% staffing cut even though the agency’s own supervisors objected.

“Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” wrote Illston.

The Department of Homeland Security and FEMA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Illston wrote that it was clear that the government violated rules established after 2005’s Hurricane Katrina that put decisions on staffing levels squarely in the hands of FEMA, not the Department of Homeland Security and that prevented DHS from “substantially” reducing the “functions” of FEMA.

Illston didn’t order a specific remedy to carry out her opinion but directed the two sides to meet and decide on a course of relief.

Although FEMA has experienced terminations, the 50% staffing cuts ultimately were not carried out. In recent months, after top leadership changes at FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security, the agency has rehired some staffers who were let go.

FEMA was one of the agencies targeted in the federal government for staff reductions as part of a broad Trump administration plan to reduce the size of government. The embattled agency has been buffeted by mass staff departures, disruptions of grant programs, and delays of disaster aid.

In May, a Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council submitted a final report recommending sweeping changes to how the agency supports states, tribes and territories in disaster.

The final version backed away from the recommendation to cut the FEMA workforce by 50%, which was included in a December 2025 draft reviewed by The Associated Press.

The council instead recommended the agency conduct a “strategic review” to determine “appropriate staffing levels.”

In an August report, the Government Accountability Office said it found the departures of thousands of staff in 2025 resulted in a “loss of institutional knowledge and experienced personnel” and “exacerbated longstanding workforce challenges.”

More than 4,300 employees, or about 17% of FEMA’s workforce, separated from the agency in the 2025 budget year, with over 1,500 through voluntary reductions. The agency also made about 2,900 new hires.

The GAO recently recommended to Congress that it “consider requiring” FEMA to base “significant workforce decisions” on a more strategic planning process.

Without it, the GAO found, “FEMA cannot be assured that the agency is positioned to effectively meet its mission needs.”
