Five protesters were arrested and an alleged “agitator” was charged Saturday during a protest outside the Atlantic City Police Department that alleged officers are aiding ICE.

The arrests included El Pueblo Unido of Atlantic City Founder Cristian Moreno-Rodriguez, who has led the call against ICE.

As protesters gathered, police told them to clear access points and not be in the street.

That is when Moreno-Rodriguez, 31, of Atlantic City, and others were taken into custody.

“The constitutional right to peacefully protest is fundamental and is respected by the Atlantic City Police Department,” Chief James Sarkos said. “That right, however, does not extend to physically obstructing access to a public safety facility, preventing police officers from safely entering or exiting the building, or interfering with the public’s ability to obtain police services.”

Moreno-Rodriguez was charged with obstruction of justice and released hours later, greeted with cheers as he stepped out of the Clayton G. Graham Public Safety Building.

The police stepped in early in the protest, after a man tried to walk into the protest after making pro-ICE statements.

Devon Barber, who has posted video showing him questioning members of El Pueblo Unido, confirmed to BreakingAC that he was pepper-sprayed by one of the protesters.

“It was a difficult position for the Atlantic City Police Department to be in once they observed the interaction between the agitator and at least on protestor,” attorney Jonathan Diego told BreakingAC. “(The police) were obligated at that point. That’s what led to the four individuals being arrested.”

Jose Salazar, 18, of Princeton, was charged with illegal possession of a chemical device for the pepper spray along with simple assault.

“They believe the focus of everybody who is becoming aware (of the incident) should be on the agitator or agitators that intentionally placed themselves in the middle of this peaceful protest by people expressing their concern about immigration procedures,” Diego said.

Barber, 28, of Atlantic City, was taken to the hospital for his injuries, but also has been issued a complaint for simple assault, police said.

The others charged and released on summonses were:

Diana Chaparro, 50, of Hammonton, charged with simple assault.

Keli Smith, 41, of Egg Harbor Township, charged with obstruction of justice and resisting arrest.

Anthony Diaz, 30, of Newark, charged with obstruction of justice.

Diego said said those arrested maintain their innocence

All are disorderly persons offenses.

Diego noted that the police stayed inside the Public Safety Building for most of the protest in what he believed was an effort not to intimidate the protestors.

“The ACPD did carry themselves very professionally,” he said. “All of my observations were that they were cordial and professional, and followed what they were supposed to do under the circumstances.”

“The individuals that are out there protesting are exercising their First Amendment rights to protest peacefully, and they will continue to do so,” Diego said.

Moreno-Rodriguez was released just before 3 p.m., but briefly rejoined the protest a couple of hours earlier via a phone call.

The holding cells do have phones, which those being held can use to make collect calls, BreakingAC was told.

Mayor Marty Small did not attend the protest, but said that the city and police department “are not against the Hispanic community in any way, shape or form.”

“We have absolutely no jurisdiction over a federal agency, and we have said that,” he said. “The Atlantic City Police Department does a fantastic job and will continue to protect and serve our community with dignity.”

Small said he understands it’s a sensitive situation and he hopes to be able to work with all parties involve to make things better.

The protest follows motor vehicle stops of at least two group members, who were cited for various traffic violations while chasing ICE vehicles throughout the city.

Atlantic City police say the traffic stops are about keeping the streets safe.

“As a reminder to the public, ACPD follows the New Jersey Attorney General’s Immigrant Trust Directive,” Sarkos wrote in a Facebook post, citing the directive that does not allow police to participate in ICE activities. “To suggest otherwise is unfair to the officer and misleading to the public.”

But Moreno-Rodriguez claims it proves police are collaborating with ICE agents to illegally target Hispanic residents.

“We’re out here warning our neighbors,” Moreno-Rodriguez tells a police officer who pulled him over. “Children are going to come home from school today and not see their parents because ICE kidnapped them because you let them get away.”

The dashboard-mounted camera video streamed live on Facebook included the alleged motor vehicle infractions as the group leader followed an ICE vehicle through at least three red lights, all while in contact with other members letting them know where ICE was.

The vehicle he is following can be seen with its emergency lights on.

Moreno-Rodriguez questioned why police did not stop the ICE vehicle for its driving.

“We called in the blue Ford Explorer running red lights. I called it in 30 minutes ago,” he tells the officer.

“So you think that gives you the right to run multiple red lights?” the officer replies.

“So now you care more about traffic than people getting kidnapped, right?” Moreno-Rodriguez shoots back.

The stop just before noon Thursday came a day after another member of the group was cited for motor vehicle violations after he was pulled over in front of the Clayton G. Graham Public Safety Building on Atlantic Avenue.

In that case, police released traffic camera footage showing the car go into the oncoming lane in an attempt to apparently confront another ICE vehicle.

The name of that driver was not released.

Now the group plans to be outside the Public Safety Building at 11 a.m. Saturday.

“Over 500 people will be out there protesting with your name on it because of the disgraceful actions you took,” Moreno-Rodriguez tells Officer Moustafa Maarouf, who the El Pueblo Unido leader calls a traitor. “We’re gonna protest you to show you how wrong you are.”

Moreno-Rodriguez received more than a dozen citations, including reckless driving, four failures to observe a traffic control device and failure to produce a driver’s license or registration, court records show.

In the video, Moreno-Rodriguez tells Maarouf that he does not have his documentation because he was in a crash a week before and the documents were in that vehicle.

He is eventually is allowed to leave.

“I’m on my way,” he tells the person he has been in contact with throughout. “They gave me tickets but I don’t give a (expletive).”

Moreno-Rodriguez also posted a photo outside the Public Safety Building with a long paper apparently listing all his citations.

“Thank you for the CVS receipt, Atlantic City Police Department,” he wrote.

The post also includes a link to donate to the group’s legal defense fund.

El Pueblo Unido also was one of 40 Atlantic City nonprofits to receive a grant from the Atlantic City Community Fund in July.

Moreno-Rodriguez also has a brother who joined the Atlantic City Police Department last year.

title: Immigration reporting measure fuels debate over Colorado's role with ICE
description:
A 2021 law blocks employees from providing personally identifiable information to immigration enforcement without a warrant or as part of a criminal investigation.
Walsh called Proposition 81 a “recipe for abuse,” saying it would inevitably lead to racial profiling and the detainment of citizens and legal residents.
Burton Brown disagreed, noting that nothing in Proposition 81 allows profiling or gives ICE agents any authority they don’t have in Colorado.
“Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement,” he said.
“If Proposition 81 passes, we would no longer be able to do that.” Larimer and Jackson County District Attorney Gordon McLaughlin also attended the rally.
text:
A coalition of advocacy groups and several district attorneys rallied outside the Colorado Capitol on Thursday to oppose a ballot measure that, if approved by voters in November, would require state and local law enforcement to cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

Backed by Advance Colorado, Proposition 81 would require local law enforcement agencies to notify Immigration and Customs Enforcement when they charge a person who is in the country illegally with a violent crime or when the individual has previously been charged with a felony. This also applies when the person’s legal status cannot be determined.

Kristi Burton Brown, executive vice president of Advance Colorado, told Colorado Politics that the group is pursuing the measure because state law now bars law enforcement from proactively reporting violent offenders or repeat felons to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

She said that, under a recent state law, an officer faces a fine of up to $50,000 for choosing to report a violent offender to federal authorities. She also noted that other “sanctuary” states, including California and New York, include exceptions in these situations that Colorado does not.

While many have characterized Colorado as a “sanctuary state,” Gov. Jared Polis has pushed back on the label, saying the state “fully cooperates with federal authorities in identifying, apprehending and prosecuting criminals – regardless of immigration status.”

Over the years, Colorado has adopted several laws whose provisions fall under the broad outlines of what constitutes a “sanctuary” state.

Notably, a 2019 law prohibits a law enforcement officer from arresting or detaining an individual solely based on a civil immigration detainer and bars a probation officer or probation department employee from providing an individual’s personal information to federal immigration authorities.

A 2021 law blocks employees from providing personally identifiable information to immigration enforcement without a warrant or as part of a criminal investigation. In 2025, Colorado’s legislators imposed the same restrictions on local government employees as well as judicial and legislative employees.

Some local governments, such as Denver, have also adopted “sanctuary” policies.

Speaking from the Capitol steps Thursday, ACLU Colorado director Olivia Mendoza said approving Proposition 81 would make communities less safe, particularly under the current administration.

“We have seen that since the beginning of the Trump administration’s second term, our communities have been gripped by the fear of ICE’s brutal immigration enforcement, from warrantless arrests to physical brutality to deplorable detention conditions,” she said. “ICE has no place in our state, and Amendment 81 invites them to take a strong foothold in Colorado.”

Mendoza argued that Proposition 81 violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits the government from taking away an individual’s life, liberty or property without fair legal proceedings.

Burton Brown countered that the allegations that the measure violates due process are unfounded because law enforcement would be allowed to report to ICE only after obtaining enough evidence to charge someone with a crime.

If the measure passed, it would require law enforcement to contact ICE every time they charge someone who has a prior criminal record, unless that person happened to have proof of citizenship with them in the form of a birth certificate or passport, according to Denver District Attorney John Walsh.

Walsh called Proposition 81 a “recipe for abuse,” saying it would inevitably lead to racial profiling and the detainment of citizens and legal residents.

“To make things much worse, this obligation triggers on charging a person with a crime, not on a conviction,” he added.

Burton Brown disagreed, noting that nothing in Proposition 81 allows profiling or gives ICE agents any authority they don’t have in Colorado.

She added, “Instead, this gives Colorado law enforcement the ability to report violent criminals or repeat felons if they are here illegally without facing a $50,000 fine from the state.”

Walsh insisted that Proposition 81 would further erode the already strained relationship between immigrant communities and law enforcement.

“Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement,” he said. “If Proposition 81 passes, we would no longer be able to do that.”

Larimer and Jackson County District Attorney Gordon McLaughlin also attended the rally.

description:

text:
By Dan Cecil

Contributing columnist

Resolving complex national matters with a whole-of-government approach is when a president uses every lever of power at his disposal to achieve a single goal. Immigration policy has been handled that way in the last two administrations, but with polar opposite effects.

Joe Biden used a whole-of-government approach to bring the maximum number of immigrants into the country as quickly as possible. Donald Trump is using it to fix the immigration mess that Biden created. The question before us now is whether we want to go back to Biden’s immigration policy, or to continue to fix the mess he made.

When done properly, immigration is a wonderful thing, but it doesn’t take a PhD in economics to know that flooding our nation with unskilled labor will create an affordability crisis for the working class. Housing prices go up, wages go down and government support becomes harder to get as millions of new immigrants vie for those limited resources. The Biden administration’s immigration policy was a disaster for America’s working class and for affordability in general.

Do you remember what Trump said about illegal immigration in his first joint address before Congress in 2025? He said, “The media and our friends in the Democrat Party kept saying we needed new legislation to secure the border, but it turned out that all we really needed was a new president.” He had been in office for just 43 days, and he had essentially ended the illegal invasion at our southern border that Biden had orchestrated and presided over for four years.

You probably remember the massive migrant caravans that were assailing our southern border during that time. Some of you may still be able to envision the videos of those caravans making their way up through Central and South America, and recall how our government seemed clueless about how to stop them. Those caravans were intentional; the direct result of Biden’s whole-of-government approach to immigration, which was designed to get as many immigrants into the country as possible during his term in office. But with Biden’s policies gone, the caravans are gone. If you don’t want them back, then vote, and vote Republican.

How bad was it under Biden? The onslaught at the southern border hit an all-time high in 2022, more than seven times higher than the 45-year low under Trump’s first administration. But even as illegal immigration hit record highs under Biden, removals fell to their lowest point in the last 30 years. Bring more in, send fewer home. The result, tracked independently by Pew, was the largest two-year increase in America’s unauthorized immigrant population. Record high net migration under Biden’s policies, record low net migration under Trump’s policies. The choice is clear this November.

Detention facilities and immigration courts were overwhelmed by the caravans, so they released migrants into the U.S. on the promise that they’d come back later for an immigration hearing. Government programs like the Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans parole process and the CBP One app allowed migrants to be flown directly into sanctuary cities and states. Border sectors and interior cities reported overloaded shelters, high costs for emergency services, public frustration with immigrants getting better treatment than citizens and concerns about who was coming in unvetted.

The Biden administration repeatedly stated that Congress needed to pass “comprehensive reforms” to give them more agents, more judges, asylum changes and emergency authority, but Trump solved the problem in just 43 days, then stood before a joint session of Congress and said “all we really needed was a new president.”

What Trump didn’t say was that he also needed a House and Senate majority, because at that time, he had both, although just barely. That’s why this election is so important. The House and Senate majority are on the line this November, and Ohio is front and center in that battle. Ohio’s conservative turnout could determine whether Trump has a majority for his last two years in office or not. If not, additional progress will be impossible and, even worse, all of the progress already made could be lost.

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown would be a thorn in Trump’s side at every turn. Sen. Jon Husted is an extremely reliable supporter of Trump’s policies. We must keep Brown in forced retirement and send Husted back to the Senate to maintain a Senate majority; if not, a Democrat majority will end Trump’s ability to fix the messes that Biden and Brown made together in Washington, D.C.

Border security isn’t the only immigration concern: Biden’s immigration policy also leveraged Temporary Protected Status to fly more foreign nationals into our country. He nearly quadrupled TPS quotas, authorizing nearly a million foreign nationals through that program alone. Trump’s second term, so far, has produced a large net reduction, ending protections for even more migrants than Biden added. Additional reductions are scheduled for later this year.

Biden also leveraged four parole programs to fly more people in: Operation Allies Welcome brought in roughly 90,000 Afghans; programs aligned with Uniting for Ukraine brought in over 650,000 Ukrainians; CHNV parole brought in over 500,000 Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans; and the CBP One app scheduled over 860,000 port-of-entry appointments. None of these required crossing the border illegally — they were all authorized by executive action, and according to the National Foundation for American Policy, they were responsible for roughly 2.7 million people being brought in or kept here by August 2024.

To right these wrongs, Trump suspended refugee admissions by executive order within a week of taking office. CHNV parole and CBP One scheduling were terminated. TPS was ended for 13 of 17 countries. Border encounters collapsed to their lowest level since 1970. For the first time since at least 2014, interior ICE removals exceeded apprehensions at the border. The government is finally expending more effort to find and remove illegals than to process new arrivals. Every immigration lever is now moving together in the right direction for the American people. Democrats and Republicans have polar opposite immigration goals. We can’t go back!

Trump’s immigration policies are common sense. We find it hard to believe that any American would want the disastrous immigration policies that the Biden administration championed. Sadly, immigration is just one of many policies where Republicans choose common sense and Democrats choose the polar opposite.

If you want to ensure we don’t go back, here is what you can do: if you’re not registered to vote, visit https://olvr.ohiosos.gov/ to register online or to find other options for registering by the Oct. 5 deadline; vote for Husted and every other Republican on your ballot; vote yes on Issue 3 to strengthen election integrity in Ohio; and tell everyone you know why this election is so important. Not voting for common sense allows the polar opposite to win.

Dan Cecil is a Christian, husband, father, grandfather and retired 30-year Air Force officer. He is chairman of the Shelby County Republican Party and a member of the bipartisan Shelby County Board of Elections. He lives in Sidney with his wife, Kim, and their herd of rescue cats.

text:
Just a year ago, Martín Soto was making breakfast at home with his wife, Gabriela, while their daughter got ready for her first day of school. But this September, Martín is in solitary confinement at the Elizabeth Detention Center (EDC) in New Jersey.

“I was crying, but my daughter, she told me, ‘Mommy, don’t cry. Daddy’s gonna come home,’” Gabriela Soto told Truthout. “I said, ‘I know, but I don’t want you to miss Daddy on your first day of school.’ And she was like, ‘It’s okay. I know Daddy’s with me.’ And then she pointed to her heart.”

On February 1, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents kidnapped Martín while he wason his way to buy diapers for their 11-month-old son. He was sent to Delaney Hall, an immigration jail in Newark run by the for-profit prison company GEO Group. At Delaney, heorganized a hunger and labor strike to protest the jail’s inhumane conditions, which sparked protests in solidarity outside the jail. In retaliation forhis organizing, he was transferred to EDC, where he has been held in solitary confinement, according to Gabriela.

In addition to the emotional impact of his absence, Gabriela is also struggling to afford rent and other necessities. Martín was the breadwinner for their family and Gabriela lost her job shortly after he was detained. She’s had to rely on donations to support their family.

“I worked as a cleaner, but the hours are not flexible,” she said. “They excused me the first week that my husband was detained, but they can’t continue, so I had to leave the job.”

Gabriela’s story is an increasingly common one. As a new school year begins, families must grapple with their loved one’s absence from yet another milestone, while also fearing that ICE will take them next. In August, ICE officersabducted parents at school bus stops in Danbury, Connecticut,setting off massive protests and eliciting condemnation from Senator Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut.)

Under the Trump administration, an estimated205,000 children have had one or both parents detained, including about 145,000 U.S. citizen children, according to a May report by The Brookings Institution. The number now is likely even higher. The Department of Homeland Security boasted in a recent press release that ICE hadarrested nearly 51,000 people in August alone, a new record for arrests in a single month.

The governmentdoes not track how many children are impacted by a parent’s detention, so the exact number of children starting off the school year with one or both parents detained is unknown.

“We see both parents taken into custody, leaving the children alone,” Sally Pillay, the director of the Mami Chelo Foundation, told Truthout. Pillay is one of the organizers of the Radical Hospitality Zone outside Delaney Hall, where visitors can get groceries, information on resources, children’s toys, and a hot lunch while they wait to see their loved one.

“We have a 15 and a 17-year-old who are fending for themselves at home because both parents are here,” she said.

Pillay also described another family where both parents of three young children, between the ages of one and seven, are detained. Friends and neighbors have taken them in.

“We do our part, a little bit, to try to support the families who are taking care of the little kids … supplementing them with grocery cards, with food when we get food donations, pantry bags, diapers, wipes, anything for that matter,” she said.

Pillay says they recently held their second annual back-to-school drive and distributed backpacks to families with loved ones at Delaney Hall. On the day Truthout visited the Radical Hospitality Zone, volunteers from Saint Anastasia’s Parish in Teaneck, New Jersey, dropped off several plastic containers filled with new clothes. The group also collected backpacks for children who have a parent at Delaney Hall.

“Every little kid should have a new outfit to wear on back-to-school day,” Judy McKay, one of the organizers, told Truthout.

Esperanza, a mother of three, says her family has been struggling to survive since her husband, who was the family breadwinner, was detained about six months ago. Esperanza is not her real name. Truthout is using a pseudonym to protect her identity. Truthout spoke with Esperanza through a translator at the hospitality zone.

“It’s so difficult — not just for school [supplies], but for daily food, paying rent, paying for everything,” she said. “I do everything I can for them — whether it’s clothes or food — I accept it with all my heart.”

Fearing ICE, Esperanza says she kept her children home all summer.

“They had to stay inside all summer,” she said, expressing how sad she felt that they were cooped up at home that entire time.

She says her husband, who has diabetes, has been experiencing pain in his kidneys and other symptoms, but is not receiving any medical care.

“Because he wasn’t getting antibiotics for a throat infection, he did what some of the men are doing inside — taking their own urine as a method to address infections,” she said.

When Truthout spoke with Esperanza, her children — ages 8, 11, and 15 — were starting school the following week. She says they’re overwhelmed with anxiety and that her eldest daughter fears what will happen if she gets of school and Esperanza is not there anymore.

Although the school is only about six or seven blocks from their home, her eight-year-old son is terrified to be that far away from home because he hasn’t been outside all summer. She says when her children hear a siren, they think ICE is coming to get their family.

“I pray a lot. I’m not Christian or Catholic, but I think about the children — waking up hungry, wanting to eat, wanting to go out, and the worry involved in sending them to school,” she said, expressing her hope that “every family take care” because “the pain is so immense” and adding, “I think that if I didn’t return home, I’d go out of my mind.”

text:
Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration.

Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.

They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.

One of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.

A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.

Donna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.

Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.

“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.

“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”

In Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.

Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.

A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.

In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) and Refugees Welcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.

Hundreds of people also gathered in Glasgow for an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.

The Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.

The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.

Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.

MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.

Prominent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.

Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.

Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”

The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.

The incident with the small boat last Sunday was thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers had been brought to Portsmouth and the first time that a significant group of anti-migrant protesters had tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.

Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.

Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.

The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.

Del Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.

Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.

The government condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters last Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth and a small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover, crowds of masked men blocked road access to the port in scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.

Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.

“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”

text:
For the first time, the Justice Department brought a case before a decades-old but until now unused special court to deport a legal US resident to Afghanistan after she conceded to being an "alien terrorist," court records show.

Prosecutors alleged Nazira Haji Zada, 47, originally from Afghanistan, supported a plan by her son and son-in-law to commit an Islamic State-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, according to court documents. Both men have already been charged and will be deported following their release from prison. Haji Zada's son, Abdullah Haji Zada, 19, was sentenced to 15 years in prison.

Haji Zada was arrested in July at her home in Fort Worth, Texas, and had an initial hearing in late July. Instead of charging Haji Zada in the criminal justice system, leaders at the Justice Department launched the first-ever civil proceedings at the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. The secretive court allows for a lower standard of proof to remove a person from American soil.

Congress created the court in 1996 to make it easier for the DOJ to use classified evidence, that they say poses a risk to national security, to deport people.

In unsealed court filings dated Aug. 20, Haji Zada waived her rights to challenge the detention and agreed to the deportation. Senior U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen ordered her removal the same day. Haji Zada's admission will not be used in criminal proceedings, and the documents were released to the public on Friday.

Haji Zada's court appointed attorneys, Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras, contested the constitutionality of the case in court filings, adding that they weren't permitted to review evidence. The evidence supporting the removal remains classified, the government said in court documents, because it poses a risk to national security.

Haji Zada's attorneys said in a statement that their client's choice to consent to the removal "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy."

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process," the statement said. "We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue."

Haji Zada came to the U.S. as a lawful permanent resident in 2018. Her husband was employed at the Bagram Air Base, the last major U.S. base in Afghanistan until it was turned over to Afghan forces in 2021, from 2009 to 2016.

As the family "matriarch," U.S. authorities alleged Haji Zada worked to "radicalize" her family and "formally pledged loyalty to ISIS." The government also alleged she and her son-in-law "worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology and have them pledge loyalty to ISIS."

Prosecutors also said the family allegedly raised funds for the terrorist attack by selling off furniture, computers, a mobile phone, and two vehicles. They added that Haji Zada signed a contract to sell the family's home, and along with other female family members and young male family members, planned to move to an ISIS-controlled location before the attack, which she hid from her "unsuspecting husband." Her son and son-in-law would remain behind to commit the terrorist attack, court documents show.

According to court records, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, Haji Zada's son-in-law, admitted that between June 2024 and October 2024, he conspired with at least one other person to purchase two AK-47 rifles, 500 rounds of ammunition and 10 magazines, with the goal of carrying out a mass-casualty attack. Court documents say Tawhedi communicated with an ISIS facilitator about his plan to buy the firearms for the plot on behalf of ISIS, "including asking the individual whether 500 rounds of ammunition would be sufficient."

Tawhedi, 28, pled guilty to two terrorism-related charges.

Attorney General Todd Blanche approved the government application before it went to the judge. In a statement, Blanche said the use of the court shows "how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Blanche said.

title: Minnesota churches roiled by legal battle over ICE surveillance and right to protest - PBS
description:
Protesters confronted federal law enforcement daily, and the killing of two protesters sparked global outcry.
The documents revealed that federal agents had conducted an undercover surveillance operation, which had targeted groups leading protests earlier this year.
The government says in court documents that its operation didn't violate the injunction because it wasn't about immigration enforcement.
Some contend the charges amounted to "selective or vindictive prosecution," and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance.
Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Court cases involving Twin Cities churches and immigration enforcement highlight how the acrimonious debate continues to roil faith communities more than six months since the federal surge turned Minnesota into a symbol of defiance of the Trump administration's policies.

In one case, a Minneapolis Baptist church — alongside congregations nationwide — asked for the government to be reprimanded after spying on protest-related activity on its property. In another, more than three dozen protesters have asked for their charges to be dismissed after they disrupted a worship service in a St. Paul church where one of the pastors was also a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official.

Even congregations uninvolved in the court cases say they're still feeling the repercussions of the weekslong surge in immigration operations last winter. Protesters confronted federal law enforcement daily, and the killing of two protesters sparked global outcry.

READ MORE: AP analysis: Justice Department went after protesters for felony assault, but juries and judges were unconvinced

Immigration agents are no longer visibly active on the same residential block as Holy Trinity Lutheran Church in Minneapolis. But its pastor says the signs that went up in January stating "Everyone is welcome here! Except I.C.E." have stayed.

"I don't foresee a time when they will come down. We want our building to remain a sanctuary for many people," said the Rev. Ingrid Rasmussen. Her church provided whistles, which protesters across the city used to alert neighbors about law enforcement presence.

Churches as safe places for migrants — and worshippers

For decades, congregations have been on the front lines of providing for immigrants and refugees, whether in their faith communities or with outreach ranging from food distribution at the U.S.-Mexico border to advocacy in Washington.

As part of its sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration, President Donald Trump's current administration gave agents more leeway to make arrests at houses of worship.

In response, dozens of religious groups sued, heralding a more openly adversarial relationship between many faith leaders and federal authorities.

READ MORE: Body camera video offers a rare look inside an immigration raid at a New York factory

That has continued through surges last fall and winter in various parts of the country, with faith leaders arrested during anti-enforcement protests and suing to make pastoral visits to detained migrants.

"There's been a pretty dramatic increase in lawsuits filed related to people of faith's support for migrants," said Elizabeth Reiner Platt, director of the Law, Rights and Religion Project at Union Theological Seminary.

Faith groups have achieved several "promising" wins, she said, adding that ongoing litigation shows how unpopular the administration's aggressive enforcement approach is with many religious people.

Both Minnesota court cases center on the idea of protecting a sacred space and people's right to worship — in one case from government intrusion and in the other, from people protesting the immigration crackdown.

Government surveillance at Minneapolis church sparks outcry

In mid-August, court documents emerged in a separate case involving 15 people charged by federal prosecutors with impeding the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. The documents revealed that federal agents had conducted an undercover surveillance operation, which had targeted groups leading protests earlier this year.

Among those charged was an organizer in a martial arts group who the government says was training protesters to physically prevent arrests. Some of the group's meetings occurred in the gym of University Baptist Church in Minneapolis, and Homeland Security agents conducted surveillance operations there four times — including once with an undercover agent inside, according to court documents.

The church is a member of American Baptist Churches USA and the Alliance of Baptists, two of several groups that in February won an injunction against most immigration enforcement at their member churches nationwide.

The groups have asked the same federal judge to rule that Homeland Security violated that order, to instruct its agents about it, as well as to disclose if any other houses of worship were part of surveillance operations.

The government says in court documents that its operation didn't violate the injunction because it wasn't about immigration enforcement. Rather, they were investigating a suspect for training "individuals to commit acts of violence against federal officers and employees."

A hearing was held Sept. 4 and a ruling is pending. A spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security said it doesn't comment "on the existence or status of specific ongoing investigations, nor on investigative methods."

University Baptist Church's interim pastor said the small congregation found the surveillance "very upsetting" — but also motivation to double down on their advocacy.

"We see the message of Jesus as compelling us to be where people are most vulnerable," the Rev. Cody J. Sanders said.

For Kevin Friedl, an attorney with the Democracy Forward Foundation that's representing the faith groups, the case is ultimately about offering sanctuary.

"For many, religion — being able to join together with others at their church or other house of worship — is an important and critical source of solace and comfort, in hard times, which these are," he said. "This administration wants to deny them that."

Protesters who interrupted Sunday worship seek dismissal of charges

The argument that churches are protected spaces and worshippers have rights against intrusion is also buttressing the case over the anti-immigration enforcement protest at Cities Church in Minnesota's capital in January.

More than three dozen people — including former CNN journalist Don Lemon and prominent local activists — are facing federal civil rights charges after entering the Southern Baptist church where one pastor was also a leader in the local ICE field office.

During Sunday worship, some walked up to the pulpit, others loudly chanted "ICE out" and "Renee Good," referring to the woman who was fatally shot on Jan. 7 by an ICE officer in Minneapolis.

READ MORE: 'A perfect tool for abuse.' Why experts are concerned about ICE's $17 million electric shock gloves contract

In August, a slew of motions to dismiss the cases were filed and will be heard in late October. Some contend the charges amounted to "selective or vindictive prosecution," and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance. They argue that the "administration's claims that this prosecution is based on a desire to protect the right to practice religion is disproved by the extraordinary freedom it has granted ICE to violate the sanctity of churches," according to court documents.

"They're using these cases to try to get information on the whole resistance movement," said Jordan Kushner, an attorney representing several defendants.

An attorney representing Cities Church countered that the issue at play is "an invasion during worship."

"Nobody has the right to storm a church," Doug Wardlow said, adding that the protest — and smaller, outdoors ones that continue to occur during worship times — "traumatically impacted the life of the church."

How fallout from the surge impacts Minnesota congregations

Faith leaders across the Twin Cities say they're still dealing with fallout from the surge, whether it's lingering fear among migrants, tensions over government surveillance, or persistent financial assistance requests.

Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev. Mariah Furness Tollgaard, senior pastor at Hamline Church in St. Paul. She was briefly detained at an anti-deportations protest at the Minneapolis airport in January.

Several Protestant congregations that were outspoken in their anti-immigration-enforcement stances have increased their security measures.

While many remain committed to their advocacy, it's taking a toll.

"The general vibe we get from leaders and congregations is just tired — there's weariness more than anything," said Nicholas Tangen of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America's Minneapolis Area Synod.

The Supreme Court will no longer hear an oral argument for a case centered on bond rights for noncitizens detained for lengthy periods, ruling the case moot after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul pardoned a lawfully present Dominican citizen, who pleaded guilty to second-degree assault.

Hochul pardoned Keisy Guerrero Mariano, who is identified in court documents as "Keisy GM," in late August, effectively killing the Trump administration's appeal to the Supreme Court arguing that noncitizens, including those with green card status, do not have a legal right to a bond hearing for a prolonged detention if they have committed crimes that are grounds for mandatory deportation.

Hochul, who is staunchly opposed to President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement crackdown, issued the pardon for Mariano just as the brief was due.

Federal Appeals Court Compares Trump Migrant Detention Policy To Japanese American Internment

Solicitor General John Sauer agreed Friday that Genalo v. Black is now moot, but said the Trump administration will seek an "alternative vehicle" to challenge the Second Circuit's 2024 ruling that prolonged immigration detention can trigger a constitutional right to a bond hearing.

Sauer said the administration intends to find another case through which the Supreme Court can resolve the issue during its 2026-27 term.

Read On The Fox News App

The lawsuit centered on the challenges of plaintiffs Carol Williams Black, a Jamaican national with lawful standing, and Mariano — both convicted criminals detained by ICE.

Appeals Court Blocks Trump Admin From Holding Migrants Without Bond For Over 90 Days

Mariano was first arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in 2020 over a 2015 second-degree assault conviction for which he served time, making him eligible for deportation.

He spent nearly two years in ICE detention, but was released in 2022 due to a nationwide injunction that required the release of detainees because of COVID-19 health risks.

Prior to his release, Judge John P. Cronan of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denied Mariano's habeas corpus request in November 2021.

But in May 2024, the Second Circuit overruled Cronan's decision, ruling that the government must grant noncitizens a bond hearing once detention becomes "unreasonably long." Failure to do so, the court ruled, would violate the Fifth Amendment's due process clause.

The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case June 15; however, the high court ruled Black's case moot because he had left the United States and filed a court declaration that he would not be returning to the country.

Black was convicted in New York in 2000 of sexually abusing a minor under the age of 11.

Hochul's decision to issue a pardon to Mariano has garnered fierce criticism from legal experts.

"Pretty wild to fully pardon an aggravated felon to (1) stop the felon from getting deported and (2) stop the Supreme Court from ruling on an issue. (Especially as this litigation has been going on for years)," Eric Wessan, Iowa's solicitor general, posted on X.

He praised Sauer's decision to fight back on the Second Circuit's ruling.

"I wonder how many non-American felons Governors like Hochul will choose to fully pardon and free to avoid them facing consequences for their actions," Wessan added.

text:
The Alexandria International Airport, which is part of England Airpark in central Louisiana, is currently known as the busiest ICE Air Operations hub for deportations in the United States. Immigration and Custom Enforcement’s Alexandria Staging Facility, a terminus for people being removed from the U.S., is reviled the world over by abused and deported refugees from Cameroon to Haiti. Even as the town’s tourism office works in overdrive to entice visitors to the area’s natural and cultural attractions — the scenic Red River, lush butterfly gardens, and historic homes such as the one where venerated Harlem Renaissance poet Arna Bontemps lived from birth to three years old — violence against immigrants keeps coming.

Last year, Alexandria was mentioned in a lawsuit regarding a child with Stage 4 kidney cancer who was deported along with two siblings in April 2025. Now, the same polarizing federal agency that has killed people on the streets and in its custody is planning to expand its operations in Alexandria. ICE has grabbed another chunk of the England Airpark, which is situated on a former U.S. Air Force base that shuttered in 1992 due to groundwater contaminated with catastrophic levels of PFAS, a class of persistent “forever chemicals” linked to cancer, reproductive harms, and other serious health problems.

If ICE has its way, as soon as the end of September, it aims to place immigrant women (including those who are pregnant), infants, and children, on top of this toxic site in a 528-bed facility, to be housed in a former military barracks. To further sully the atmosphere, ICE has contracted with the LaSalle Family Foundation, an affiliate of the private prison operator LaSalle Corrections, which runs the Irwin Detention Center in Georgia. A congressional investigation found ample evidence of rampant medical abuse at the facility, including medically unnecessary gynecological procedures performed on migrant women.

Louisiana residents are mobilizing in opposition to the immigration jail with the help of CENLA Activism, a grassroots group of concerned residents that mobilizes activists in central Louisiana and organizes mutual aid for communities under siege by ICE.

At the center of this scheme is England Economic and Industrial Development District (EEIDD), an independent political subdivision of the State of Louisiana charged with taking over and redeveloping the England Air Force Base after it was decommissioned.

EEIDD, the governing authority for England Airpark, has a board of commissioners who are all appointed by the mayors of Alexandria and Pineville, the Central Louisiana Regional Chamber of Commerce, and Rapides Parish officials. The 10 commissioners, all men, were persuaded last February to rubber-stamp the contract for the ICE jail. Their executive director Ralph Hennessy told Verite News that “the facilities are set up like a traditional dorm room,” and said to ABC affiliate WBRZ that it would bring an economic benefit to the Airpark.

As Hennessy put it: “There are a lot of people in Central Louisiana that make a living off of the immigration world, the prison world.” ICE will pay EEIDD, the district he works for, $530,000 annually. In May, Hennessy’s own base salary rose from $209,615 to $240,000.

Since learning of EEIDD’s plan to allow ICE to detain children in their community, mothers, grandmothers, Christian clergywomen, and educators organizing with CENLA Activism have showed up to EEIDD board meetings, and they have no intention of letting up. They’ve channeled their fury into demonstrations to raise public awareness in heavily trafficked parts of town on the National Day of Action: ICE Out Visibility Event, and have held prayer services that have often brought participants to tears. Pastor Leah Rachal said at an August 25 service she helped organize: “We might disagree on some of the other minutiae of immigration policy. But not this. Nobody wants children to be detained.”

At an August 27 EEIDD board of commissioners meeting, where more than 100 Louisianans packed the overflow room, Rose Marie Norton greeted board chair Oday Lavergne as “the heart of Alexandria” and reminded him, “The protests aren’t necessarily against you; they’re against the system.”

Other community members addressed board members as “brothers,” and cautioned them to think carefully about who will be blamed for any tragic mishap. In every possible way — through prayer, song, even curses — the participants suggested that the board may be taking moral or legal liability by attaching themselves to ICE’s towering pile of collateral damage.

“This will come back to haunt you,” Colleen Buras from Baton Rouge said to the board. “The administration has gone rogue. There’s a lot of policy that is being condemned in the courts. It takes a long time for these things to be adjudicated. Ultimately, you guys will be responsible for what happens in your detention centers.”

Bentley Hensel, a local accountability journalist, explained in his piece for The Kingfish Project how the murkiness of many of the terms and unusual conditions in the “cooperative endeavor agreement” for the jail seemed structured to disadvantage EEIDD’s board over LaSalle or ICE. For instance, Hensel noted, EEIDD has a right to inspect the premises, but not to audit LaSalle’s operating books. Hensel, who grew up in the area and has recently returned, said that in addition to the “unauditability” red flag, there has been an opaque process in which crucial documents were not shared as the board of commissioners went headlong toward an almost unanimous approval.

Marty Floyd, a veteran, retired biologist, and longtime resident of Rapides Parish, told Truthout he fears Alexandria will be permanently stained by what ICE is doing in the town he’s lived in since the 1990s, and he considers it “un-American.”

“I swore an oath to protect the public from foreign and domestic problems. And to me, this is going against that oath. I’ve got to stand up and say something.”

ACLU Louisiana’s communication specialist Jesse Vad drove from New Orleans to attend the August 27 meeting in Alexandria because the board was considering an anticipatory 19-page ordinance curtailing protest at the England Airpark. It unanimously passed, over an avalanche of community objection. Vad said the move to stifle the right to assembly appeared to many of the attendees as if the board were preemptively acknowledging that there will be atrocities that merit mass protest. A number of commenters scoffed at the ordinance and said that if children are harmed, nothing will stop them from assembling freely to demand accountability wherever and whenever necessary.

Vad told Truthout he doesn’t think the board has been given all the facts about the reality of Louisiana’s detention centers.

“I don’t think there’s a single facility in this state that isn’t just absolutely atrocious, unlawful conditions. You know, horrendous incidents at every single one … the board of commissioners and ICE have tried to dress this up as something different,” Vad said. “Nobody believes that. There’s just no reason to believe that.”

Daniel Nakamura drives two hours from the small city of Ruston whenever CENLA Activism puts the word out. But he came specifically to the August 27 meeting because of his family’s experience during World War II. His parents, Yosh and Grace Nakamura — both born in the U.S., both American citizens — were nevertheless rounded up with other 120,000 Japanese Americans and interned in concentration camps when they were in their late teens.

“My dad’s family was at Gila River in Arizona and my mother’s in Manzanar in California,” he said.

Writing in Years of Infamy: The Untold Story of America’s Concentration Camps, author Michi Nishiura Weglyn, describes the harrowing reality at Manzanar: “A WRA investigation conducted in the summer of 1942 had revealed: The guards have been instructed to shoot anyone who attempts to leave the Center without a permit, and who refuses to halt when ordered to do so. The guards are armed with guns that are effective at range of up to 500 yards.” Later that same year, sentries shot and wounded 10 people and killed two — Henry Ito, a 17-year-old from Los Angeles and James Kanegawa, 21 from Tacoma.

“They had a kind of trick question: Do you renounce your loyalty to them? It seems like there’s a lot of trickery with the way immigration’s practiced right now,” Nakamura said.

Nakamura says he’s buoyed by the idea that odious places such as Alligator Alcatraz were closed by a lot of scrutiny. “But you know,” he said, “a lot of pain happened up to that point, and knowing that it might happen to women and children, this is unacceptable.”

A Chance to Walk Back the Deal

Mich González, an attorney at the Southern Poverty Law Center in New Orleans, assists immigrants who are voluntarily deporting themselves to keep their families safe and intact. He was invited to Alexandria by the locally led movement to help them share expert information about the reality of the new ICE jail and how bad it would be for the town’s image and, as some said, its soul.

González, who was escorted out of the previous board meeting while delivering passionate testimony, told Truthout he’s already conveyed to the commissioners that the deal they made with ICE is by no means a “done deal” unless they want it to be. “I already let them know at the July meeting, attorneys can help get them out of the contracts,” he said.

After his second look at the board in action, González responded with sympathy: “These guys are in over their heads, and I think some of them know it in their guts.”

He said about the commissioners, “It would be a mistake for them to think there is any serious oversight over ICE from the U.S. Office of Inspector General or the U.S. Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. They no longer do that. ICE is its own overseer. The commissioners must know this already; it’s old news that there is no oversight.”

González told Truthout that if the commissioners were his clients, he would advise them to unwind these contracts on the basis that they did not have sufficient information and understanding to vote for them on behalf of the town. Later they won’t be able to say they didn’t know.

“At the end of the day, you know what it is. You know it’s an arm of a private prison company. You know it’s an intergovernmental service agreement. You know that it’s an ICE detention center.”

Erin Tracy, who moved back home to Alexandria permanently in 2024, and founded CENLA Activism with her mother in advance of the first No Kings Rally in June 2025, is also noticing a change due to activism.

“We are seeing some of these board members start … to ask more questions,” Tracy told Truthout. “Because something they have not been doing is asking the right questions. They just see the money and think it’s going to help people, but it’s not. It’s just negative attention on our town, and we don’t want that. We have to live here. This is not the economy we want. This is not what we want to profit off of.”

She said that ICE abuses in Alexandria are not limited to the holding station at the Airpark.

“I have a friend whose entire family essentially has been taken and deported to Mexico,” she said. “We have a big community where there’s a bunch of plant nurseries that are staffed by Latinos, and they are very much in danger. One of our local Hispanic markets has had to close. I know of another one where the owner’s husband is now in ICE detention.”

It’s seemingly made no difference to ICE when immigrants have documents or when they have no criminal record. “There’s no discretion,” she said.

“Organizations that are responsible for a lot of death and violence are coming in and saying ‘We’re gonna hold children here and don’t worry we’re gonna protect them,’” she said. “Why would I ever believe that?”

In fact, she thinks that’s backwards.

“It’s we who have to protect our neighbors,” Tracy said.

Tracy was happily surprised that at the August 27 meeting it was announced that a special meeting would be held on September 8 to give everyone an opportunity to speak about the proposed staging area — something they had not previously allowed. But as the days passed, she became concerned that though a majority of the board members signed a letter in favor of the special meeting, one week later it had not been publicly announced.

Sheri Scallan, England Airpark’s Communications Manager wrote in an email to Truthout that she had no details about the time or venue for the special meeting. Two days letter a press release announced the meeting’s cancelation with no explanation. Scallan did not respond to a follow-up email asking for comment in response to activists’ concerns.

Now, CENLA Activism is sponsoring a community-led community forum of its own to call for an end to child detention.

“Our work will not end until this detention center project is shut down for good,” Tracy said.

text:
A Cary pastor who suffered a medical emergency while detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been released and will be going to rehabilitation, according to his daughter.

Gabri Johnson, 30, said her father, Gabriel Johnson III, a 55-year-old Cary pastor, was released from ICE custody on Wednesday evening and would be transitioning to a 24-hour rehabilitation center for medical treatment.

“He’s just so excited to be allowed to go to therapy. A big fear of his was having his body not fully work and be sent to a country he’s never been to before without his family. So that just took such a huge toll, and now, for the time being, that is not a threat,” Gabri told The News & Observer on Saturday, while driving to the Dallas hospital with her mother to visit Johnson.

Johnson is still at a Dallas hospital and will likely be moved to the rehabilitation facility within three days, pending administrative matters like insurance verification, Gabri said. The N&O reached out to ICE on Saturday but has not received a response.

Gabri said doctors initially believed that her father had had a stroke, but brain scans showed that he had an acute neurological event, which has led to partial paralysis on the whole left side of his body, preventing him from moving his left arm or leg and more issues.

“It’s (rehab) something to look forward to for him. So that’s just been taken off of our shoulders, and we’re so, so grateful to everyone involved who made it possible,” she said, referring to community members in Cary who showed up, including from churches, as well as congressional members, her lawyer, activists and others who were vocal about his situation.

Johnson’s medical event occurred on July 30, after he had been in detention in Georgia for about half a month. His family says that he did not receive proper care in custody; ICE and CoreCivic, which runs the Stewart Detention Center in Georgia detention facility, have disputed those allegations, as previously reported by The N&O.

As for why he was detained, ICE previously said Johnson has been under a removal order since 1991, having overstayed a six-month permission to stay, and has a criminal record. The N&O could not independently verify that record, nor would Gabri comment on it.

Gabri said previously he was granted protection from deportation in 2004 and has complied with requirements stemming from that since.

Johnson, who has been married for 30 years and has four children, came to the U.S. from Liberia at age 16 in the 1980s, a decade that began with a violent military coup and grew into political repression before erupting into civil war by its end. Since his arrival, he graduated from N.C. Central University in 2002 and has been a pastor for about 20 years.

More details on detention and medical emergency

Johnson was detained by ICE around 8:30 a.m. on July 15. He was taken to the Cary detention center, where he soon experienced a blood pressure crisis — stage 2 hypertension — and was admitted to WakeMed. Johnson had previously suffered a series of strokes in 2020 that led to brain damage, requiring him to take six to eight medications a day, Gabri previously told The N&O.

After being released that evening from WakeMed, he remained in ICE custody and was transferred to Stewart Detention Center in Georgia the following day. While there, Gabri said her father told the family he was not consistently given his blood pressure and stroke medications. She said he also sometimes went without food or water during transfers, including one instance when agents took him to a military base and pressured him to sign deportation papers and board a plane, two days before a hearing to halt his deportation.

On July 29, ICE flew Johnson to Texas, where he ended up at Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, about 40 miles south of Dallas. The next morning, Gabri said Johnson called his family and told them he loved them and was not feeling well. She said he told them he had not received food or medication in the 24 hours since he was flown from Georgia to Texas.

Around 11 a.m. July 30, Johnson was admitted to a Dallas-area hospital. ICE confirmed at the time to The N&O he was hospitalized for “stroke-like symptoms” but denied allegations that he was denied medical care. ICE did not directly address The N&O’s questions about Johnson’s treatment before his hospitalization.

Gabri and her family traveled to Texas on Aug. 1 and went to the hospital, where she said they were initially not allowed to see Johnson. They were ultimately allowed a one-hour visit and eventually traveled back to the Triangle — though they later returned to visit him again — to continue to advocate on Johnson’s behalf. That included via a federal court case filed in Texas. Johnson’s request for a temporary restraining order was filed on Tuesday, and the court ordered the following day that federal officials cannot deport him, including to another country apart from Liberia, or transfer him out of the court’s jurisdiction while the case proceeds.

Gabri said she got a call from her father’s lawyer around 3 p.m. on Wednesday.

Expecting bad news, she told the attorney, “Honestly, I don’t have the capacity.” But the attorney said she’d want to hear it.

After the Wednesday order from the judge, ICE issued Johnson’s release.

What’s next

The immediate focus of the family right now is getting Johnson into therapy, said Gabri.

“It’s been over a month of him being told (by doctors) that he needed to go to rehab, and that not getting the treatment that he needed could be holding him back from recovery,” Gabri said Saturday, adding that it’s not clear whether he’ll be able to make a full recovery.

Still, now that he can finally access care, Gabri said they just want to support him, having found a place to stay close to a first cousin who lives in the area. They don’t have plans to bring him back to the Triangle, as doctors haven’t given the OK for that and he can’t presently walk.

Gabri previously told The N&O in mid-August that, based on conversations with nurses, it was her understanding that her father was receiving very limited physical therapy at the hospital. She also said Johnson’s right leg was secured to his bed with an ankle cuff, so he rarely left his bed. Gabri said nurses told her the cuff could increase the risk of another stroke because Johnson was taking anticoagulant medication.

The hospital planned to transfer Johnson to a rehabilitation facility, Gabri said at the time, but the facility did not want ICE agents there. ICE requires agents to accompany detainees receiving outside care. Gabri said ICE then canceled the transfer and told the hospital Johnson would remain in its care. ICE said in a previous statement that it does not make clinical decisions or interfere with medical treatment.

But once the judge’s order was issued, Gabri said ICE left promptly, and Johnson has been “a normal patient at the hospital for the first time since he was taken in.”

“It was such a huge relief,” she said.

Still, she can’t fully breathe yet. As for whether ICE can take him back after rehab, that’s currently unclear, Gabri said.

“We’re not fully out of the woods legally, nor with his health,” said Gabri. “We’ve won a battle but not the war. We’re still talking to the lawyers to figure out what our next step is.”

She’s also looking to make emergency arrangements for passports, should her father end up getting deported to a third country that is not Liberia, a practice the Trump administration has escalated.

“The main thing our family is really looking forward to is just being able to have a family dinner at home; it’s just something that we took for granted,” Gabri said, with her family often grilling and her father making pepper soup.

“It started to feel like that would never happen again, and we were all grieving that so heavily. And now that that seems to be possible again, we just want to look forward to family dinner again and the home we’ve lived in for 22 years,” she said.

Twumasi Duah-Mensah contributed to this report.

text:
The United States Supreme Court rendered a high-stakes immigration lawsuit moot after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul granted an executive pardon to Keisy Guerrero Mariano, a lawfully present Dominican citizen who previously pleaded guilty to second-degree assault.

The legal fight in Genalo v. Black examined whether long-term detained noncitizens facing mandatory deportation maintain a constitutional right to a bond hearing under the Fifth Amendment's due process clause.

Gov. Hochul issued the full pardon in late August, effectively preventing the federal government from pursuing its appeal before the high court. The Trump administration had sought to overturn a 2024 ruling from the Second Circuit Court of Appeals that required bond hearings for noncitizens whose immigration detentions become unreasonably long.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers initially arrested Mariano in 2020 following a 2015 assault conviction. Although a federal district court originally denied his habeas corpus petition in November 2021, Mariano was later released from an ICE facility in 2022 under a nationwide COVID-19 health order.

The Second Circuit subsequently ruled in May 2024 that failing to provide bond hearings during prolonged detentions violated constitutional due process rights. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the appeal on June 15, but the case involving co-plaintiff Carol Williams Black was dismissed earlier when the Jamaican national departed the United States.

Following the dismissal of Mariano's case, federal officials affirmed their intent to continue challenging the appellate decision through alternate judicial channels.

Solicitor General John Sauer acknowledged on Friday that the current litigation had become moot due to the pardon.

However, Sauer stated the administration intends to find another case through which the Supreme Court can resolve the issue during its 2026-27 term.

The governor's decision to pardon an aggravated felon drew sharp pushback from state legal officials who criticized the maneuver to derail federal litigation.

"Pretty wild to fully pardon an aggravated felon to (1) stop the felon from getting deported and (2) stop the Supreme Court from ruling on an issue. (Especially as this litigation has been going on for years)," Eric Wessan, Iowa's solicitor general, posted on X.

Wessan commended the solicitor general's commitment to contesting the underlying constitutional ruling in future court sessions.

"I wonder how many non-American felons Governors like Hochul will choose to fully pardon and free to avoid them facing consequences for their actions," Wessan added.

Gov. Hochul's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding the pardon or its impact on the high court proceedings.

text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal authorities are investigating allegations surrounding Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar's immigration history and a disputed claim that she married her brother to help him enter the United States.

Speaking with conservative commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican National Convention on Thursday, Mullin said the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is examining not only Omar's alleged past marriage but also broader questions.

"We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States," Mullin said. "There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with." Mullin described the matter as an "ongoing investigation" and said authorities would only proceed if they could establish evidence of wrongdoing.

Read More on Politics

The allegations involving the Minnesota Democrat have circulated for years in conservative media and political circles. However, they have never been proven in court, no federal agency has publicly released findings substantiating them, and Omar has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Newsweek reached out to Omar's office for comment Friday afternoon via email.

DHS said it could not comment on specific investigations, with a spokesperson adding, “No one, including members of Congress, are above the law.”

The comments mark one of the strongest public statements yet from a senior Trump administration official regarding allegations surrounding Omar.

The issue has resurfaced amid broader administration efforts to investigate potential immigration fraud cases. Mullin suggested investigators are examining whether any false information was provided during the immigration process and said such violations could remain actionable years later if proven.

The remarks also come weeks after reports that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) declined to release certain records related to an Omar-related inquiry, citing ongoing enforcement proceedings.

What Are the Allegations?

The central allegation concerns Omar's 2009 marriage to British citizen Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

Critics have claimed for years that Elmi was actually Omar's biological brother and that the marriage was entered into for immigration-related purposes. Under that theory, the marriage would have constituted immigration fraud.

The accusation gained national attention in 2019 after then-President Donald Trump and several conservative organizations called for further investigation. At the center of the dispute are questions about family relationships, immigration records, and inconsistencies that critics say appear in public documents.

No evidence has been produced to substantiate the claims. The couple divorced in 2017.

What Evidence Has Been Reported?

Several investigations have examined the claims.

In 2019, the Minneapolis-based Star Tribune reviewed newly obtained records and communications related to Omar's marital history. The newspaper reported that some documents raised additional questions about the timeline of Omar's marriages and divorces, but it did not establish that Elmi was her brother.

The New York Times similarly examined the accusations and reported that while questions had been raised about Omar's personal history and marriage records, there was no evidence publicly demonstrating that Elmi was her sibling.

Omar has consistently characterized the allegations as false and politically motivated.

What Has DHS Said?

Mullin said investigators believe they have reason to continue examining the case but emphasized that no enforcement action would be taken unless evidence supports it.

"If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case," Mullin said. "It's an actual case because they did things wrong."

He added that investigators are looking beyond the marriage allegation itself and assessing whether there were broader irregularities associated with the family's immigration history.

“As a matter of policy, DHS does not comment on specific investigative techniques, ongoing investigations, or potential future actions," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek Friday.

The secretary did not provide documentary evidence supporting his assertion that Omar married her brother, nor did he identify any charges under consideration.

What Has Omar Said?

Omar has repeatedly denied that Elmi is her brother and has rejected allegations of immigration fraud.

When the issue resurfaced during her earlier political campaigns, she dismissed the claims as baseless attacks. She has referred to the allegations as "lies."

The Minnesota Democrat has said the allegations are attempts to distract from other administration activity.

What Happens Next

It remains unclear whether federal investigators will ultimately bring any civil or criminal case against Omar.

While DHS says an investigation is ongoing, no court has ruled that Omar committed immigration fraud, and no government agency has publicly released evidence proving the claim that her former husband was her brother.
