text:
A U.S. District Court judge has issued an order forbidding enforcement of a bipartisan Kansas law adopted in 2004 that allowed certain immigrant students at public colleges and universities to pay in-state tuition rates rather than higher out-of-state rates.

Beneficiaries of the controversial state statute have been community college or university students who were brought to the United States as children, completed a high school education in Kansas and agreed to seek citizenship while pursing a higher education degree.

The judge’s injunction takes effect immediately, but it was unclear how it would be implemented on individual campuses across Kansas.

The state law was challenged by the U.S. Department of Justice based on a premise the program violated federal immigration law, incentivized illegal immigration and unconstitutionally discriminated against U.S. citizens.

U.S. District Judge Holly Teeter, a nominee of President Donald Trump, issued a permanent injunction Wednesday night that relied on the Justice Department’s arguments to justify invalidation of the Kansas tuition program.

“The central problem here is that there are United States citizens and nationals who pay full nonresident tuition when an unlawfully present alien is eligible to pay a lower rate on the basis of residence,” the judge said in the decision.

Teeter said state statute was preempted by federal law “because it confers a postsecondary education benefit on an unlawfully present alien based on a state-defined residency conclusion without making that same benefit generally available to United States citizens and nationals regardless of their residence.”

Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach, a longstanding opponent of the tuition statute, collaborated with the DOJ on the legal challenge and jointly proposed a consent judgment blocking the law.

Ryan Kriegshauser, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Kansas, said during a news conference Thursday that the court ruling meant Kansas couldn’t extend in-state tuition benefits to immigrant students without providing the same benefit to U.S. citizens.

“No longer will illegal aliens enjoy the benefit of lower in-state tuition in Kansas,” Kriegshauser said. “This decision has been a long time coming. In fact, I looked at this statute 20 years ago as a law student and a law clerk. It violated the supremacy clause then as it does now.”

In defense of the state’s tuition statute, Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly sought to intervene and seek dismissal of the lawsuit. She was rebuffed by the judge.

“As I said at the onset of this case,” the governor said, “the use of federal government resources to target Kansans, brought to the United States through no will of their own and who only seek to be productive members of society, does nothing to solve any of the fundamental immigration issues we face as a country.”

She said the DOJ’s legal maneuver would hamper the ability of Kansans to secure the education and training required to be valuable members of the state’s workforce and contributors to the economy.

Jessica Swonger, staff attorney with the ACLU of Kansas, said the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund and the ACLU of Kansas filed a motion in July to intervene on behalf of students impacted by U.S. v. Kansas.

“This is a disappointing denial of the rights of those most impacted by the current administration’s cruel crusade against students in Kansas to participate in a lawsuit that will directly impact their future,” Swonger said. “The court has allowed the Department of Justice, in collusion with Attorney General Kobach, to slam the door on hardworking Kansas students, even though Kansans have long supported providing all children in our state the opportunity to learn.”

In June, the DOJ filed its complaint against Kansas and endorsed a proposed consent decree to permanently forbid future use of the tuition law.

“Kansas’ unconstitutional and un-American laws should never have been passed in the first place and are prohibited by federal law,” said Brett Shumate, an assistant attorney general in the DOJ’s civil rights division. “The Department of Justice has won on this exact issue in Texas, Oklahoma, Kentucky and Nebraska, and we will take this fight to any states that fail to put American citizens first.”

During the 2026 session of the Kansas Legislature, the House and Senate passed Senate Bill 254 to prohibit people without authorization to be in the United States from receiving state and local public benefits, including in-state tuition at public colleges and universities.

Kelly vetoed the measure and the Republican-controlled Legislature didn’t assemble the two-thirds majorities necessary to override the governor.

In February, Kobach issued a nonbinding legal opinion that concluded the tuition law known as KSA 76-731a conflicted with federal law.

“For years, Kansas universities have been violating federal law by giving in-state tuition rates to illegal aliens, while nonresident U.S. citizens have to pay much more in tuition,” Kobach said. “The governor tried to intervene in this case, because she wanted to continue giving in-state tuition benefits to illegal aliens. With this decision, the court rejected her illogical arguments, and once again, U.S. citizens will be treated better than illegal aliens by Kansas universities.”

Violet RoumeliotisCEO, Settlement Services International

No spreadsheet could capture how it felt to be one of the 150 Hazara men, women and children stepping down onto the deck of the Norwegian cargo boat MV Tampa in 2001, after their rapidly sinking refugee boat was rescued in the middle of the Indian Ocean.

The image of Australian soldiers helping them to take a leap of faith is seared into my memory still now, 25 years later.

No accountant’s ledger can measure the relief those families who came so close to safety on our shores felt when they were offered a new home in New Zealand.

But if their story was to be reduced to dollar figures, they would have more than paid their new country back. The boys and girls from those families who grew up in Auckland studied hard, went into professions, learned trades, raised families and contributed to the country that gave them a home. They were the children Australia rejected and New Zealand welcomed.

Advertisement

At the time, decision makers in Australia determined the cost in political complications of allowing them to settle here was simply too high. One of those at the helm was then-foreign affairs minister Alexander Downer, who argued last week that Australia’s legal and moral obligation to refugees should be temporary because of their negative lifetime fiscal contribution.

But his logic would also see us deprioritise the average Australian newborn, who enters this world with a negative lifetime fiscal impact, too.

Yet no sane government would reduce an Australian child to a line-item liability or measure their value by their predicted lifetime tax contributions – because we instinctively understand that a nation’s soul and its future strength also can’t be tapped into an accountant’s desktop calculator.

Downer went on to argue that “we do not have an obligation to settle refugees permanently as migrants in our country. Our obligation is to protect them from whoever they are fleeing, not to turn them into migrants”.

Advertisement

I disagree. Resettlement is an act of nation building, firmly planted in our proudest traditions. Australia was one of eight nations that helped draft the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 and played a leading role in establishing the 1951 Refugee Convention.

We should not become a country that sees our responsibility as ending at temporary shelter rather than extending to the possibility of permanent belonging. Because to do so overlooks an economic irony: Australia did not avoid a negative fiscal contribution by turning those children away on the Tampa - we turned away future civil engineers, health professionals, tradespeople and loyal taxpayers to contribute to New Zealand at zero cost to Wellington.

In recent weeks, we have seen voices from across politics argue over whether Australia should cut its humanitarian intake or maintain it at 20,000 places. What has often been missing from that debate is an understanding that humanitarian resettlement is a distinct, human-rights response to persecution and conflict.

That does not mean economics is irrelevant. Refugees work, pay taxes, start businesses, raise families and contribute to their communities, just as generations of humanitarian entrants have done before them. But their right to safety should not depend on whether a Treasury model predicts they will eventually return a fiscal dividend.

Advertisement

Permanent resettlement recognises a basic truth that temporary arrangements ignore: protection is meaningless if human beings are condemned to spend their lives in legal, social and psychological limbo.

Twenty-five years after frightened children and their families took a leap of faith, we remember what is really at stake. A country is more than its balance sheet. When Australia extends a welcoming hand to a child – or a doctor, or engineer or teacher – seeking safety, we invest directly in the strength, character and future of our country.

Violet Roumeliotis is chief executive of Settlement Services International, a community-based organisation that works to overcome inequality.

text:
An Afghan national who was the first-ever case before the federal Alien Terrorist Removal Court has been deported, the Justice Department announced Friday.

The big picture: The DOJ win before the previously dormant court could give the administration a path to remove people it links to terrorism while keeping much of its evidence secret, Axios previously reported.

"It'll be interesting to see what they do next," says Jess Dawgert, a former DOJ attorney and now founding partner at a firm focused on federal immigration litigation. "I can't imagine that now that they've done this and got this confession fairly quickly that they're not going to use it again."

Driving the news: Chief Judge Joan Ericksen directed the removal of Nazira Haji Zada, a lawful permanent resident whom the government accused of assisting her son and son-in-law's foiled 2024 shooting plot, in a recently unsealed August 20 order.

The DOJ said "the government used classified information to establish that Zada is an alien terrorist" and that Zada accepted that designation and waived appeal of the removal order.

Zada's lawyers had previously argued the government violated her due process rights.

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

Catch up quick: The unclassified summary filed in the case accused Zada of being an ISIS supporter who worked to "radicalize the family" and backed her son and son-in-law's conspiracy.

It further said the underlying information was classified "because disclosure would enable terrorists and terrorist organizations to avoid preventative or detection measures" or could reveal FBI or other intelligence sources.

What they're saying: Zada's public defenders, Mary Petras and Matthew Farley, said in a statement to Axios that her "choice to consent to removal should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy."

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process," they continued.

Friction point: The case's result alarmed immigration attorney Eric Lee, who says "the very fact that they were able to achieve their goal without the constitutional question even being tested is deeply concerning."

Pointing to the administration's aggressive immigration crackdown and its propensity to label people as terrorists, he says "it defies logic ... in this particular moment in American history to believe that somehow the invocation of this court could be a positive step, or that ... we should assume it's going to be very very limited."

The other side: Aram A. Gavoor, a former senior counsel for national security in the DOJ Civil Division who has long researched the court and argues it works, describes the case as "a success story in national security."

"[The Alien Terrorist Removal Court is] never going to be a high volume court, nor should it be," he says.

He notes the court's judges are appointed by the Supreme Court's chief justice and calls it "perhaps the last body that I would ever ... even think of cutting corners in as a Justice Department prosecutor looking to effectuate favorable national security outcomes."

The big question is what comes next, Dawgert says: "Are we going to see a stream of them, or is this really going to be a unique court that is only used in ... unique circumstances?"

title: Loss of legal immigrant caregivers puts America's seniors at risk - The Hill
description:
The elder care industry should move swiftly to address current and future staffing gaps — something it has been slow to address previously.
The same research found that, when the immigrant population increases in a metro area, elderly mortality in long-term care facilities measurably declines.
Additional research analyzed by the Kaiser Family Foundation shows that immigrants make up about 30 percent of direct long-term care workers overall, and 41 percent of home health aides.
Legal immigration pathways for healthcare workers deserve recognition as a necessity for care quality, not a peripheral policy debate.
Lawmakers debating these pathways in the abstract are also, whether they realize it or not, deciding who answers the call button at 2 a.m. in long-term care facilities across the country.
text:
The quality of long-term care depends heavily on appropriate staffing levels and continuity of care, as residents fare best when they are routinely treated by the same trained caregivers who know their needs and notice warning signs.

Many documented instances of elder abuse and neglect trace back to facilities that either lacked sufficient staffing or could not maintain a stable, trained team over time. In fact, that pattern that shows up repeatedly in lawsuits involving vulnerable residents.

What often goes unspoken in these cases is the identity of the caregivers themselves. In skilled nursing homes and assisted living facilities across the country, a large share of the workforce providing hands-on care to aging residents is made up of legal immigrants, including visa-holders, green card-holders, naturalized citizens and workers who hold lawful humanitarian status such as temporary protected status.

That workforce is now shrinking. The elder care industry should move swiftly to address current and future staffing gaps — something it has been slow to address previously.

Roughly one in three home care workers and one in five nursing home workers are immigrants, according to research from Harvard, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of Rochester. The same research found that, when the immigrant population increases in a metro area, elderly mortality in long-term care facilities measurably declines. This is because a larger immigrant population expands the overall pool of available caregivers rather than displacing native-born workers from a fixed number of jobs.

Additional research analyzed by the Kaiser Family Foundation shows that immigrants make up about 30 percent of direct long-term care workers overall, and 41 percent of home health aides. Further, a significant rise in a given community’s immigrant population decreases the likelihood that an elderly person will be moved into an elder care facility at all, as immigrant caregivers often make it possible for older Americans to remain safely and receive care in their own homes.

When legal immigration pathways are disrupted, facilities lose trained staff overnight, and residents pay the price in broken continuity of care. In an interview with PBS, a senior care leader described facilities losing between 16 and 40 workers overnight when protections such as temporary protected status have lapsed. This occurred not because those workers had done anything wrong, but because their legal status expired and there was no pathway to renew or reapply.

A loss on that scale does not give a facility time to recruit and train replacements before the next shift. The immediate response is almost always for each staff member to absorb more residents, which is precisely the staffing dilution that is a common thread in elder abuse and neglect cases.

This is happening at a moment when the population needing care is growing faster than the workforce that provides them with care. It is pushing facilities toward a staffing crisis that the industry is poorly positioned to absorb. The fallout from these losses is systemic and devastating for the people caught in the middle, as care teams that residents had come to trust are broken apart and residents are forced to adjust to unfamiliar caregivers who do not yet know their needs or history.

Even skilled, well-trained caregivers become less effective under these conditions, because quality care depends on having enough time with each resident to understand their needs and potential risks, not just rely on credentials to do the job. This leaves facilities in a position where they must consider reducing the number of beds they can safely staff or, in some cases, close entire wings of facilities.

Legal immigration pathways are critical to the elder care infrastructure. Providing quality care to the seniors who depend on skilled nursing homes and assisted living facilities requires treating adequate staffing and continuity of care as a critical part of the elder care infrastructure.

Legal immigration pathways for healthcare workers deserve recognition as a necessity for care quality, not a peripheral policy debate. Every lapsed visa or expired protection is a resident who loses the person who knows their routines, care needs and potential risks best.

Lawmakers debating these pathways in the abstract are also, whether they realize it or not, deciding who answers the call button at 2 a.m. in long-term care facilities across the country. That decision will be felt in individual rooms, and by some of our nation’s most vulnerable individuals, long before it ever shows up in a policy report.

Edward Dudensing is the founder and lead counsel at Dudensing Law.

text:
GREENSBORO, N.C. —

A now-former detention officer in Guilford County has been charged with forgery after the sheriff said 20 court documents for ICE detainees were falsely signed.

According to the Guilford County Sheriff’s Office, GCSO Detention Officer Michael Diehl was fired Friday during an investigation that stemmed from one court document issued for inmate Claudio Nepornuceno.

Get the latest news stories of interest by clicking here

Sheriff Danny Rogers said the Guilford County Magistrate’s Office notified the sheriff’s office that document AOC-CR-662 – which is an Order After Receipt of ICE Detainer and Administrative Warrant – intended for Nepornuceno had the signature of a magistrate who did not process the inmate’s initial arrest.

North Carolina law required Nepornuceno to be brought before a magistrate with a copy of the ICE detainer to authorize a 48-hour hold in the detention center to allow ICE to arrive and assume custody. However, the sheriff alleges that Diehl forged a magistrate’s signature on the AOC-CR-662 form – which violated immigration law in the United States.

Keep up with the latest news and weather by downloading the WXII app here.

Further investigation by the sheriff’s office found that 19 other AOC-CR-662 forms had forged signatures tied back to Diehl. Deputies arrested Diehl and charged him with 20 counts of felony common law forgery. Sheriff Rogers said Diehl received a $5,000 secured bond and was released from Guilford County custody.

Sheriff Rogers said the investigation remains ongoing and additional charges could come forth.

name: Human Rights
title: Everyone should be concerned by ICE agents' brutality | Opinion - The Portland Press Herald
description:
Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero isn’t the first person killed by immigration officials, and without action, he won’t be the last.
This year, we’ve seen bystanders and targeted individuals alike shot in the street by ICE.
Recently, the United Nations has been calling out the United States for its violations of these laws, including the unmerited use of force in immigration enforcement.
Every single one of us should be outraged about the public killings committed by ICE agents and the deaths of those in ICE custody.
Until we have addressed the issue by halting government-sanctioned force, we’re not a free country at all.
text:
Rachael Haskell lives in Portland.

Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero isn’t the first person killed by immigration officials, and without action, he won’t be the last.

This year, we’ve seen bystanders and targeted individuals alike shot in the street by ICE. While many Americans have voiced their outrage, too many continue to support the violence or “do not do politics” or “prefer to remain neutral,” even though we’ve entered a time in which “remaining neutral” means condoning the unbridled government force against those we call neighbors.

As Archbishop Desmond Tutu said, “If you are neutral in situations of injustice, you have chosen the side of the oppressor.” If we choose to ignore and distance ourselves from the brutality being executed by our government, we feed it. We feed it with our silence. We feed it with the blood of our neighbors. We feed it with blind faith that the government is doing what it must, while ignoring the simple truth in our hearts: this is not about politics.

This is about humanity. This is about morals and the crucial promises upholding society. We call these international human rights laws. Recently, the United Nations has been calling out the United States for its violations of these laws, including the unmerited use of force in immigration enforcement.

The rest of the world has been raising alarm bells at the actions of the U.S., but still, many of us remain unmoved. We’re sitting in a burning building and closing our eyes simply because the flames haven’t reached us yet. They will, most likely, because that is fire’s nature. But even if they didn’t, how can we still sit there, knowing that our neighbors are burning around us, hearing them, and doing nothing to help? If we have the means to extinguish the fire — which I believe we do — then choosing not to is the same as setting them on fire ourselves.

So why are so many choosing to sit here? The answer is that we labeled this a political issue, when in reality, it’s a moral issue. Our country has become so polarized that conversation is difficult. This may seem like a condemnation of conservative politics, but I’ve said nothing about politics.

You may be for or against increasing pathways to citizenship or for immigration reform. There is plenty of room for discussion on those topics. We are caught in the political language that surrounds immigration so much so that we avoid the human rights crisis in front of our eyes.

It is perfectly possible to be strict on immigration without utilizing extreme force. But that discussion can only happen if we uphold the basic principles upon which our society and our human decency is founded: the right to just treatment and freedom from cruelty and violence for all human beings, regardless of citizenship. Every human being deserves to be treated as a human being. That isn’t — or shouldn’t be — political.

Our country is divided, and thus, everything gets split into one end of the spectrum, and people become too polarized to take a step toward the other direction. Somehow, in this process, the idea that human beings should not be shot in the street or face excessive force became an idea “belonging” to the left.

I hope to take that idea back and offer it to every person within the United States. Because if we don’t secure human rights, we lose all basis for any policy. We lose our democracy. Holding the government accountable and denying it the right to terrorize its people is the most central component of our political freedom.

Every single one of us should be outraged about the public killings committed by ICE agents and the deaths of those in ICE custody. We describe ourselves as a free society, but as Maya Angelou said, “No one of us can be free until everybody is free.” This includes freedom from unjust harm, cruelty and violent force. Until we have addressed the issue by halting government-sanctioned force, we’re not a free country at all.

We’re beholden by violence, content to watch it burn everything around us.

text:
This is The Marshall Project’s Closing Argument newsletter, a weekly deep dive into a key criminal justice issue. Want this delivered to your inbox? Sign up for future newsletters.

As a transgender woman, Channel Ferro Badell has spent her life fleeing discrimination, trafficking and abuse — first in Uruguay, where she was born, then in Argentina, where she is a citizen. But few experiences compare to what she suffered during her time in ICE custody, she told me. “In six months I was taken to six facilities,” she wrote in Spanish in messages to The Marshall Project. “In every one, the situation is the same: Violence is tolerated within ICE.”

The second Trump administration has singled out immigrants and transgender people — among others — for particular scorn and scrutiny. People at the intersection of those two identities have become a target in ICE custody, and many have described harassment, humiliation, assault and denial of medical care in interviews with The Marshall Project and other news outlets. The administration denied the allegations.

Last month, The New York Times spoke to Camila Toro de Paula, a 25-year-old transgender woman who has spent more than a year in an immigrant camp for men despite a pending asylum claim. She and other women in at least 10 ICE detention camps across the country have had their access to gender-affirming hormone therapy abruptly cut off, the Times reported.

“I’m afraid of dying here,” she told the paper.

Lookout News identified at least 20 transgender women that ICE detained across Arizona and Colorado alone, and found that many had experienced devastating effects from a sudden stop to hormone therapy, including “rapid, menopause-like symptoms, spiking suicidal ideation and severe psychological distress.” As one transgender woman told Lookout: “It messes up your body … Like it’s eating you up inside.”

In interviews, emails and letters with more than half a dozen transgender women in three ICE immigrant camps in Louisiana and Texas, as well as court documents and testimonials, I heard stories of sexual assault, constant harassment — both by staff and fellow detainees — and a sense of betrayal that the country where they had sought refuge and safety was treating them like criminals.

“It was humiliating to see myself with chained arms, waist, and legs, like if I were an animal,” said Mia, detained at River Correctional Center in Louisiana, run by the for-profit LaSalle Corrections. She asked The Marshall Project to withhold her last name because she fears retaliation from staff at that facility. She said her Real ID identifies her as female and reflects her current name, Mia, but ICE staff insist on calling her by her previous name anyway.

Toro de Paula, speaking in Spanish in a telephone interview from the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, run by GEO Group, told me that she “came to the United States because I heard that here they respected the laws for trans women.” In New York, she found doctors who prescribed her hormones and helped her begin the process of medical transition. “I felt cared for, protected, loved, respected. And truly, I will never forget what’s happening to me now.”

This month, two transgender men and a nonbinary person held at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, a GEO Group-run ICE facility for women, filed a civil rights complaint alleging that the warden targeted them for an unsanctioned overnight “work crew,” forcing them to work without protective equipment, taunting them about their gender identities, and sexually harassing them.

At the South Texas ICE Processing Center, also run by GEO Group, Ferro Badell said she slept in an open dorm with 70 men, who called her crude names and said things like “I’ll rape you tonight,” or “I’ll tear you to pieces.”

“Sometimes I go two or three days without eating because they make fun of the way I eat, the way I sit, or they simply don't allow me to sit at the table,” she said. She was deported to Uruguay in August. She’s currently being held in a prison there pending removal to Argentina, according to her friend Déa Thatcher.

Other men’s facilities routinely keep transgender women in isolation cells. This is ostensibly for their safety, but also feels like punishment, said several of the women being held there.

It’s well established that even short stints in solitary confinement can be psychologically damaging, especially for people with a history of trauma — which many in ICE custody have.

Irene Flores Mendoza suffers from PTSD and depression related to her childhood in El Salvador, where she was “continually targeted for violence and threats by MS-13 gang members because she is transgender,” according to legal filings by her attorney. She has been in an isolation unit for months. Flores Mendoza said a psychologist had told them that, because of their mental health conditions and medications, they should not spend prolonged periods in segregation. Nevertheless, she said in Spanish that they had remained there so long that “we see shadows and hear voices and suffer delirium.”

The Department of Homeland Security, in a statement, said that “these claims that there are ‘inhumane’ conditions at ICE detention centers are categorically false … No lawbreakers in the history of human civilization have been treated better than illegal aliens in the United States.” The statement also said, “We are NOT wasting U.S. taxpayer dollars to provide hormone therapy to illegal aliens seeking to change their sex.”

Few of the women in these cases would have been held in detention at all before the second Trump administration, say attorneys and former ICE officials.

People with pending asylum claims, for example, were rarely detained in previous administrations, said Allegra Love, an attorney who specializes in asylum cases. “Most trans people have extremely well-articulated claims to asylum in this country,” she said. “The women I work with almost categorically have been victims of police violence, gang violence, sexual abuse. That’s why they’re fleeing their countries.”

The Trump administration’s policy is to detain almost all unauthorized immigrants, regardless of their individual circumstances, and to hold them as long as it takes for their cases to move through immigration court — often months, or even years. But ICE always has the discretion not to detain someone, and prior administrations often used that discretion in cases where an immigrant might be unsafe in detention, said Claire Trickler McNulty, who served as assistant director of ICE and other top positions under Presidents Obama and Biden. “When you were looking at reasons to release people, vulnerabilities like transgender identity would have been part of the decision,” Trickler McNulty said. “It’s not anymore.”

Before January 2025, ICE published the number of transgender people in custody each month, which rarely climbed above a few dozen, according to ICE data archived by the Vera Institute, a criminal justice reform think tank. The Trump administration stopped publishing that data shortly after the president’s second inauguration. But experts say the numbers are likely higher now, because ICE is detaining more people in general.

The current policies are a marked reversal from guidelines the Obama administration issued in 2015, determining how ICE would treat transgender people, including safe housing decisions, access to undergarments that align with their gender identity and access to hormone therapy. The Trump administration functionally rescinded that policy and removed it from the DHS website in February 2025.

Beginning in the Obama administration, transgender detainees had the option to stay in a dedicated housing unit. The first was in the Santa Ana City Jail, in Southern California. Other units followed in Cibola County, New Mexico, and Aurora, Colorado.

The “trans pods,” as they were called by ICE, had many of the same problems that plague ICE detention centers in general. At the time, lawsuits and news reports documented overuse of solitary confinement, medical neglect, discrimination and poor living conditions. But there was a sense of safety in numbers, and a basic validation of identity that’s gone now, said several people who have been in both places.

Irene Flores-Mendoza was detained in the transgender unit in Colorado before it closed. There, she said, “They treat me like Irene.” At the South Texas men’s facility where she is now, “They treat me like a man. You are Ricardo. We cannot call you Irene. You cannot use makeup or nothing here. If you use makeup, you go to the hole,” she wrote to me in a message. “They don't give me razors. They don't give me hormones. They mock me.”

text:
Four Maryland residents and the immigrant rights group We Are CASA have filed a proposed federal class-action lawsuit seeking to stop alleged warrantless immigration arrests by ICE.

The lawsuit comes as TheGrio has reported on a surge in street arrests affecting Black immigrants and a recent Maryland airport detention involving Johns Hopkins researcher Fatima Ameaka.

The case, Guzmán v. DHS, was filed Sept. 9 in U.S. District Court in Maryland. It challenges what the plaintiffs call an “arrest first, ask questions later” policy and asks a judge to declare the practice unlawful, block it while the case proceeds, and require ICE to comply with federal law and the Fourth Amendment.

Federal law permits an immigration arrest without a warrant only when an officer has probable cause to believe a person is in the country unlawfully and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. The lawsuit alleges ICE agents in Maryland have routinely skipped those determinations.

The complaint says that nearly 7,000 arrests have been made under the challenged practice since January 2025. Plaintiffs accuse agents of following work trucks in unmarked vehicles, boxing in cars, smashing windows and detaining people without first establishing who they are or whether they pose a flight risk.

Samuel Guzmán, 24, is among the named plaintiffs. Guzmán, who was born in Maryland and is a U.S. citizen, alleges masked ICE officers surrounded him outside a 7-Eleven in Annapolis, handcuffed him and held him for more than an hour. He says an officer questioned why he did not speak better English after he said he was an American citizen.

The lawsuit also includes a Latino man identified as J.M.R., who alleges agents pulled him from his car, threw him to the ground and shocked him with a Taser before detaining him. A federal judge later ruled his detention unlawful and ordered his release.

The Washington Post reported that attorneys for the plaintiffs say the enforcement is placing Black, Latino, Afro-descendant and immigrant Marylanders in fear of arbitrary arrest. DHS rejected allegations of racial profiling, saying immigration status, not race or ethnicity, determines who is targeted for enforcement.

The lawsuit seeks a preliminary injunction and class certification. The allegations have not been adjudicated, and the case remains pending in federal court.

text:
A federal judge ordered a UW Medical staffer be released Friday from detention after being convinced the Kenyan immigrant had an elevated chance of a stroke while being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

U.S. District Court Judge Tiffany Cartwright said at a midafternoon hearing that Robert Sidhe should be freed within six hours of her order. His fiancee confirmed Friday evening he was home.

The government has not formally initiated deportation proceedings, but that is still expected to happen.

Sidhe, a 43-year-old who worked as a doctor in Kenya and founded a nonprofit devoted to expanding healthcare access, had a medical crisis at the Tacoma facility that included extremely high blood pressure and strokelike symptoms, according to information discussed at Friday’s hearing. He was taken by ambulance to St. Joseph’s Medical Center in Tacoma

Imaging showed he did not have a bona fide stroke, but the possibility of a future stroke remained, Sidhe’s lawyer argued. Cartwright agreed, saying the consequences could be “catastrophic” given the difficulty of accessing emergency care in detention.

She also noted Sidhe is a caretaker for his partner, a disabled U.S. citizen who uses a wheelchair. Sidhe helps her with bathing, dressing and cooking.

The judge therefore said she was granting a temporary restraining order, reserved for extraordinary circumstances, before a full hearing on a habeas corpus, or unjust imprisonment, petition Sidhe had filed.

Sidhe came to the United States legally five times on visas, according to a legal filing submitted on his behalf. During one visit, he served as a fellow in a U.S. Department of State program for outstanding young African leaders, which enables professional development at an American educational institution.

He last entered the U.S. in February 2023 and later that year filed an asylum application that remains pending.

UW Medicine spokesperson Susan Gregg said Sidhe has worked there since 2025 as a patient care technician. That position involves helping nurses with tests, treatments and other tasks.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement stopped Sidhe on Aug. 26 as he was driving on 68th Avenue in Lynnwood, according to his legal filing. He had just left a grocery store and was on his way home from the gym.

The officers who arrested him said he had overstayed his visa, Sidhe told one of his lawyers, Peter Omari. When Sidhe replied that he had a pending asylum application, the officers told him to tell that to a judge.

Advertising

An ICE spokesperson later said Sidhe was authorized to remain in the U.S. until August 2023 and “did not depart as required.”

The spokesperson referred to a previous statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security: “To be clear, a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States. Any application for asylum does not preclude immigration enforcement.”

ICE did not cite any criminal history when asked about Sidhe, as it invariably has when someone has such a record.

Under previous administrations, ICE did not typically detain people with pending asylum applications and no criminal history. The Trump administration, despite saying its enforcement efforts are focused on immigrants who commit crimes, is different.

ICE last year detained Fernando Rocha, a theater manager at Juanita High School in Kirkland, who also overstayed a visa and had a pending asylum application.

Omari, based in Minneapolis and asked by the Washington Federation of State Employees to represent Sidhe, said he has seen ICE arrest others with pending asylum applications.

To qualify for asylum, people must show they were persecuted, or fear persecution, in their country of origin because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group.

As a Kenyan doctor, Sidhe treated victims of a 2011 pipeline explosion and fire that killed hundreds and injured thousands. He also testified on their behalf in a lawsuit by survivors seeking government compensation, noting their need for specialized surgery.

The survivors won their case, angering many in the Kenyan government who sought revenge against Sidhe, he claims in his legal filing. He links that to the subsequent murder of his brother and a warning he said he received soon after last coming to the U.S. that his life was in danger.

Three years after the pipeline explosion, Sidhe founded the Hawi Global Foundation “with the goal of bridging the gap between healthcare services and those who need it most,” according to the nonprofit’s website. Originally serving Kenyans, the foundation established a Washington outpost in 2023 that provides food and medical services to families here, according to his legal filing.

UW Medicine issued a brief statement after Sidhe’s arrest saying it cares deeply about the well-being of its employees and “hopes for a swift resolution to this matter.”

Gregg, the spokesperson, said she couldn’t elaborate on Sidhe’s tenure at the University of Washington because the university can’t comment on personnel matters. Neither she nor another UW spokesperson answered questions about whether the university is concerned about how immigration enforcement activity affects its staff and students.

Immigration authorities arrested Lewelyn Dixon, a UW lab technician and then green card holder, at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport last year. Government officials cited a 2001 conviction for embezzling $6,500 from Washington Mutual bank when she was a bank teller. Held for three months in ICE detention, Dixon won her case in immigration court and has since become a U.S. citizen.

Sidhe does not appear to be at risk of losing his job, at least in the short term. An email from a UW human resources staffer to a Washington Federation of State Employees representative confirmed the university will not consider him a no-show and will use his accrued leave while he is detained. If he needs more leave, union members have said they want to donate some of theirs.

Mike Yestramski, president of the statewide state employees union, said Sidhe is “exactly who we want” in the United States, “a leader within our union, within his church, within his community.”

He was elected a delegate to an international union convention last month in Chicago, noted Paula Lukaszek, president of the union local that represents UW Medical Center employees. He came a day late because he had a biometrics appointment with immigration authorities, often a routine procedure where fingerprints, photo and the like are taken.

ICE has started arresting people with pending immigration cases and no criminal record at airports, including at Sea-Tac. But Sidhe flew to Chicago without incident.

“He really seemed to enjoy the convention,” Lukaszek said, noting Sidhe went around introducing himself to people and talking about the need for increased healthcare access.

He flew back to Seattle, again without incident.

At Friday’s hearing, Cartwright said Sidhe’s habeas case was likely to succeed. She cited previous decisions granting release to immigrants who had overstayed visas and pending asylum applications. As with Sidhe’s case, long periods of time had gone by without any government effort to detain them. Due process, judges have ruled, requires the government give such immigrants notice and an opportunity to be heard before switching course and taking them into custody.

text:
GUILFORD COUNTY, N.C. (WGHP) — A former Guilford County detention officer faces forgery charges in connection to alleged forged ICE detainment documents, according to a Guilford County Sheriff’s Office news release.

Around 8 a.m. on Friday, the Guilford County Magistrate’s Office told the GCSO about a potentially forged court document submitted by GCSO Detention Officer Michael Shaun Diehl Jr.

The document, entitled Order After Receipt of ICE Detainer and Administrative Warrant, was associated with an ICE detainer issued for an inmate.

The magistrate’s office and GCSO detention staff reviewed the document and determined that it had the allegedly forged signature of a different magistrate who didn’t process the initial arrest.

Under North Carolina law, when certain inmates are subject to an ICE detainer, they must be presented before a magistrate with a copy of the ICE detainer.

The magistrate can then issue a form that authorizes the detention center to hold an inmate for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would otherwise be entitled to be released from custody.

The 48-hour window allows ICE an opportunity to take custody of the inmate.

In this case, it was determined that the inmate mentioned above was not presented before the magistrate with the detainer.

Instead, a form containing the magistrate’s allegedly forged signature was submitted, according to the GCSO.

A further review of jail booking records identified 19 more forms associated with 19 more inmates that contained allegedly forged signatures of magistrates.

The GCSO says that it appears that in each of the 20 cases, ICE had issued a detainer based on evidence that the inmate who was the subject of the detainer violated US immigration law.

The GCSO began a criminal investigation, and Diehl, 40, was fired from the sheriff’s office.

He was arrested and charged with 20 counts of felony common law forgery.

He was given a $5,000 secured bond and has since been released from custody.

Additional charges may be forthcoming.

name: Litigation
title: Website Tracking Class Actions: Courts and Legislatures Push Back, but Risks Remain
description:
Over the past month, courts and legislatures took critical steps to help stem the recent wave of class action litigation targeting websites with wiretapping claims.
As these lawsuits proliferate nationwide, businesses across New England should carefully evaluate their website technologies and related compliance practices.
The California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA), an all-party consent statute, has become one of the primary tools for website tracking litigation.
Plaintiffs have brought CIPA claims nationwide challenging the use of website tracking technologies.
Massachusetts Courts Develop Defenses to Website Tracking Claims Recent Massachusetts decisions have also developed potentially significant defenses.
text:
Common website technologies have become the target of rapidly increasing class action litigation in recent years. More than 5,700 "wiretapping" cases have been filed to date. Companies that deploy tracking pixels, analytics tools, chatbots, session replay software, and similar technologies increasingly face demand letters and class action lawsuits.

Over the past month, courts and legislatures took critical steps to help stem the recent wave of class action litigation targeting websites with wiretapping claims. First, California passed Senate Bill 690, which would limit private lawsuits based on website tracking if signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom by the September 30, 2026 deadline.

Second, the Business Litigation Session of the Suffolk Superior Court recently enforced a Massachusetts choice-of-law provision contained in a website’s terms of use and dismissed a California plaintiff’s CIPA claim. The decision builds on the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court’s earlier holding that the Massachusetts Wiretap Act does not extend to ordinary website browsing activity.

These recent developments provide much-needed reform and clarity, but do not eliminate litigation risk for Massachusetts-based companies. Businesses with websites accessible across state lines may still face claims under federal law and broader state wiretapping statutes, particularly CIPA. Courts remain divided on many key issues, and the law continues to evolve rapidly. As these lawsuits proliferate nationwide, businesses across New England should carefully evaluate their website technologies and related compliance practices.

How Plaintiffs Use Wiretapping Laws to Challenge Website Tracking

Plaintiffs have increasingly sought to apply decades-old federal and state wiretapping statutes to commonplace website technologies that collect and transmit user interaction data.

The targets are familiar digital tools used by businesses across virtually every industry, including:

Tracking pixels and cookies

Session replay technologies

Online chat and customer service tools

AI-powered technologies

Plaintiffs generally allege that these technologies permit third-party vendors such as Meta, Google, TikTok, or LinkedIn to unlawfully intercept electronic communications between website visitors and operators without consent. The claims are often framed as unlawful "eavesdropping" or "interception" of electronic communications in violation of federal and state wiretapping laws.

Federal and State Wiretapping Laws: CIPA, ECPA and the Massachusetts Wiretap Act

The federal Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) prohibits the intentional interception of wire, oral, or electronic communications unless at least one party consents. Several states, including Massachusetts, impose more restrictive consent requirements. Critically, in Vita v. New England Baptist Hospital, Massachusetts’s highest court held that general web browsing is not a protected "communication" under the Massachusetts Wiretap Act.

The California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA), an all-party consent statute, has become one of the primary tools for website tracking litigation. Plaintiffs have relied on several provisions of the California statute, including:

CIPA Section 631, which prohibits the intentional interception of communications in transit without the consent of all parties;

CIPA Section 632, which addresses recording or eavesdropping on confidential communications; and

CIPA Section 638.51, which regulates the use of pen registers and trap-and-trace devices.

Notably, CIPA Section 637.2 authorizes statutory damages of $5,000 per violation or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, creating potentially substantial exposure in putative class actions. Plaintiffs have brought CIPA claims nationwide challenging the use of website tracking technologies. Plaintiffs also bring ECPA claims, including in Massachusetts federal courts, arguing that the statute’s consent exception does not apply where an interception is undertaken for the purpose of committing a criminal or tortious act. The First Circuit is poised to weigh in on that interpretation in Goulart v. Cape Cod Healthcare, Inc.

California SB 690 Could Reshape CIPA Website Tracking Claims

If signed into law by Governor Newsom before October, SB 690 would materially narrow one of the principal theories underlying recent CIPA website-tracking litigation. SB 690 would apply retroactively and eliminate the private right of action, and only the California Attorney General would be empowered to bring a Section 638.51 claim based on website or app tracking. However, SB 690 does not restrict the ability of private litigants to bring Section 631 and 632 interception claims. If signed and once in effect, SB 690 should nonetheless reduce new private website tracking claims and result in the dismissal of Section 638.51 claims filed two or fewer years earlier.

Massachusetts Courts Develop Defenses to Website Tracking Claims

Recent Massachusetts decisions have also developed potentially significant defenses. Federal judges have divided over the application of ECPA’s crime-tort exception, while the Business Litigation Session recently enforced a website’s Massachusetts choice-of-law provision to dismiss a California plaintiff’s CIPA claim.

Unresolved Questions and Emerging Threats: AI Notetakers as the Next Wiretapping Risk

Despite these promising developments, significant uncertainty remains. It is unclear whether SB 690 will substantially stem wiretapping claims or merely refocus them on other CIPA sections. It also remains uncertain how the First Circuit’s decision in Goulart will affect ECPA website-tracking claims in New England federal courts.

AI tools are also generating new applications of traditional wiretapping statutes. In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation is notable; in August 2026, a federal court allowed ECPA and CIPA claims against AI meeting-assistant provider Otter.ai to proceed based on allegations that its tool recorded and processed virtual meeting communications without sufficient consent. The decision signals heightened litigation risk for companies deploying AI tools that record, transcribe, or process communications.

What Businesses Can Do Now

Despite recent legislative and judicial developments, federal and state wiretapping statutes continue to present litigation risk for businesses across industries and jurisdictions.

Particularly pending the enactment of SB 690 and issuance of the Goulart decision, businesses should consider the following steps:

Inventory pending CIPA claims. For suits brought under CIPA Section 638.51 within the past two years, assess for potential dismissal after SB 690 becomes operative.

Conduct a risk assessment of website functionality, tracking technologies and consent mechanisms. Inventory website tracking technologies, analytics tools, chatbots, note-taking and other third-party services; identify what data they collect and transmit; and evaluate applicable consent requirements, including potential CIPA Section 631 exposure.

Update website terms of use and privacy disclosures. Review consent and contract-formation mechanisms, tracking disclosures, choice-of-law provisions, and appropriate arbitration and class-action-waiver provisions.

Monitor legal developments. Businesses should continue to monitor developments under the CIPA, ECPA, and similar state privacy and wiretapping laws, as this area of law continues to evolve rapidly.

For the above steps or a broader privacy risk checkup, our team can help assess exposure, prepare responses, and harden your data flows and disclosures against the next wave of plaintiff demands.

text:
Federal immigration agents detained a man in midtown Friday morning, according to Steven Davis, a volunteer with Rapid Response Tucson, a community network that monitors ICE enforcement operations.

Around 7:24 a.m., at least nine vehicles left the ICE Tucson Field Office, Davis told AZPM. Photos provided by Rapid Response displayed an armored ICE vehicle, emblazoned with the label “Special Response Team.” Another photo displayed a white van outfitted with a ladder and resembling a utility truck.

The man detained on Friday, Davis said, owns and operates a food truck with his wife.

Reached Friday afternoon, an ICE spokesperson would not confirm information about the Friday incident without additional personal details about the detained individual, which have not yet been verified.

“We are out every day conducting enforcement activity,” ICE spokesperson Fernando Burgos said in an email.

Since immigration agents fatally shot Minneapolis residents Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January, the Department of Homeland Security has scaled back on the highly visible enforcement tactics seen in Minnesota last winter.

But despite the more discreet approach, ICE arrests and detainments have not dwindled. Instead, they’ve surged — both nationally and statewide.

Rapid Response observes and documents ICE activity in Tucson. The community network also provides a bilingual hotline for witnesses and those affected by ICE operations. And as arrests climb nationwide, the local group continues to see detainments on the ground, Davis said.

“I can say that these raids and detentions are a daily occurrence,” he noted.

ICE arrests continue to soar

Davis is not alone in that observation. The Deportation Data Project, a research initiative at UCLA and UC Berkeley, logged 2,190 ICE arrests across Arizona in July — the highest monthly statewide arrest rate in years.

The records also show the sweeping majority of those detained by ICE in Arizona that month either had a nonviolent criminal conviction or no criminal conviction at all — despite the Trump administration’s repeated pledge to detain “the worst of the worst.”

ICE enforcement operations also surged on a national scale in July, with agents arresting nearly 50,000 people. Those numbers continued to soar in August, with ICE arresting nearly 51,000 people last month, according to a recent press release from DHS.

The Data Deportation Project has not yet released state-level records for August.

Note: A previous version of this story stated that the man’s wife was also detained. This story has been updated to correct that error.

text:
The State Bar of California has seized what it alleged was an unauthorized law practice from a Chula Vista business it accused of wrongly acting as a provider of immigration legal services, but an attorney representing the business said its owner and other employees acted only as immigration consultants who never claimed to be practicing law.

The State Bar filed a petition last month in San Diego Superior Court seeking to assume jurisdiction over Superior Immigration Services. The state agency alleged that Gabriel Luna de la Fuente, the owner of the H Street business, was “engaged in the unauthorized practice of law” without being a licensed attorney.

A San Diego judge granted the petition last week, and on Tuesday investigators from the State Bar seized thousands of records from Superior Immigration Services. State Bar officials said the records included roughly 1,300 client files and a computer with a massive amount of data.

Defense attorney Kerry Steigerwalt said he believed the matter was a “big misunderstanding,” and that Luna de la Fuente was offering a valuable service to his customers without ever claiming to be a lawyer.

“Gabriel and everyone else in his office are following and complying with his position as an immigration services consultant,” Steigerwalt said. “He’s not in the business of practicing law. Whenever anyone asks, he tells them he’s not a lawyer. Nowhere on his website does it say he’s a lawyer.”

Steigerwalt said California’s Business and Professions Code allows for non-attorneys such as Luna de la Fuente to act as immigration consultants.

“It’s an incredibly valuable service for many, many people,” said Steigerwalt, who said he is representing Luna de la Fuente and his business for now while evaluating whether to take on the case. “He’s helped untold numbers of people.”

Court records showed that no attorney or representative for Superior Immigration Services was present at the Sept. 3 hearing when a San Diego judge authorized the State Bar to seize the business.

Steigerwalt said that raised potential due-process concerns.

“They yanked this business out from under him,” Steigerwalt said. He added that immigration attorneys are “overwhelmed right now” because of the Trump administration’s crackdown, arguing that immigration services consultants, therefore, “serve a very, very valuable role.”

The State Bar’s Office of Chief Trial Counsel argued that Luna de la Fuente and Superior Immigration Services went beyond simply acting as consultants. Attorneys and investigators from the state agency argued that Luna de la Fuente filled out and filed legal forms for clients and offered clients legal advice. The State Bar also alleged that the business advertised to potential clients that they could speak with “Licenciados,” a Spanish term likely to be understood in context as a licensed attorney.

A woman whose complaint helped launch the State Bar investigation asserted that Luna de la Fuente charged her $4,000 for various services between 2021 and 2024, but did not deliver on his promises to help her and her daughter improve their immigration status.

“The complaining witness trusted Mr. Luna de la Fuente with her family’s future and paid thousands of dollars for immigration services she believed were being handled by qualified professionals,” State Bar Chief Trial Counsel George Cardona said in a statement. “Instead, her daughter’s immigration petition was never filed, her daughter’s file was withheld, and she was misled into believing licensed attorneys were assisting her.”

According to the State Bar and court documents, that woman filed a complaint against Luna de la Fuente and his business in October 2024. Earlier this year, a State Bar investigator launched an investigation that lasted through August.

That investigation found that Luna de la Fuente “is engaging in the unauthorized practice of law by advertising and providing legal services to the public in California, engaging in legal analysis and studying the facts of clients’ cases, conducting client consultations, giving legal advice to clients, charging legal fees, and falsely claiming that attorneys are available to speak with potential clients,” an attorney for the State Bar wrote in the petition.

Luna de la Fuente “has never been admitted to practice law by the State Bar of California and is not otherwise authorized to practice law,” the State Bar attorney wrote. “(He) is also not being supervised by any licensed attorney.”

name: Litigation
title: Minnesota churches roiled by legal battle over ICE surveillance and right to protest
authors: Giovanna Dell'Orto, the environment, apnews.com, giovanna-dell-orto
description:
Protesters confronted federal law enforcement daily, and the killing of two protesters sparked global outcry.
Immigration agents are no longer visibly active on the same residential block as Holy Trinity Lutheran Church in Minneapolis.
The government says in court documents that its operation didn’t violate the injunction because it wasn’t about immigration enforcement.
Some contend the charges amounted to “selective or vindictive prosecution,” and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance.
Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Court cases involving Twin Cities churches and immigration enforcement highlight how the acrimonious debate continues to roil faith communities more than six months since the federal surge turned Minnesota into a symbol of defiance of the Trump administration’s policies.

In one case, a Minneapolis Baptist church — alongside congregations nationwide — asked for the government to be reprimanded after spying on protest-related activity on its property. In another, more than three dozen protesters have asked for their charges to be dismissed after they disrupted a worship service in a St. Paul church where one of the pastors was also a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official.

Even congregations uninvolved in the court cases say they’re still feeling the repercussions of the weekslong surge in immigration operations last winter. Protesters confronted federal law enforcement daily, and the killing of two protesters sparked global outcry.

Immigration agents are no longer visibly active on the same residential block as Holy Trinity Lutheran Church in Minneapolis. But its pastor says the signs that went up in January stating “Everyone is welcome here! Except I.C.E.” have stayed.

“I don’t foresee a time when they will come down. We want our building to remain a sanctuary for many people,” said the Rev. Ingrid Rasmussen. Her church provided whistles, which protesters across the city used to alert neighbors about law enforcement presence.

Churches as safe places for migrants — and worshippers

For decades, congregations have been on the front lines of providing for immigrants and refugees, whether in their faith communities or with outreach ranging from food distribution at the U.S.-Mexico border to advocacy in Washington.

As part of its sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration, President Donald Trump’s current administration gave agents more leeway to make arrests at houses of worship.

In response, dozens of religious groups sued, heralding a more openly adversarial relationship between many faith leaders and federal authorities.

That has continued through surges last fall and winter in various parts of the country, with faith leaders arrested during anti-enforcement protests and suing to make pastoral visits to detained migrants.

“There’s been a pretty dramatic increase in lawsuits filed related to people of faith’s support for migrants,” said Elizabeth Reiner Platt, director of the Law, Rights and Religion Project at Union Theological Seminary.

Faith groups have achieved several “promising” wins, she said, adding that ongoing litigation shows how unpopular the administration’s aggressive enforcement approach is with many religious people.

Both Minnesota court cases center on the idea of protecting a sacred space and people’s right to worship — in one case from government intrusion and in the other, from people protesting the immigration crackdown.

Government surveillance at Minneapolis church sparks outcry

In mid-August, court documents emerged in a separate case involving 15 people charged by federal prosecutors with impeding the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. The documents revealed that federal agents had conducted an undercover surveillance operation, which had targeted groups leading protests earlier this year.

Among those charged was an organizer in a martial arts group who the government says was training protesters to physically prevent arrests. Some of the group’s meetings occurred in the gym of University Baptist Church in Minneapolis, and Homeland Security agents conducted surveillance operations there four times — including once with an undercover agent inside, according to court documents.

The church is a member of American Baptist Churches USA and the Alliance of Baptists, two of several groups that in February won an injunction against most immigration enforcement at their member churches nationwide.

The groups have asked the same federal judge to rule that Homeland Security violated that order, to instruct its agents about it, as well as to disclose if any other houses of worship were part of surveillance operations.

The government says in court documents that its operation didn’t violate the injunction because it wasn’t about immigration enforcement. Rather, they were investigating a suspect for training “individuals to commit acts of violence against federal officers and employees.”

A hearing was held Sept. 4 and a ruling is pending. A spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security said it doesn’t comment “on the existence or status of specific ongoing investigations, nor on investigative methods.”

University Baptist Church’s interim pastor said the small congregation found the surveillance “very upsetting” — but also motivation to double down on their advocacy.

“We see the message of Jesus as compelling us to be where people are most vulnerable,” the Rev. Cody J. Sanders said.

For Kevin Friedl, an attorney with the Democracy Forward Foundation that’s representing the faith groups, the case is ultimately about offering sanctuary.

“For many, religion — being able to join together with others at their church or other house of worship — is an important and critical source of solace and comfort, in hard times, which these are,” he said. “This administration wants to deny them that.”

Protesters who interrupted Sunday worship seek dismissal of charges

The argument that churches are protected spaces and worshippers have rights against intrusion is also buttressing the case over the anti-immigration enforcement protest at Cities Church in Minnesota’s capital in January.

More than three dozen people — including former CNN journalist Don Lemon and prominent local activists — are facing federal civil rights charges after entering the Southern Baptist church where one pastor was also a leader in the local ICE field office.

During Sunday worship, some walked up to the pulpit, others loudly chanted “ICE out” and “Renee Good,” referring to the woman who was fatally shot on Jan. 7 by an ICE officer in Minneapolis.

In August, a slew of motions to dismiss the cases were filed and will be heard in late October. Some contend the charges amounted to “selective or vindictive prosecution,” and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance. They argue that the “administration’s claims that this prosecution is based on a desire to protect the right to practice religion is disproved by the extraordinary freedom it has granted ICE to violate the sanctity of churches,” according to court documents.

“They’re using these cases to try to get information on the whole resistance movement,” said Jordan Kushner, an attorney representing several defendants.

An attorney representing Cities Church countered that the issue at play is “an invasion during worship.”

“Nobody has the right to storm a church,” Doug Wardlow said, adding that the protest — and smaller, outdoors ones that continue to occur during worship times — “traumatically impacted the life of the church.”

How fallout from the surge impacts Minnesota congregations

Faith leaders across the Twin Cities say they’re still dealing with fallout from the surge, whether it’s lingering fear among migrants, tensions over government surveillance, or persistent financial assistance requests.

Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev. Mariah Furness Tollgaard, senior pastor at Hamline Church in St. Paul. She was briefly detained at an anti-deportations protest at the Minneapolis airport in January.

Several Protestant congregations that were outspoken in their anti-immigration-enforcement stances have increased their security measures.

While many remain committed to their advocacy, it’s taking a toll.

“The general vibe we get from leaders and congregations is just tired — there’s weariness more than anything,” said Nicholas Tangen of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America’s Minneapolis Area Synod.

text:
A San Francisco-based federal immigration judge was fired after she questioned Trump administration legal tactics and resisted a request from Immigration and Customs Enforcement to fast-track the deportation of a teen asylum seeker, a lawsuit claims.

In the complaint, filed Thursday in federal court, Chloe Dillon alleges she was fired roughly 48 hours after sending a message to a superior relating her concerns over an August 2025 incident. In the message, Dillon wrote that she was alarmed a teenage asylum seeker had been arrested by ICE after they left her courtroom, where she had just delayed ICE's request to dismiss the individual's case and place them into expedited removal proceedings.

Prior to the arrest, Dillon gave the individual, who had been representing themselves, time to find a lawyer.

"When you have judges who are in fear that they will be fired for the decisions that they're making, it has completely undermined the basic principles of judicial adjudication," Dillon told SFGate. "I don't see how you have fair and unbiased tribunals in the immigration court when there is this atmosphere of fear and intimidation."

The asylum seeker had originally shown up to court representing themselves, and Dillon concluded the individual was "almost certainly a designated unaccompanied minor who could not be placed into expedited removal proceedings, and who thus had the right to have his already-filed asylum application decided first by an asylum officer, and then, if necessary, by the Immigration Court," according to the suit.

The San Francisco immigration court was already under pressure from the Trump administration to comply with requests from ICE to transfer cases to other venues, according to the suit. Dillon alleges a superior told her in spring of 2025 that the White House "was watching the issue and cautioned her against resisting the directive."

Nonetheless, Dillon refused to comply with some of these requests, and she similarly pushed back in cases where she felt ICE lacked the jurisdiction to re-calendar cases involving unaccompanied minors.

In her August email to her superior, Dillon argued ICE had been "disrupting the orderly administration of justice," the suit claims.

The complaint, which names the Justice Department and Attorney General Todd Blanche, among others, seeks to have Dillon reinstated and given back pay, damages and a declaration the firing was unlawful. The lawsuit argues Dillon's constitutional rights under the First and Fifth Amendment were violated, along with federal law, and it alleges the judge was fired without notice or an opportunity to challenge the decision.

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

"While we do not typically comment on pending litigation or personnel matters, we can tell you that this allegation is patently false," a DOJ spokesperson told The Independent in a statement.

"After four years of the Biden Administration forcing Immigration Courts to implement a de facto amnesty for hundreds of thousands of aliens, this Department of Justice is restoring integrity to our immigration system and encourages talented legal professionals to join in our mission to protect national security and public safety," the official added.

Over the last year-and-a-half, the Trump administration fired most of the immigration judges in San Francisco and shuttered one of the main immigration courts there.

Under the Trump administration, immigration officials have stepped up arrests near courthouses, schools and other sensitive locations. Numerous individuals have reported being arrested after appointments checking in with immigration officials about their pending legal status that had previously occurred without incident.
