text:
I. Introduction

Roxanna Flores-Alvarado was convicted of (a) conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute cocaine, and (b) possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of cocaine, after a traffic stop uncovered approximately four kilograms of cocaine in a vehicle she was driving with her boyfriend, Christian Mendez, as a passenger.

The core factual dispute at trial was knowledge: Flores-Alvarado maintained she believed Mendez was working in construction and did not know drugs were involved; the government relied heavily on circumstantial evidence (travel patterns, warning texts about police, photos, proximity to drugs, and testimony from cooperator Wuesley Pelaez-Vela) to show she knowingly and voluntarily joined the drug activity.

On appeal, Flores-Alvarado raised two issues:

Sufficiency: whether the evidence proved she knew of and voluntarily joined the cocaine conspiracy (and knowingly possessed cocaine with intent to distribute).

Sentencing legality: whether the district court erred by treating the jury’s verdict as binding when denying safety-valve relief under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(5) and U.S.S.G. § 5C1.2(a)(5).

II. Summary of the Opinion

The Eleventh Circuit affirmed both the convictions and the 60-month sentence.

Convictions affirmed: The court held that, viewing the evidence in the government’s favor, a rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that Flores-Alvarado knowingly participated in the conspiracy and knowingly possessed cocaine with intent to distribute.

Sentencing affirmed (harmless error): The court held the district court made a legal error by concluding it was bound by the jury’s verdict when assessing safety-valve eligibility, because safety-valve compliance requires independent judicial determination. The error was nonetheless harmless because the sentencing judge expressly stated that if the judge were the factfinder, the judge would find Flores-Alvarado knew she was involved in drug dealing—so the result would be unchanged on remand.

III. Analysis

A. Precedents Cited

1. Sufficiency of the evidence framework

United States v. Robertson (quoting United States v. Tinoco): Supplies the standard appellate lens—view evidence in the light most favorable to the government and credit verdict-supporting inferences.

United States v. Defilippis, United States v. Trujillo (quoting United States v. Suba): Reiterates the controlling question—whether any rational trier of fact could find the elements beyond a reasonable doubt; the government need not disprove every innocent hypothesis.

United States v. Guevara (quoting United States v. Mieres-Borges): Confirms no special discounting of circumstantial evidence; direct and circumstantial evidence are evaluated under the same sufficiency test.

United States v. Mendez: Adds the limiting principle—when relying on circumstantial proof, convictions must rest on reasonable inferences rather than speculation.

2. Elements of conspiracy and the “mere presence” caution

United States v. Badolato: Provides the Eleventh Circuit’s familiar § 846 elements—(1) conspiracy, (2) knowledge, and (3) voluntary participation.

United States v. Miranda: Establishes that mere presence/association is insufficient, but can be probative when combined with other evidence.

United States v. Colston: Explains how juries may infer guilty knowledge—instrumentality to the plan, opportunities to learn the “critical fact,” and frequent contact with someone who knew it.

3. The defendant’s testimony as affirmative evidence of guilt if disbelieved

United States v. Brown: Key doctrine—if a defendant testifies and the jury disbelieves the testimony, the jury may treat the denial as substantive evidence of guilt (the “opposite may be true” inference).

United States v. Beaufils: Reinforces United States v. Brown in a modern Eleventh Circuit formulation.

United States v. Murray and Globe Indem. Co. v. Richerson: Emphasize credibility allocation—juries can accept all, some, or none of a witness’s testimony.

Bonner v. City of Prichard, Ala.: Explains why former Fifth Circuit decisions like United States v. Murray and Globe Indem. Co. v. Richerson remain binding in the Eleventh Circuit.

4. Prosecutorial argument and curative instructions

United States v. Almanzar and United States v. Verdeza: Supply the presumption that juries follow limiting instructions.

United States v. Lopez (quoting United States v. Smith): States the remedial rule: improper statements in closing are often cured by instructing that lawyer arguments are not evidence.

5. Safety valve: who decides, what is required, and how errors are reviewed

United States v. Pulido: Used rhetorically to frame the parties’ mismatch: the government argued clear-error review (factfinding), while Flores-Alvarado alleged a legal misunderstanding (de novo review).

United States v. Little: Recognizes deferential clear-error review for sentencing factfinding—relevant only if the issue were factual rather than legal.

United States v. Dubois and United States v. Defilippis: Support de novo review for statutory interpretation and legal questions at sentencing.

United States v. Mathews: Establishes the “authority misapprehension” principle—sentencing courts err when they believe they lack discretion/authority that the law actually grants.

Pulsifer v. United States: Cited for the structural point that the safety valve enables courts to impose lighter terms.

United States v. Brownlee: Treats truthfulness/completeness of a safety-valve proffer as a factual finding for the district court.

United States v. Espinosa: Holds it is error for a district court to defer to the government on truthfulness; the court must make the determination.

United States v. Sherpa: Persuasive (Ninth Circuit) support for the specific proposition that safety-valve compliance is a separate judicial determination not required to match a jury’s findings.

United States v. Johnson (quoting United States v. Yate): Defines § 3553(f)(5) as an affirmative disclosure duty—defendant must truthfully disclose all information about the offense and relevant conduct.

6. Harmless-error review at sentencing

United States v. Rodriguez: Notes the government typically bears the burden to show harmlessness.

United States v. Adams and United States v. Graham: Recognize the appellate court’s ability to raise harmlessness sua sponte, especially where it is “patently obvious,” and caution when harmlessness is uncertain.

United States v. Keene and United States v. Robles: Provide the operative harmlessness logic—when the district court’s stated reasoning makes the result on remand certain, an error that would not change the outcome is harmless.

7. Plain-error standard (unpreserved objections)

United States v. Utsick (as quoted in United States v. Defilippis): Supplies the four-part plain error framework for issues not raised below, relevant to Flores-Alvarado’s challenge to the prosecutor’s closing argument.

B. Legal Reasoning

1. Why the evidence was sufficient

Applying the sufficiency standard from United States v. Trujillo and United States v. Suba, the court treated the record as a collection of mutually reinforcing circumstantial facts rather than a single dispositive “smoking gun.” The opinion identifies multiple inference-supporting strands:

Travel and logistics: evidence that she drove with Mendez during trips linked to cocaine procurement, including border/checkpoint evidence.

Proximity and transport: she was driving when four kilograms were found behind the driver’s seat, near her child.

Warning texts: messages like “Babe, cops are outside… Be careful,” which the jury could interpret as countersurveillance or awareness of illicit activity.

Photos and hotel context: pictures of money; her presence in a hotel room associated with drug packaging; and communications among conspirators.

Witness testimony: Pelaez-Vela’s account that she accompanied Mendez to McAllen and was present during drug-related discussions.

Credibility and adverse inference from her testimony: under United States v. Brown and United States v. Beaufils, the jury could treat her blanket denial of knowledge as evidence supporting knowledge if disbelieved.

Critically, the court used United States v. Miranda to acknowledge that “mere presence” is not enough, but then treated her actions (driving, warnings, contextual photographs, and repeated proximity to drug-related conduct) as the “something more” that converts presence into probative participation. And consistent with United States v. Colston, the court emphasized opportunities to discover the “critical fact” (that drugs were involved) and close contact with someone who knew it (Mendez), allowing an inference of knowledge.

2. Prosecutor’s closing argument did not warrant reversal

Flores-Alvarado argued the prosecutor improperly reframed culpability as “unreasonableness” rather than knowledge/voluntary participation. Because no contemporaneous objection was made, the court invoked plain-error review per United States v. Defilippis.

The court then resolved the issue largely through the curative-instruction line: under United States v. Almanzar and United States v. Verdeza, juries are presumed to follow instructions that counsel’s arguments are not evidence; and under United States v. Lopez (quoting United States v. Smith), improper closing statements are typically cured by such instructions. That doctrinal move allowed the panel to avoid an extended inquiry into the precise phrasing of the rebuttal argument.

3. The safety-valve legal error—and why it did not matter here

The opinion’s most concrete legal clarification concerns the institutional role in safety-valve determinations. The district court denied relief because the jury found knowledge beyond a reasonable doubt, and the judge believed the jury verdict was “binding” on the truthfulness element of § 3553(f)(5). The Eleventh Circuit held that was a legal mistake.

Rule articulated by the panel: Safety-valve compliance—especially whether the defendant “truthfully provided” all information under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(5) and U.S.S.G. § 5C1.2(a)(5)—requires an independent judicial determination; the sentencing court is not bound by the jury’s verdict when making safety-valve findings.

The panel grounded that conclusion in:

Statutory text and structure: § 3553(f) repeatedly assigns findings to “the court,” and does not incorporate jury determinations.

Supreme Court framing: Pulsifer v. United States describes the safety valve as a mechanism enabling courts to impose lighter terms.

Eleventh Circuit authority on who decides: United States v. Espinosa (no deference to government) and United States v. Brownlee (truthfulness/completeness is for the district court) support the principle that the judge must decide.

Persuasive reinforcement: United States v. Sherpa explicitly states safety-valve compliance is a separate judicial determination not required to match a jury’s findings.

Legal-error framing: Under United States v. Mathews, a court commits legal error when it mistakenly believes it lacks authority to grant relief.

Even so, the panel affirmed on harmless-error grounds. The district court did not merely rely on the jury; it also stated on the record that if it were the factfinder it “would find” she knew she was assisting drug dealing. Under United States v. Keene and United States v. Robles, when the district judge’s stated view makes the remand outcome certain, the legal error does not affect substantial rights and is harmless. The panel also relied on its discretion to consider harmlessness sua sponte under United States v. Adams, noting harmlessness was “clear,” consistent with the cautionary framing in United States v. Graham.

C. Impact

1. Sentencing practice: safety valve is a judge’s call—even after a guilty verdict

The opinion reinforces (and operationalizes) a practical sentencing rule: safety-valve eligibility is not mechanically foreclosed by the jury’s guilty verdict. The sentencing court must independently decide whether the defendant met the affirmative disclosure obligation of United States v. Johnson (quoting United States v. Yate), even when that inquiry overlaps with contested trial facts (e.g., knowledge).

That said, the harmless-error affirmance also signals a litigation reality: where the sentencing judge clearly indicates the same adverse factual finding would be made independently, appellate relief may be unavailable even if the judge misstated the “bound by jury” rationale.

2. Trial strategy: defendant testimony can be a double-edged sword

The sufficiency analysis underscores the continuing importance of United States v. Brown: when a defendant testifies and denies knowledge, the jury’s disbelief may become affirmative evidence of guilt. In close knowledge cases built on circumstantial evidence, this doctrine can materially increase the risk of conviction.

3. Prosecutorial-argument challenges: instructions remain a powerful shield

The panel’s reliance on United States v. Almanzar, United States v. Verdeza, and United States v. Lopez suggests that absent a preserved objection and demonstrable prejudice, closing-argument complaints will often be neutralized by standard jury instructions.

Note on precedential weight: The decision is labeled “NOT FOR PUBLICATION,” which typically limits its binding precedential force. Nonetheless, its reasoning may be cited as persuasive authority and as an indicator of how the Eleventh Circuit applies established safety-valve and harmless-error doctrines to common trial-and-sentencing fact patterns.

IV. Complex Concepts Simplified

“Sufficiency of the evidence” review: The appellate court does not re-try the case. It asks only whether a reasonable jury could have convicted when viewing the evidence in the prosecution’s favor.

Circumstantial evidence: Proof by inference (texts, travel patterns, photos, proximity), not direct admission. The law treats it as fully valid if the inferences are reasonable and not speculative.

Drug “conspiracy” (21 U.S.C. § 846): An agreement to commit a drug offense plus knowledge of that agreement and voluntary participation. You do not need to handle drugs personally to be guilty.

“Mere presence” doctrine: Being near criminals or drugs is not automatically guilt; but presence combined with actions that advance the scheme (driving, warnings, repeated involvement) can support conviction.

Safety valve (18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)): A statutory escape hatch from mandatory minimums for certain drug defendants who meet all criteria—including, importantly here, truthfully telling the government everything they know about the offense and related conduct.

Harmless error: Even if a judge makes a legal mistake, an appellate court may affirm if the mistake would not change the result (e.g., the judge would deny relief anyway based on independent findings).

V. Conclusion

United States v. Roxanna Flores-Alvarado delivers two principal takeaways. First, convictions for drug conspiracy and possession may be sustained on layered circumstantial proof—particularly when the jury can reasonably infer knowledge from conduct and context and can treat a disbelieved denial as substantive evidence under United States v. Brown. Second, and more distinctly, safety-valve eligibility under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(5) requires independent judicial factfinding; a sentencing court errs by treating a jury verdict as “binding” on the safety-valve truthfulness inquiry. Yet the case also illustrates the limiting doctrine of harmless error: when the sentencing judge makes clear the same factual findings would be made independently, appellate courts may affirm despite the legal misstatement.

text:
As Stowe police exit their agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement for a second time, the small riverside borough of Versailles has moved to cooperate with the federal agency.

Officials in both municipalities — among a small list of Allegheny County communities that have entered into controversial cooperation pacts with ICE, known as 287(g) agreements — said the deals have had little practical effect.

Versailles Council President Lisa Fleckenstein said the Democratic-majority borough council unanimously voted to approve the pact after weeks of discussion. ICE records show the borough entered the agreement Sept. 4.

“We all knew it could be a controversial issue,” she said.

The council vote sets Versailles apart from other municipalities in Allegheny County — like Springdale and Pitcairn — which entered into agreements without a vote by elected officials. Springdale and Pitcairn officials have both said a vote was not required by their borough codes.

In Versailles — a community of around 1,500 along the Youghiogheny River south of McKeesport — the primary reason for signing the agreement was for the training it would provide the borough’s five-person police force, according to Linda Sheedy, council vice president.

To her knowledge, there are no undocumented people in Versailles, nor has there been any previous ICE activity in the borough, Sheedy said.

“We don’t have a problem,” she said. “We’re proactive. This training protects our residents.”

The agreement “allows local officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties, such as identifying an alien at a DUI checkpoint and sharing information directly with ICE,” according to an ICE website.

In such cases, an ICE supervisor would determine next steps, according to the site. Officers “may also exercise limited immigration authority as active participants on ICE-led task forces,” the site says.

Fleckenstein said almost all the training offered by ICE would be virtual and free, though it’s unclear what it would include. Versailles Police Chief Charles Roka could not immediately be reached for comment Friday.

ICE’s tactics and training of new recruits, part of a massive recruitment effort under the second Trump administration, have come under fire from national lawmakers and local immigrant advocacy groups, including one former ICE lawyer who called the current training regimen “deficient, defective and broken.”

Though they see the ICE training as beneficial for Versailles officers, both Fleckenstein and Sheedy said they don’t expect any agency activity in what Sheedy called the “sleepy little borough.”

“My own personal opinion was I don’t think we’ll ever see an ICE officer because I don’t know why we would,” Sheedy said.

In Stowe, however, pushback from numerous residents led township commissioners to rescind a 287(g) agreement that has been in place since last December, according to Commissioner Tyler Kochirka.

In the more than nine months since signing on with ICE, Stowe Police hadn’t participated in any operations with the agency, Kochirka said.

“It was an easy decision to withdraw because nothing was happening anyway,” he said.

It’s the second time the township — located along the Ohio River between McKees Rocks and Robinson — has withdrawn from the pact. It signed on Nov. 18 before backing out and rejoining Dec. 11., according to ICE records.

Stowe police initially signed the agreement unilaterally, which Kochirka said was caused by a miscommunication with federal authorities. But after discussions in December, borough officials opted to rejoin.

Stowe police Chief Matt Preininger did not immediately respond Friday to a TribLive request for comment.

Kochirka said he initially supported the idea because he thought it would allow local officers to handle potential immigration issues rather than ICE agents coming to Stowe, providing a “shield” for the township.

But after around two dozen people showed up to Stowe’s Tuesday meeting, many of whom spoke out against the agreement, he said he and his fellow commissioners decided to reverse course.

“Immigration and illegal immigration is not an issue in Stowe Township,” Kochirka said. “I think this is done and over with.”

In Springdale and Pitcairn, though, the agreements have led to multiple detainments.

Springdale Borough police, who signed the agreement last November, have been involved in the arrest of at least two people who they later handed over to ICE — a local father of two and a visiting laborer who ICE says has a criminal record.

The pact has led to concern among local immigrants and continued discord in the Allegheny Valley borough.

Pitcairn police, which also cover nearby Wilmerding, have also been involved in multiple detainments, Mayor Margaret Stevick told TribLive last month.

Several Allegheny County municipalities — of which there are 130 distinct local governments — have passed resolutions forbidding local officers from assisting ICE, including Oakmont, Fox Chapel, Plum and McCandless.

title: Minnesota churches roiled by legal battle over ICE surveillance and right to protest - WCBD
description:
Protesters confronted federal law enforcement daily, and the killing of two protesters sparked global outcry.
Immigration agents are no longer visibly active on the same residential block as Holy Trinity Lutheran Church in Minneapolis.
The government says in court documents that its operation didn’t violate the injunction because it wasn’t about immigration enforcement.
Some contend the charges amounted to “selective or vindictive prosecution,” and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance.
Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Court cases involving Twin Cities churches and immigration enforcement highlight how the acrimonious debate continues to roil faith communities more than six months since the federal surge turned Minnesota into a symbol of defiance of the Trump administration’s policies.

In one case, a Minneapolis Baptist church — alongside congregations nationwide — asked for the government to be reprimanded after spying on protest-related activity on its property. In another, more than three dozen protesters have asked for their charges to be dismissed after they disrupted a worship service in a St. Paul church where one of the pastors was also a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official.

Even congregations uninvolved in the court cases say they’re still feeling the repercussions of the weekslong surge in immigration operations last winter. Protesters confronted federal law enforcement daily, and the killing of two protesters sparked global outcry.

Immigration agents are no longer visibly active on the same residential block as Holy Trinity Lutheran Church in Minneapolis. But its pastor says the signs that went up in January stating “Everyone is welcome here! Except I.C.E.” have stayed.

“I don’t foresee a time when they will come down. We want our building to remain a sanctuary for many people,” said the Rev. Ingrid Rasmussen. Her church provided whistles, which protesters across the city used to alert neighbors about law enforcement presence.

Churches as safe places for migrants — and worshippers

For decades, congregations have been on the front lines of providing for immigrants and refugees, whether in their faith communities or with outreach ranging from food distribution at the U.S.-Mexico border to advocacy in Washington.

As part of its sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration, President Donald Trump’s current administration gave agents more leeway to make arrests at houses of worship.

In response, dozens of religious groups sued, heralding a more openly adversarial relationship between many faith leaders and federal authorities.

That has continued through surges last fall and winter in various parts of the country, with faith leaders arrested during anti-enforcement protests and suing to make pastoral visits to detained migrants.

“There’s been a pretty dramatic increase in lawsuits filed related to people of faith’s support for migrants,” said Elizabeth Reiner Platt, director of the Law, Rights and Religion Project at Union Theological Seminary.

Faith groups have achieved several “promising” wins, she said, adding that ongoing litigation shows how unpopular the administration’s aggressive enforcement approach is with many religious people.

Both Minnesota court cases center on the idea of protecting a sacred space and people’s right to worship — in one case from government intrusion and in the other, from people protesting the immigration crackdown.

Government surveillance at Minneapolis church sparks outcry

In mid-August, court documents emerged in a separate case involving 15 people charged by federal prosecutors with impeding the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. The documents revealed that federal agents had conducted an undercover surveillance operation, which had targeted groups leading protests earlier this year.

Among those charged was an organizer in a martial arts group who the government says was training protesters to physically prevent arrests. Some of the group’s meetings occurred in the gym of University Baptist Church in Minneapolis, and Homeland Security agents conducted surveillance operations there four times — including once with an undercover agent inside, according to court documents.

The church is a member of American Baptist Churches USA and the Alliance of Baptists, two of several groups that in February won an injunction against most immigration enforcement at their member churches nationwide.

The groups have asked the same federal judge to rule that Homeland Security violated that order, to instruct its agents about it, as well as to disclose if any other houses of worship were part of surveillance operations.

The government says in court documents that its operation didn’t violate the injunction because it wasn’t about immigration enforcement. Rather, they were investigating a suspect for training “individuals to commit acts of violence against federal officers and employees.”

A hearing was held Sept. 4 and a ruling is pending. A spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security said it doesn’t comment “on the existence or status of specific ongoing investigations, nor on investigative methods.”

University Baptist Church’s interim pastor said the small congregation found the surveillance “very upsetting” — but also motivation to double down on their advocacy.

“We see the message of Jesus as compelling us to be where people are most vulnerable,” the Rev. Cody J. Sanders said.

For Kevin Friedl, an attorney with the Democracy Forward Foundation that’s representing the faith groups, the case is ultimately about offering sanctuary.

“For many, religion — being able to join together with others at their church or other house of worship — is an important and critical source of solace and comfort, in hard times, which these are,” he said. “This administration wants to deny them that.”

Protesters who interrupted Sunday worship seek dismissal of charges

The argument that churches are protected spaces and worshippers have rights against intrusion is also buttressing the case over the anti-immigration enforcement protest at Cities Church in Minnesota’s capital in January.

More than three dozen people — including former CNN journalist Don Lemon and prominent local activists — are facing federal civil rights charges after entering the Southern Baptist church where one pastor was also a leader in the local ICE field office.

During Sunday worship, some walked up to the pulpit, others loudly chanted “ICE out” and “Renee Good,” referring to the woman who was fatally shot on Jan. 7 by an ICE officer in Minneapolis.

In August, a slew of motions to dismiss the cases were filed and will be heard in late October. Some contend the charges amounted to “selective or vindictive prosecution,” and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance. They argue that the “administration’s claims that this prosecution is based on a desire to protect the right to practice religion is disproved by the extraordinary freedom it has granted ICE to violate the sanctity of churches,” according to court documents.

“They’re using these cases to try to get information on the whole resistance movement,” said Jordan Kushner, an attorney representing several defendants.

An attorney representing Cities Church countered that the issue at play is “an invasion during worship.”

“Nobody has the right to storm a church,” Doug Wardlow said, adding that the protest — and smaller, outdoors ones that continue to occur during worship times — “traumatically impacted the life of the church.”

How fallout from the surge impacts Minnesota congregations

Faith leaders across the Twin Cities say they’re still dealing with fallout from the surge, whether it’s lingering fear among migrants, tensions over government surveillance, or persistent financial assistance requests.

Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev. Mariah Furness Tollgaard, senior pastor at Hamline Church in St. Paul. She was briefly detained at an anti-deportations protest at the Minneapolis airport in January.

Several Protestant congregations that were outspoken in their anti-immigration-enforcement stances have increased their security measures.

While many remain committed to their advocacy, it’s taking a toll.

“The general vibe we get from leaders and congregations is just tired — there’s weariness more than anything,” said Nicholas Tangen of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America’s Minneapolis Area Synod.

More than three dozen people — including former CNN journalist Don Lemon and prominent local activists — are facing federal civil rights charges after entering the Southern Baptist church where one pastor was also a leader in the local ICE field office.

During Sunday worship, some walked up to the pulpit, others loudly chanted “ICE out” and “Renee Good,” referring to the woman who was fatally shot on Jan. 7 by an ICE officer in Minneapolis.

In August, a slew of motions to dismiss the cases were filed and will be heard in late October. Some contend the charges amounted to “selective or vindictive prosecution,” and cite the University Baptist Church surveillance. They argue that the “administration’s claims that this prosecution is based on a desire to protect the right to practice religion is disproved by the extraordinary freedom it has granted ICE to violate the sanctity of churches,” according to court documents.

“They’re using these cases to try to get information on the whole resistance movement,” said Jordan Kushner, an attorney representing several defendants.

An attorney representing Cities Church countered that the issue at play is “an invasion during worship.”

“Nobody has the right to storm a church,” Doug Wardlow said, adding that the protest — and smaller, outdoors ones that continue to occur during worship times — “traumatically impacted the life of the church.”

How fallout from the surge impacts Minnesota congregations

Faith leaders across the Twin Cities say they’re still dealing with fallout from the surge, whether it’s lingering fear among migrants, tensions over government surveillance, or persistent financial assistance requests.

Many congregants wonder who else was under federal surveillance, said the Rev. Mariah Furness Tollgaard, senior pastor at Hamline Church in St. Paul. She was briefly detained at an anti-deportations protest at the Minneapolis airport in January.

Several Protestant congregations that were outspoken in their anti-immigration-enforcement stances have increased their security measures.

While many remain committed to their advocacy, it’s taking a toll.

“The general vibe we get from leaders and congregations is just tired — there’s weariness more than anything,” said Nicholas Tangen of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America’s Minneapolis Area Synod.

text:
Political leaders in Maryland are calling for investigations into the conduct of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers as they clashed with protesters during a federal operation in a local community.

Residents of Frederick, a city about 50 miles north-west of Baltimore, are still shaken more than a week after ICE officers arrived in numerous vehicles and could be seen on video footage using batons on members of the public and driving their cars on to the sidewalk towards people.

At one point during the occurrences last Thursday and Friday, approaching the Labor Day weekend, protesters sat down in a line across the road linking arms, and also tried to block the doorway to a residential address as ICE personnel approached. Officers went inside the home but left without appearing to have made any arrests.

Federal officers arrived last Thursday, attracting grassroots activists who watch out in communities and warn people when ICE vehicles or agents are spotted. Protests quickly began and then grew.

Cesar Diaz, the president of Frederick city council, heard news of a confrontation and said he rushed to the scene. He said he had to step out of the way to avoid being hit by an ICE vehicle and saw a colleague, Katie Nash, the vice-president of the council, have to do the same.

“I had to move so I wouldn’t get hit, and the vice-president did too. There was no warning at all. The vehicle was one foot away from her,” Diaz told the Guardian earlier this week.

“We were there to show people that they had our support, and so the officers would see it too,” he said. Diaz estimated around 200 protesters gathered quite quickly, carrying signs and singing.

At that point, four or five ICE vehicles were in the area, he said, a number that grew to eight or nine by last Thursday evening.

Other witnesses reported that some residents were scared to leave their homes and go to work. Some required help to make sure their kids, who were coming off the school bus on Thursday afternoon, would be safe walking home.

Protesters can be heard on video footage of the demonstration chanting “Go home”, “Leave Frederick” and “Leave Maryland” at the gathered federal personnel.

ICE said in a statement to local media that they were in the area in “an effort to arrest a man” during a vehicle stop last Thursday morning but the man fled the scene, the Frederick News-Post reported. After that more ICE officers arrived and tensions escalated.

In the evening, ICE officers confronted protesters by driving their vehicles towards them, as seen in bystander footage, and videos shared by the Hagerstown Rapid Response activist group also showed officers approaching a home. It was then that some protestors tried to stop them from reaching the building by creating a human chain, and violence erupted.

Officers in tactical vests can be seen raising batons and hitting at least one protester about their body, while others are dragged and shoved.

“The level of violence went beyond what the situation called for. It was too much. It exceeded what is permitted,” Diaz said, saying that at least two people had to go to the hospital due to injuries. “There are many other options when dealing with unarmed people.”

He called for an investigation, as did Congresswoman April McClain Delaney, whose district includes the city, calling the incidents deeply concerning.

In a statement, Delaney said: “No family should be afraid to leave their home or feel unsafe in their own neighborhood … I am especially disturbed by reports that ICE agents used force against Frederick residents. These allegations demand immediate answers and a full, transparent investigation.”

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.

In an earlier statement to local network WBAL-TV, the agency declined to comment “for operation security” and “the safety” of their personnel.

DHS told the outlet that “criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US”.

Frederick authorities said they were not aware of any ICE or local arrests. Frederick police said personnel were dispatched to try to de-escalate the situation.

Police chief Kevin Meyer said his officers asked ICE whether they had an arrest warrant but that federal officers refused to discuss it.

Soolah Kemp, a member of Hagerstown Rapid Response, said she was recording video when an ICE car drove in her direction. “I heard the siren, I turned, and he was coming at me. He sped up, so I jumped out of the way. He had enough room on the street to not have an issue. He didn’t have to do what he did,” she said.

She has filed a report of the incident with the state attorney general’s office, she said.

US senator Chris Van Hollen has demanded an immediate investigation into events and said “[Donald] Trump’s ICE operations are not about making our country safer, they are about creating chaos and instilling fear in our communities”.

Tatiana Santos, of the activist network Indivisible Frederick Forward, said that the ICE conduct she witnessed was “unconscionable”.

“These people were so peaceful in the defense of their immigrant neighbors. They were simply standing and chanting things like: ‘We shall not be moved,’” she said.

She has asked Maryland governor Wes Moore to speak out and called for him to conduct an investigation.

Moore’s office said in a statement the governor was working with local leaders to “address what happened and make sure that there is real accountability”.

Lex McMenamin contributed reporting

text:
Immigration arrests in Oregon nearly doubled during the first seven months of 2026 compared to the same time period last year, state officials told members of the House Interim Committee on Human Services on Wednesday.

Federal authorities made 682 immigration arrests between January and July of this year compared to 349 during the same time period in 2025, said Jessica Ventura, director for the state’s Office of Immigrant and Refugee Advancement and the chair of the state’s Interagency Council for Immigrant and Refugee Coordination. The council, which presented the update to lawmakers Wednesday, was created by Gov. Tina Kotek in January in an effort to better coordinate the state’s response to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

There were only 119 immigration arrests in Oregon in 2024 before Trump retook office and his immigration dragnet began, Ventura said an analysis of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement data shows.

Rep. Ricki Ruiz, D-Gresham, expressed alarm at the figures, warning that they could foreshadow an even steeper increase in arrests this fall than Oregon saw at the end of last year. He suggested creating a state hotline that would allow immigrants to report arrests and access services through a single point of contact.

“That data could probably tell us that there’s going to be a big spike, probably a bigger spike than last year,” Ruiz said during Wednesday’s meeting. “How do we get our brains together to figure out, like, could there be … a resource number that anybody can call and they get linked to basically a 211 for this type of situation?”

Ventura said people can currently call the 211 community resource hotline to get some services, but must get connected to other assistance through different avenues, such as community organizations. People can call the Portland Immigrant Rights Coalition to report immigration arrests.

“But I’m not aware about a specific immigration-related resource hotline,” she told lawmakers. “I’m happy to take back that idea to our team.”

Kotek’s office didn’t answer questions about whether she would support the establishment of an immigration-related hotline or seek funding for it. But in a general statement, Kotek said “with dangerous, unpredictable policies from President Trump changing from day to day,” Oregon will continue to coordinate and work to “provide as much certainty as possible to our community partners and Oregon’s immigrant and refugee families.”

Rep. Lamar Wise, D-Portland, said immigration enforcement came up during a town hall he recently took part in with Attorney General Dan Rayfield.

“It was clear that our community wanted more,” he said. “My question to you all is, you know, what is needed to continue to strengthen and sustain this coordination effort and would also love to continue to just have open conversations about what defensive measures … we can be deploying to ensure that we’re keeping Oregonians safe.”

The interagency council is made up of leaders from 10 state agencies, including health, education, housing, transportation and human services. The group works to ensure Oregon’s response to immigration-related disruptions aligns with state law and that families can continue to access basic services without fear.

S7: Right. Sorry. Yeah. Says Garcia.

S8: I would say that the public perception of the INS was , um. No , uh , it was it was nonexistent for the vast majority of people in the United States. Yeah.

S7: Yeah. Compare that to Ice today. I don't think anyone would call the public perception of ice to be null or nonexistent. Right. It's top of mind right now , especially during this administration. So it kind of shows how in the last 25 years , just how the government thinks about immigration and how we think about immigration has totally changed.

S1: And , Andrew , for the military at that time , again , we're in this sort of like pre nine over 11 moment. You say nine over 11 took place after what had been a relatively kind of calm era with limited combat. Sure.

S6: Sure. You know , I mean , obviously coming out of Vietnam , Vietnam was a very bloody conflict and a very unpopular draft. Um , well , you know , in 1973 , they ended the draft , and we've been an all volunteer military ever since. There was , you know , some downsizing in the 70s. And , um , unless you were part of , like , uh , like some kind of special operations unit , um , there wasn't a whole lot of on the ground combat. You know , um , there was , you know , the invasion of Grenada. Uh , there was , uh , we were in Panama for a little bit.

S1: Very like short term actions. Right.

S6: And it wasn't until Desert Shield , Desert Storm that , uh , you know , we had an actual war. Um , but even that was a very short conflict. And , um , yeah , there was the , uh , operations , like in Somalia , obviously. Um , but there wasn't a whole lot of , uh , prolonged exposure to combat , prolonged , um , accounting of of casualties and everything like that. So , um , you could go , you know , you could spend a 20 year career in the military and never , never see combat. Never , never take place or never participate in a real world like kinetic operation. Um , which after nine over 11 wasn't the case. Yeah.

S1: Yeah. So , Gustavo. Now , that brings us to September 11th , 2001. What happens soon after at our borders?

S7: It was interesting to me to hear from folks who were on the ground like for this series. We talked to to the the acting port director in San Ysidro that day , and the supervisor , inspector , supervisor , she supervisor , people in the booths. And there was just this feeling of fear , anxiety and a little bit of guilt because like , this happened on our watch , right? For a good 5 or 6 month period , two of the 911 hijackers were living in Claremont , and then they crossed that border that they were working at. And it was this hypervigilance , um , you know , even today , there's always this balance when you're looking at the border. Right? We have to balance being safe with keeping it moving along. Right. We can't keep get the wait lines. But after nine over 11 , for those good three months , they had this policy of stop every car open every trunk , right. It took forever to cross. But that's kind of that was the mentality and that idea that that fear , anxiety , a little bit of guilt was felt throughout the federal government and that kind of created , you know , helped create this vision for DHS , the Department of Homeland Security. The very name implies some kind of threat and connects that threat to immigration. So that was the fundamental shift in immigration became a threat that needs to be managed in a way that it wasn't before. Um , and , uh , Garcia , that the professor I talked to explained it in a way like , like this used to be housed in the Department of Justice. Before then , it used to be housed in commerce , setting up this separate agency that is a law enforcement agency tasked and led by law enforcement professionals , means that your entire view of immigration is going to come through a law enforcement view. And a lot of the solutions to the problems you face are going to be law enforcement problem or I'm sorry. Law enforcement solutions. And that mentality alone has guided a lot of the policy decisions that we see today. So there's you can point a direct line between the aggressive enforcement we're seeing today and the decisions that were made post 911 , especially if you count the hundreds of billions in funding that this agency has gotten over the years as well.

S1: Andrew , you touched on this earlier , how , you know , maybe your expectation of joining the military before nine over 11 was quite different from what happened afterwards. You may never see combat. Obviously , that relative calm you spoke about ended soon after the attacks. Right.

S6: Right. And I think nobody was surprised. You know , whenever , whenever I joined the Navy , like the idea was that you're going to do something like we're going to do something. We didn't know that exactly what was going to happen , but something was going to happen like that was very clear from very early on. And , um. People like my age at the time , like a lot of the people that came into the service when I did , like , wanted to be part of that. Right. And , um , you know , uh , operations in Afghanistan were fairly limited in the early stages of that , uh , that conflict. It didn't get really bad over there until later. Um , but in 2003 , with the invasion of Iraq , is when that real ground war long , uh , kind of conflict started. And you could expect to , at least in the Navy , be on a , on a ship that maybe you go a couple times to the Middle East for operations , maybe you go to shore duty and then you go back to sea duty , and now you're going back to the Middle East for more operations , like you could rely on , you know , spending time in the pond over there , the Persian Gulf. Um , if you're on a especially in a West Coast carrier.

S1: So , like , more deployments , longer deployments.

S6: You know , I don't know the number because you would deploy , you know , pre nine over 11 , there was always carrier deployments. We maintained this global presence that the Navy does. Um , and you know the Marines deploy with their with the expeditionary unit to , you know , maintain their proficiency and be ready if combat starts. Um , what changed after nine over 11 was that these weren't just training , you know , deployments. These were deployments where you were going into to do what you trained to do. Mhm.

S1: Mhm. And many who served , you know , came from places like Camp Pendleton came in and around San Diego as well. Yes.

S6: Yes. So Camp Pendleton is home of one Marine Expeditionary Force. This is about a quarter of the Marine Corps. Um , you have the air element with the air wing. You have the infantry with the first Marine Division. You have supply. Um , you have everything with with one MEF. And these units , um , rotated to Iraq multiple times , Afghanistan multiple times. And , um , if you had a career as a marine , especially an infantry marine , if you stay in for 20 years , you can expect to see combat , you know , multiple times over , over that career.

S1: You know , for this story that you did. Um , looking back at nine over 11 , you spoke with one long serving marine , Hector Rivera , about his multiple tours. But one thing that , you know , he talked about was you spoke about a memorial dedicated to Marines and sailors killed in in the global war on terror.

S9: Those names that you see in the world. They are not statistics only. They were sons and daughters. Fathers. They were somebody special to their families.

S1: So , you know , I'm just wondering if you can reflect on a little bit what the lasting impact from the global war on terror has been for our nation's military members and veterans?

S6: Well , I think that it depends on how you it kind of depends on how you look at things , because , um , you know , Sergeant Major Rivera , when I asked him about that , he said it made it better. It made the Marines better because we went into combat multiple times. We knew what we were doing. We got better and better at it as we went. And because you have these senior. um , people like him who have seen multiple combat tours. Now they are training , you know , younger Marines today , those younger Marines are benefiting from from that experience. Right. Um , and so that's how he looks at having a career deploying multiple times to combat. But there's there's other issues , um , obviously , that come along with that. Um , we have a large disabled veteran population , 1.5 million veterans who served in the world's New York and Afghanistan have some kind of service connected disability that is , you know , that's like half of the disabled veterans that the VA serves. Um , you know , there's been obviously issues with with mental health and suicide. Um , you know , these folks in special operations especially , you know , seals , these these people were put into not just these big formation combat ground operations , but , you know , really dangerous , really precarious , um , operations multiple times over the years. So , you know , it really did do it. It just changed what your military career would look like. So if you were in the military between 2000 and 2021 , like , I don't know if somebody that joins the military in 2021 , if they're going to look back at things in 2040 , you know , they're not going to look back on on , I think multiple combat tours. I don't know if if the country has an appetite for for that again.

S1: Well , you know , here we are 20 years on now from this milestone. And I want to take a look maybe to the next 25 years. Just , Andrew , like you were kind of thinking about Gustavo , what comes to mind for you when it comes to the future of our borders and immigration?

S7: Yeah , I think that's really tough to say. Um , right. When you look into the future , I do think we're at a pivotal moment now where , you know , we've been building this massive infrastructure of enforcement in the last 25 years. Right. We've DHS has just grown and grown and grown with the technology of surveillance. The number of people , especially with this $260 billion funding that was approved by Congress last year. But the unpopularity of the agency , I mean , you just had a segment here before us right about this Ice detention , but by City College , um , it's giving everyone a moment of pause and reflection. Right. Is this the way we want to go , especially after last year with what happened in Minneapolis to US citizens killed by federal agents? There are people , even former DHS officials , who are who are saying , you know , maybe that approach of linking immigration to terrorism threats is a little bit outdated. Um , and I think it is kind of interesting. We have this moment where we know what this looks like. Taken to an extreme , we're experiencing it right now and is the problem. The executive that's taking it to the extreme , or is the problem the way that this agency is built and laid out , that allows somebody to take it to an extreme. And I think that's a really interesting conversation we're having right now.

S6: You know , when you asked about the impact of 9/11 on the military , you know , the that is also impacted , uh , DHS and law enforcement in general. You know , we've seen since the drawdown of these wars all kinds of surplus military equipment acquired by police departments. Um , you now have an agency , DHS , that acted like an occupying force , like we did in Baghdad , in Minneapolis. So , um , it did change that , that mindset.

S1: We'll have to leave it there. I want to thank you both for being here , and you're listening to KPBS roundtable. We'll be back. Thanks.

S10: Thanks.

S1: Welcome back to KPBS roundtable. I'm Andrew Bracken. On September 11th , 2001 , Rosina Alley was a teenager growing up in California's San Joaquin Valley. Soon after the attacks , her father instructed her to hide her Muslim identity out of a concern for her safety. Now , 25 years later , Rosina , a journalist out with a new book that traces our country's long history with Islamophobia. It's called Seasons of Fury for families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. Rosina , welcome to roundtable.

S11: Thank you so much for having me here.

S1: I'm wondering if you can start by just taking us back to that day , September 11th , 2001. What do you remember? Yeah.

S11: Yeah. So I was actually in I was a teenager and I was getting ready for school , and it was early in the morning , and all I remember was my parents just watching the news in the living room , looking completely petrified. and I had never seen them this shocked before , and I had never been to New York City , and I. I didn't really understand what had happened until later on that day. But it was until it wasn't until I got home that evening when my father sat me down and said , you know , if anyone asks , tell them that you're Hindu , don't tell them you're Muslim. And we were one of about 3 or 4 Muslim families in town. And the fear was palpable.

S1: And of course , we're having this conversation on the 25th anniversary of nine over 11. Reflecting back on that time. Now , what did the post 911 period mean for Muslim Americans?

S11: I think I didn't quite appreciate it until much later. You know , I , um , I remember actually going back to school a few weeks or even just a few days after nine over 11 , and one of my classmates actually asked the teacher if Muslims would be interned now and I. That was never a possibility to me until she said it. And it wasn't until I started reporting and researching that I realized how close that possibility had been , because one of the things that the government did was actually round up people , round up muslims , and started a registry of Muslims , and it really created a chilling effect. I mean , one of the big things that I kept hearing at home was the walls have ears , as in the government is probably listening. And I realized a lot of Muslim households across the country were saying the same thing. You know , don't don't talk about Osama bin laden at home. Don't talk about George W Bush , because someone might be listening.

S1: In the prologue of your book , Seasons of Fury , you write about this enduring legacy of nine over 11 for Muslim Americans. And I'm wondering if you could read a little bit of that. Read us a passage from that prologue. Yeah.

S11: Yeah. Thank you. Conversations about the post nine over 11 period tend to relegate the uncertainty that Muslims face to that was then , or it was a different time. But such demarcation is an illusion. There was no celebration to mark the end of the war on terror. No newspaper headline that declared the fight against Islamic fundamentalism over. There has also been little reckoning of what took place in the United States over the last several decades.

S1: I mean , there's so much in those words , you know , not only that , just lack of a defining end point that I think just resonates in a lot of ways. But you mentioned there this idea of of lack of reckoning. What would that reckoning look like for you? What would you like to see?

S11: I think first and foremost is actually a acknowledgment of the lives that had been completely destroyed in the years after nine over 11 , so many Muslim families were forced to leave the United States , or they voluntarily departed because they were so afraid , or they were deported , even though they had not been guilty of anything. And there really hasn't been , and I should say , a lot of people were actually put in jail for years without any charge. And there really hasn't been a nationwide apology for it , nor much recognition or narrative about it. Um , I think the second thing that I would love to see is actually an acknowledgement that Muslims were victims on nine over 112 , in the sense that this is our country. And we were also attacked. And one of the difficulties about this period is not having been able to grieve the way that the rest of the country did , because we were always put under this lens of suspicion. And even now , as we see Mayor Zoran Mamdani in New York , has been dealing with a lot of criticism for even wanting to attend the memorial ceremony. Right.

S1: Right. I think yeah , absolutely. Um , now , you know , on your book , I think this was something of a bit of a surprise to you is , is , you know , Islamophobia obviously did not begin with nine over 11. And your book kind of takes us far before that time. Why did you feel that was important to , you know , explore that history?

S11: Well , one of the defining features of Islamophobia has been that this consideration of Muslims as a national security threat. And I wanted to understand , when did we actually start thinking of Muslims with suspicion? And I realized as I dig in that it actually didn't start at nine over 11. But the government has been considering Muslim communities with an eye of suspicion for decades. Actually , they have been monitoring and surveilling them even since starting in the late 60s and early 70s. And I was quite shocked by this history.

S1: And your book , it follows four Muslim American families across several decades. What common threads connect their stories? Yeah.

S11: Yeah. One of the reasons I actually wanted to follow these four families was because I wanted to show one that there is such diversity among Muslim Americans. They are not diverse just in terms of race , but or ethnicity , but also in their political beliefs , in their political motivations , even in their religious beliefs , how spiritual they are , even in their party. Right. I have one character who is so progressive and so democratic , and another character who is very staunchly Republican and supported Bush's war against terror. And ultimately , the thing , the threat that combines all of them is that they were somehow all impacted by anti-Muslim sentiment in this country , and it manifested in different ways. You know , one was surveilled , another was entrapped and convicted. Another was terrorized by their neighbor for many , many years and another had his community turn against him.

S1: I'm wondering , you know , here on roundtable , we talk with reporters , we talk with storytellers. And I just wondering what role you feel the mainstream media journalism has played in the rise of anti-Muslim sentiment post nine over 11?

S11: Yeah , I have to say , you know , I'm I'm a journalist myself , and I have such deep respect for my colleagues , I really do. And certainly after nine over 11 , there was so much incredible coverage. But one of the things that media as a whole did was , you know , before nine over 11 , there were just we didn't know that much about Islam. A lot of Americans hardly knew any Muslim. They hardly knew about their religion. Even law enforcement and government officials didn't really know much about the religion. And so it seemed natural after nine over 11 to try to explain the religion. And so we had any like media outlets from the Guardian to MTV to CNN publishing explainers about Islam. But the problem with that was , was that we ended up emphasizing the religion rather than the political aspects of this war. Right? Because we were launching a war on terror , that enemy was so broadly defined that the media , rather than confine our conversations or analyses to al-Qaida , for example , or Iraq and Afghanistan. We started really analyzing what is this religion , what does it mean? And I think one of the issues was that or the other issue is that journalists really didn't push back enough on Bush's war on terror , which was a policy decision. You know , he started he launched this war on terror. And a lot of journalists , reputable journalists , went along with that without really pushing back on what it meant and what the parameters of , of success would be to this war. Absolutely.

S1: Absolutely. And it was , um , overwhelmingly popular , at least in the , you know , those early years , right? I mean , what about today? I mean , how do you see the , you know , the media has it improved? You know what what how do you reflect on it back now? Yeah.

S11: Yeah. I mean , I think it's improved remarkably. I do think that there is a lot more appetite for pushing back and challenging government , government policies , government rhetoric , government narrative. But when it comes to covering Islamophobia , I still feel like there is a lot to be done. One is that we still don't have a good definition or understanding with what we mean by terrorism. You know , everything can be called a terrorist. And unfortunately , we see a lot of people in the Republican Party and right wing folks doing that to a lot of Democrats and anti-choice activists even. Um , but the other problem is , is that when there is anti-Muslim rhetoric peddled by policymakers. It's really pushed back upon from their colleagues or media. And even going back to the example of Zoran Mamdani , I noticed that a lot of journalists were asking him how he felt about whether he should attend the memorial service or not. Rather than asking the critics why the mayor of New York City should not attend the memorial service , and I think we need to flip the calculus a bit and really be pushing back and challenging this anti-Muslim rhetoric.

S1: I mean , it does strike me , you know , 25 years ago you were living in California , but now you're in New York. You've mentioned New York City. Mayor Mamdani is the first Muslim mayor of New York City. Um , I'm just wondering what's coming up for you this year on nine over 11 , actually being in New York.

S11: Yeah , I really appreciate that question , because I really have struggled with feeling like I don't know how to grieve today , because so much of my memory of that day and what has come after , has been shaped by the fear of being attacked by neighbours , by colleagues or by the government. And I can't help but think of not just the tragedy of today , but the tragedy of the days after when so many people did die in the days and weeks after nine over 11. And so I think , you know , I can't help but reflect that this was such a heavy day for so many people. And I , I feel so , um , I still struggle with how to remember and grieve today.

S1: Well , I just want to say thanks for , you know , taking time today for actually speaking with us and sharing some of those , those thoughts with us. I've been speaking with Rosina Ali. She's an investigative journalist and author of the book Seasons of Fury for families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. And we'll have a link to that on our website , KPBS. Rosina , thank you so much for being here today.

S11: Thank you so much for having me.

text:
No, ICE agents are legally not allowed at voting sites this November — and Denver wants to make sure the question isn’t even in the air.

The City and County of Denver joined civil rights organizations, the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause and UnidosUS in a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 10 after the Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin allegedly clarified the department’s “Polling Place Policy” on Sept. 1, according to the lawsuit.

The policy allegedly authorizes armed ICE officers to go to polling places in the November midterm elections to respond to “threats,” serve warrants and conduct civil immigration arrests.

Surprise: that isn’t legal. In fact, it’s directly against 18 U.S.C. § 592, which was enacted in 1865 and blatantly says that members of the Army, Navy, civil, military or naval service of the United States will be fined or imprisoned if they “order, bring, keep, or have any troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Open and shut, right? Not at all. In fact, during New York’s primaries back in June, ICE agents entered a polling location because they believed Paigelynne Gonyea, a poll worker, was “violating federal law,” according to reporting by Spectrum News.

At the beginning of the month, Mullin told the media that “the only reason why we would be at polling places, if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.” He later added: “If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be.”

ICE has made arresting illegal immigrants (and sometimes completely legal citizens) its crusade since Trump retook office in 2025. He even called a mass deportation plan Operation Aurora after the media frenzy that was the Tren de Aragua Venezuelan gang “taking over” the entire city. But noncitizens aren’t allowed to vote and haven’t been able to in any of the 50 states since 1924. In fact, under Bill Clinton’s administration in 1996, Congress added criminal penalties for noncitizens who even attempt to register to vote.

So, technically, there shouldn’t be anyone for ICE to arrest at the polls, anyway.

The lawsuit claims the idea is a scare tactic, potentially “threatening” the election, due to the 170 legal citizens who had been arrested by ICE in the first nine months of Trump’s administration and multiple citizens who have been shot and killed while protesting ICE activity.

“The right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy and to being an American,” Mayor Mike Johnston said in a press release. “Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes. We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it.”

It’s unclear whether Denver polling centers were planned to be explicitly targeted by ICE, but polls will be busy, with around 90% of voters who cast a mail ballot in Denver returning their ballot to one of the drop boxes throughout the city, according to the lawsuit.

A spokesperson from DHS tells Westword “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”

“Our right to vote is powerful and enshrined in the U.S. Constitution and U.S. Code,” Denver Clerk and Recorder Paul López said. “Denver is the vanguard of democracy, and with cast-iron certainty we will protect our free and fair elections from any and all attempts at federal intimidation and intrusion.”

All in all, the lawsuit is asking DHS to drop the policy and only enter polling areas if it is to “repel armed enemies.”

text:
She was seen in her round glasses near the DBK4 warehouse in the quiet Queens neighborhood of Maspeth, alongside Amazon workers frustrated with the multinational that dominates e-commerce in the United States. She was seen at a popular Starbucks in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn, with baristas disappointed by the world’s largest coffee chain. She was also seen at a strike in Harlem alongside members of the Neighborhood Defender Service union. On each of those occasions, working people were asking for the same thing workers throughout history have demanded from their bosses: decent working conditions and a livable wage.

Claire Valdez can relate. She herself has worked at Taco Bell, Pizza Hut and the supermarket chain Trader Joe’s and, should she win a seat in Congress, she hopes to achieve two essential goals: making it easier for workers to unionize and ensuring that the federal minimum wage in the United States is no longer stuck at $7.25 an hour, where it has remained since 2009, when it was increased by 75 cents.

Valdez is a politician today because she was first, and for a long time, a worker. She has been employed since the age of 14 and is someone who, as she puts it, has had to “clock in and do oftentimes difficult or exhausting labor.” But her understanding of the country around her first took shape in Lubbock, a conservative enclave in West Texas, where she grew up with Democratic parents in a world that already followed a different order. “I’m a millennial, so I grew up in the wake of the September 11 attacks and the beginning of the war on terror, the invasion of Afghanistan and Iraq. Witnessing our country murder a million people overseas in the name of safety for the United States was something that really radicalized me at a very early age.”

By the age of 25, in 2015, she had become a visual artist and moved to New York to work at a small museum in Queens. “The work was rewarding, but really very hard. I worked a lot, at night and on weekends; there was a lot of unpaid overtime,” she says. It was also difficult to develop her own artistic practice at the same time, so she left the position and took another one in Columbia University’s visual arts department. That job changed the course of her life. At the time, she had no idea that, a few years later, as a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), she would win the Democratic primary to represent New York’s 7th Congressional District.

Joining Columbia’s UAW Local 2110, an affiliate of the United Auto Workers (UAW), one of the country’s most important labor unions, proved decisive. Valdez became increasingly involved, and the fight for workers gradually eclipsed her artistic practice. Even so, when she thinks about it, there is much in common between being an artist and being a politician. “You have to rely on other people; you have to be creative, problem-solve. You’re building something collaboratively with others. The union gave me the same joy and purpose that art did.” Among the priorities she plans to pursue in Congress is advancing the PRO Act, legislation designed to make it easier to form unions, hold employers accountable and restore dignity to workers.

Question. Championing workers’ rights is something that set you apart from the other candidates in New York’s Democratic primary. Why has it been such a central part of your political life?

Answer. Organizing with my co-workers was really important because being part of the union gave me a living wage, time off the job, and a sense of purpose that I’d never had before. I always expected that hours would be long, wages would be low, protections would be few and far between. The union changed my relationship to not just my bosses and my work, but to my co-workers. It taught me to see them also as very politically powerful people who deserve excellent working conditions and good wages. We’ve all had shitty jobs and we’ve all had bad bosses, but very few people have had the experience of being transformed by their union. What’s so important to me about being in Congress, and earlier in the State Assembly, is getting as many people as possible to be able to organize, change their lives and recognize their power.

Q. You in particular, and the DSA more broadly, speak about empowering the working class, which has sparked a debate about where the working class begins and ends in the United States. What is your view?

A. I believe the working class is defined by control. Do you have control over what you do at your job? Do you have control over your schedule? Your hours and your wages? For most people, the answer is no. That can include janitors, clerical workers like I was at Columbia University, and even software engineers. I think the category can be very broad because what we’re talking about is how much power you have to dictate the conditions of your workplace and your life. The working class needs to be as broad a category as possible because it’s going to take millions and millions of people organizing together to win the world that we deserve. The more that we can relate to one another across these differences that have been imposed on us by bosses, the more power that we’ll have.

Q. Socialists have recently won some major electoral victories in the United States, though they also draw strong opposition from other sectors. What is your vision for making this a better country?

A. For me, democratic socialism is about expanding democracy — making sure people can organize in their workplaces, their neighborhoods and their apartment buildings, and be political actors in their own lives. It’s about universal programs like universal childcare, free public education and higher education, universal healthcare, expanding rent stabilization and rent control, and making sure people can afford to live their lives and have real dignity.

Our goal, and certainly my goal as someone going to Congress as a democratic socialist, is to prove we can govern effectively and deliver for the working class. Every time we win a race, we’re demonstrating that there is a constituency for democratic socialism. Polling nationally shows that people are moving on this subject; they’re more willing to identify as democratic socialists and less afraid of the term. I think that’s partly due to the work Mayor Zohran Mamdani has done to successfully run the city for the past eight and a half months,

Q. This resurgence of the left has also come as a response to the political system and the administration. But if a campaign and an election like Zohran Mamdani’s had not happened, would we still have seen this surge?

A. It’s hard to imagine this political moment without last year’s successes. Zohran’s victory was really momentous for the movement. It gave us a roadmap for 2026, when we were deciding where to run, which districts might be good places to challenge incumbents or where open seats might be advantageous for us. He’s done a pretty good job as mayor, effectively communicating and rolling out very popular programs early in his tenure. His bus network improvements to make buses faster, universal childcare… those things are incredibly popular and show people that Democratic Socialists can govern well. So I think his success has paved the way for us to take bigger swings to take on bigger challenges.

Q. You were arrested at 26 Federal Plaza, the immigration court building where so many migrants have been detained recently, and one of your battles is to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). How do you plan to make that possible?

A. With news of a new federal investment in electric shock gloves that ICE agents will be deployed with, it’s clear that until we end this agency, it will just continue to be expanded, to be militarized, to be funded, and there will be no accountability until it’s done away with. Knowing that our taxes are funding this agency instead of universal healthcare or public infrastructure investment is really despicable. There are things we can do to create more oversight and accountability for this agency, but ultimately it just shouldn’t exist.

Q. So if the Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives, do you think there will be a real opportunity to make progress on your priorities, such as ICE and workers’ rights?

A. I don’t think ICE will be abolished under this administration, but we have to plan for what life is going to look like after the Trump administration is done in a couple of years and be ready to do as much as we can to transform America’s life. That also includes passing the PRO Act to make it easier for people to organize in their workplaces and raising the minimum wage. In the grand scheme of defending our democracy against rising fascism and authoritarianism, making sure that we have a really thriving labor movement is paramount. We must push for a humane, welcoming immigration policy. If we are going to address the root causes of migration, we need to start by understanding our foreign policy and the things we’ve done for many years to destabilize other countries.

Q. That was clear in your campaign and in those of many other socialists when you called for an end to the genocide in Gaza, an issue many avoid discussing or distance themselves from, but one that you turned into a major front in your campaigns...

A. Palestine was an important part of our campaign because it repeatedly came up when we were door-knocking. When we spoke with people at their homes, they wanted to talk about Palestine. Nearly three years of genocide is hard to reconcile, and it’s painful to know our taxes are funding the bombing of refugee camps and upholding an apartheid state. Since this genocide began and unfolded under a Democratic president, Joe Biden, the Democrats missed an opportunity to stop the worst of this atrocity while in power. We want to see that change. I also think people want to see real moral leadership. We saw a lot of that during Mamdani’s mayoral race. Palestine wasn’t the central issue — affordability was — but people who had been disengaged from politics or hadn’t voted in 2024 and were outraged by the genocide in Gaza saw his consistency on this issue and came back into politics. We saw the highest voter turnout the city has seen in decades, and I think that’s what people are hungry for right now.

text:
Six employees of GLC Property Maintenance in Highland Township, Michigan, were stopped by nine U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles on their way to work Thursday morning, in what the landscaping company's owner believes was a targeted raid.

The company says all six employees are legally working in the U.S. on H-2B visas. Video taken by one of the workers and obtained by CBS News Detroit shows the encounter with federal agents.

"In the meantime, give me the phone, put the phone down," an ICE agent said in the video.

Eventually, the agents let the workers go after reviewing their official paperwork, but the landscaping company says it is now frustrated and trying to figure out why it was stopped in the first place.

Tyler Ralko, whose parents started the company 25 years ago, posted a TikTok on Friday that has received hundreds of thousands of views, in which he describes what happened and what he's doing to support the employees.

"They're some of the hardest working people I've ever met. They pay their taxes like anybody else," Ralko told CBS Detroit.

He has since contacted an immigration attorney and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin's office.

"Senator Slotkin's office has been super helpful today. We'll see if that leads to anything, but I just think our employees deserve, you know, some clarity on why they deserved that," said Ralko.

Ralko says he also reached out to ICE about why they would stop the workers, but he says he hasn't heard back. CBS News Detroit reached out to ICE and has not received a response.

"I think if you're going to ask people to do things the right way, then when they do them the right way, they shouldn't be treated disrespectfully. Anybody should be treated respectfully," Ralko said.

Ralko also tells CBS News Detroit that other landscaping businesses in the area have reached out to him, saying this story is a good reminder for all H-2B visa employees to keep their paperwork on hand at all times.
