text:
“I’m taking this risk because I know we have to fight hard to make changes that we need, to make changes that we deserve,” said Eustaquio Orozco Verdusco, a Minnesota labor organizer who was abducted by ICE on January 9 during Operation Metro Surge. He was giving testimony at the Minnesota Truth Council on August 21, one of numerous people speaking about the ordeals they went through as a result of the federal crackdown.

On March 25, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz issued an executive order creating the “Governor’s Council to Record the Truth of Operation Metro Surge and Operation PARRIS,” also known as the Minnesota Truth Council. The goal of the Truth Council is to produce a historical record of experiences of Operation Metro Surge that will include a report with findings and recommendations for policymakers. Orozco Verdusco gave his testimony to the Truth Council at an event hosted by the Advocates for Human Rights, a nonprofit organization located in Minnesota that has been collecting stories since mid-May.

Orozco Verdusco said that when he first learned about Operation Metro Surge, he didn’t leave his house for more than 20 days. “I left because I had a work meeting. I was followed just a few blocks from our home. They followed me for about eight miles before pulling me over and arresting me,” said Orozco Verdusco.

He says the next day they were flown to Texas. “After 72 hours we were told we could talk to our families which didn’t happen. Three or four days later we had the opportunity to talk to them for three minutes. Only three minutes,” he said. Three weeks later, they were moved to New Mexico. “During that move, we were given no food, no drinks, all day and night,” he continued. “They stopped at a gas station. They got food, they got drinks, they ate and drank in front of us. They said when we arrived we would be given food and drinks. Well it was not that way. It wasn’t until the next morning that we could have breakfast. Finally we could call our families and talk for a little bit longer. When I talked to my family they told me my lawyer had presented a habeas corpus which had been denied. Every time I had an opportunity to talk to my family, they were telling me stories about people, organizations, communities, supporting me.”

Orozco Verdusco was released in June after being in detention for almost six months. In May, a federal judge ordered that anyone who was in the process of obtaining a T or U visa should be taken out of detention. A T or U visa enables immigrants who are victims of trafficking to remain in the U.S. for a period of time and grants them protections. Because Orozco Verdusco and his wife are in the process of getting a T visa, he was released. “This is a bad moment we are living in, but it’s going to be better because of the people that live here,” he said. “I’m thankful to all those who prayed for me to come back, to join my family again.”

The event where Orozco Verdusco spoke took place at the first ever Convergence for Democracy at the Minneapolis Convention Center in downtown Minneapolis, Minn. The Convergence, hosted by Tending the Soil and co-sponsored by May Day Strong and Freedom Trainers, served as a national gathering for labor, community, faith, and legal advocates devoted to defending democracy in a moment of increasing authoritarianism and fascism. Speakers iterated that defending democracy means defending each other. The gathering was full of learning and trading resistance stories, and the opposition and resistance to Operation Metro Surge was highlighted in many of those stories.

Six more people testified to the Truth Council at the Convergence, including Christin Crabtree, a grassroots community organizer and Minneapolis resident and parent who cofounded Minneapolis Families for Public Schools. She gave testimony about the day ICE swarmed upon Roosevelt High School in South Minneapolis on January 7, which was also the day ICE shot and killed Renee Good.

Crabtree says that she was at work the day that Renee Good was killed, and she had not planned to be at school dismissal, but showed up anyways. As students were exiting, a convoy of SUVs stopped in front of the main entrance of the school. “I ran faster than I ever had in my life,” said Crabtree. “I saw masked men with giant guns and in my mind visualized what had happened to Renee Good just hours before. Agents tackled our educators, aimed guns at our kids, and used chemical agents on our community, on our kids who were just trying to go home. I was mere inches from Greg Bovino. I remember the sound of a gun being cocked.”

Crabtree referenced the detention of Quentin Williams, an assistant teacher at Roosevelt who is now pursuing a lawsuit against the federal government after being tackled by agents. “He was a Black man being attacked by militarized police as high school students bore witness,” said Crabtree. “I felt echoes of 2020.”

Gabby Benavente Hobart is an educator at a high school in North Minneapolis working with Spanish-speaking students who are learning English and math. After the 2024 election, educators organized meetings to develop safety protocols for what to do if ICE showed up at school. “Still this preparation would not prepare us for the scale of the horror that was about to unfold,” said Benavente Hobart in her testimony to the Truth Council. “I am deeply grateful to my fellow educators at my side and in my union as well as community members in all walks of life.”

She recalled how one student apologized for having to log out of Zoom because ICE was in the street nearby. She shared how she consoled a mother whose son and husband were detained and separated by ICE. “To this day I think of him, how he was denied the joy of walking alongside classmates during graduation.”

Matt Allen is a local hip hop artist who goes by Nur-D. He gave testimony about his ICE detention after attending a protest after Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti.

“I watched on my phone as Alex Pretti was murdered in cold blood,” Allen said. “When I went out to have my voice be heard, I was attacked violently from behind by more than half a dozen men with guns who threw me to the street. They beat my body, they sprayed acid in my face, they told me I was being arrested for assaulting an officer, a charge I have yet to see.”

Allen said agents put him in a vehicle and he was released later. “We are living the worst case scenario,” he said. “What are you willing to do to stop it? They are killing people. And they will continue to capture and kill people not because a law says they can, but because they want to.”

Garrison Gibson Brown gave testimony about his arrest and time in ICE detention. Gibson Brown said he was born in Liberia, that he has resided in the U.S. since four years old, and that he has been checking in with ICE regularly since 2009. He said on January 11, his family was woken up by ICE agents who had entered his house without a warrant and broke down the front door. The agents cuffed him in front of his family.

“After being at Whipple for a couple hours, the next morning they put some of us on a plane and sent us to Texas,” said Gibson Brown. “It was no better in Texas than it was at Whipple. The cells were dirty, the [correctional officers] they talk to you like you’re not human.”

On the day ICE agents shot and killed Renee Good, civil rights attorney Nicole Salonek Schladt was at Powderhorn Park bringing her child to therapy when she saw three large SUVs in the parking lot surrounded by masked agents. She approached the vehicles and noticed three teens huddled in the back seats. “They were all my children at that moment,” she said.

After an ICE agent told her to get out of the way, she began walking alongside the vehicle from a distance when another agent approached her from behind. “A gun appeared less than 12 inches from my face. I had no time to react, no time to panic,” she said. “The agent shot me in the face at point blank rage with what I learned were two projectile pepper balls. Everything went black. When I came to, lying in the snow, I could hardly breathe, I could hardly think.”

She vomited, removed all of her clothes, and was frothing at the mouth. “A park employee ushered me out of the cold into the rec center, a street medic emerged from literally nowhere and began flushing my eyes, a neighbor brought me a sheet and held it around my naked body,” she said. Her child’s therapist did breathing exercises and several people offered to share video recordings of the incident. It was then that they received news about Good’s killing.

“Another queer white woman, a mother like me, was dead, and I by the grace of God or something was not,” she said. Although she was alive, she experienced the impact of being shot by pepper balls, and was later diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury and cervical radiculopath that gave her nerve pain throughout her arms and hands. “My nail beds and scalp blistered,” she said. “I learned intimately why pepper ball projectiles are prohibited as chemical weapons in international armed conflict.”

Benjamin gave testimony about his father who was detained and deported during Operation Metro Surge. He says he grew up in Honduras learning about movements for equality in the U.S. He says his father was often working with Fe y Justicia, a nonprofit in central Minnesota that provides training and clinics for community members. On January 10, Benjamin says his father was driving when he was pulled over and his seatbelt was cut and he was abducted by masked men. After being detained, he was moved to Texas where his attorney had no jurisdiction, and then they moved him to New Mexico. “During the 43 days my dad spent in detention he tried to stay sane, he held back his tears because he did not want us to worry,” he says.

Eventually, his father was deported to Honduras. “When someone comes from a country where access to healthcare, freedom of speech is limited, I cannot blame my dad for wanting something different,” he said. “I’m not here to pretend my dad did not overstay his visa. I’m here to tell you that breaking an immigration rule should not take someone’s humanity away. Behind every case number, there is a person and behind them is a family loving them and waiting for them to be treated as a human being.”

Formed in 2018, Tending the Soil is an alignment of nonprofits and labor organizations in the Twin Cities that includes CTUL, Inquilinxs Unidxs por Justicia/Renters United for Justice, New Justice Project, SEIU Local 26, and Unidos MN. Cat Salonek Schladt, executive director of Tending the Soil, said that the goal of the conference was to build the national movement to resist authoritarianism. “We sit in the reality that the government is fueled by corporate greed that is killing everything in this young country,” she said in the opening plenary.

Ricardo Levins Morales, visual artist, organizer, and author based in Minneapolis, whose work inspired the name Tending the Soil, spoke during the closing plenary at the Convergence. “What we live under is a system for whom the basic hardline non-negotiable is the permanence of a permanent underclass. It cannot survive without that,” said Levins Morales. “Waves of movement ebb and flow, but they can still be part of a rising tide. People can often get really scared when a movement ebbs away and think, ‘oh it’s over now,’ when it could sometimes only be the first wave of a rising tide that will continue to climb. That’s what we’ve been experiencing.”

Amie Stager is the Associate Editor for Workday Magazine.

It laid the groundwork for what exists now,” says Hiroshi Motomura, a UCLA law professor and author of several books on immigration in the United States.

text:
The September 11, 2001 attacks brought about major social, political, and judicial changes in the United States. It was an unprecedented event and the enormous impact and trauma it caused forced a thorough examination of how the United States operated to prevent terrorism and to ensure a similar tragedy would not happen again. One of the most significant changes was the creation of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in March 2003, which followed congressional investigations into the attacks that lasted two years.

Something had failed in the system. The terrorists had obtained visas to enter the country and, ultimately, had easily evaded airport passport control. “The failure revealed by the September 11 attacks was that those hijackers were not prevented from entering the country and, subsequently, boarding the planes,” says Doris Meissner, who was commissioner of the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) between 1993 and 2000 during Democratic President Bill Clinton’s administration. Responsibility for issuing visas lay with consular officers under the State Department, but entry into the country was permitted by immigration inspectors.

The fact that the terrorists were foreign nationals changed immigration priorities. U.S. immigration control became directly linked to national security and the fight against terrorism. As a result, in the following decade, deportations rose to 2.3 million people compared with 1.6 million expelled in the previous 10 years.

Meissner left her post at the INS months before the attacks occurred. While she led it, the INS was part of the Justice Department and was responsible for enforcing immigration laws, patrolling the border, and processing applications for legal status and citizenship. After 9/11, the INS disappeared and its functions were split into three agencies: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), responsible for granting visas and residence permits; Customs and Border Protection (CBP); and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“There is now far less coordination and coherence in immigration policy — now that these areas have been separated — compared with the era when they depended on a single commissioner; that person could weigh options to determine the best allocation of resources and set priorities that balanced, for example, legal immigration against control and law enforcement functions. From a bureaucratic standpoint, this is much harder to achieve today because the work is split into three separate parts within the Department of Homeland Security,” Meissner says.

The split into three agencies meant separate budgets. In an administration like Donald Trump’s, in which the campaign against immigration dominates the presidential agenda, ICE, which is responsible for detentions and deportations, has seen its available funds surge to unprecedented levels, larger than the military budgets of most countries in the world. “The structural change allowed a massive increase in funding for ICE and created an independent law-enforcement apparatus that did not exist before. It laid the groundwork for what exists now,” says Hiroshi Motomura, a UCLA law professor and author of several books on immigration in the United States.

Thanks to funds approved in 2025 in the budget bill (the Big Beautiful Bill), which provided $170 billion, and to this year’s Reconciliation Act, which supplied an additional $70 billion for the immigration agenda, ICE has been able to multiply the number of agents, open new detention centers, forge partnerships and acquire intelligence programs and equipment to carry out Trump’s goal of effecting the largest deportation in history. “In law-enforcement terms we now have levels of resources that post-9/11-era lawmakers would never have imagined,” says Meissner, who is currently director of the migration policy program at the Migration Policy Institute (MPI).

That enormous injection of money has also been accompanied by what has been perceived as a license for ICE to operate with impunity. The DHS has so far defended the actions of its immigration agents in the most controversial cases. The department has supported the officials who killed U.S. citizens Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January of this year, and also those responsible for the deaths of Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Colombian Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both of which occurred in July. “They certainly enjoy immunity and, under the second Trump administration, they have been empowered to carry out law-enforcement activities in ways that are incompatible with the professional standards established for police,” Meissner contends.

By dividing the INS’s functions into agencies, policing operations were strengthened. “The real problem lies in the separation of ICE and CBP, on the one hand, and USCIS — that is, the service-provision branch — on the other. I believe this structure has allowed both ICE and CBP to expand further, while insufficient funding for USCIS has created an imbalance and led to a prioritization of national security to an extent that, in my view, is excessive,” Motomura says.

Applications to adjust immigration status and apply for permanent residency are piling up at USCIS, where cases accumulate for years without resolution.

Biometric control

In the 25 years since 9/11, the United States has not suffered another terrorist attack of that magnitude. The country implemented measures such as biometrics and interactive databases, and the resources devoted to travel management and cooperation, both internationally and among U.S. agencies themselves, have proven effective. However, in the last 18 months the current administration has used national security to detain and deport migrants it has accused of terrorism without providing evidence. The government has used outdated laws, such as the 1798 Alien Enemies Act, which was only applied in wartime cases, to deport Salvadoran and Venezuelan migrants without due process and has activated the Foreign Terrorist Removal Court, created 30 years ago but never operational.

Moreover, it has intimidated people into self-deportation and revoked visa approvals, making it very difficult to enter the United States and deterring the arrival of students and workers who contribute benefits to the country — certainly not the kind of foreigners Congress had in mind when creating the DHS. “We are a country that is safer from international terrorism. Today, security threats in the United States come from within the country, not from abroad; they stem from internal tensions, gun violence and polarized public opinion. These are, therefore, different and novel challenges,” Meissner says.

text:
Immigrant-advocacy group We Are CASA and four Maryland residents sued the Department of Homeland Security to force it to stop what the complaint calls an “arrest first, ask questions later” policy by immigration enforcement officers.

The lawsuit, filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland, alleges that DHS agents are using warrantless arrests to meet quotas. It seeks a preliminary injunction to halt the practice while the litigation plays out.

The plaintiffs say the manner in which the tactic has been employed in Maryland is “particularly disturbing.”

“Each morning, as community members drive to work and take their children to school, masked agents in unmarked cars stalk them like prey, identify drivers they perceive to be Brown or Black immigrants, and stop their vehicles,” the plaintiffs said in their memorandum supporting a preliminary injunction.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in private, unmarked vehicles are boxing cars in, smashing car windows, and drawing their weapons to make the unlawful arrests, they wrote.

“They arrest everyone in the vicinity, regardless of who they intended to stop, without probable cause, and in many cases without asking any questions at all,” the plaintiffs said.

Immigration arrests generally require a warrant. In the absence of a warrant, an agent must have reason to believe the person is violating immigration laws and is likely to escape before a warrant can be issued.

The complaint cites a January 28 memo from then-acting ICE Director Todd Lyons that acknowledged the law requires probable cause of escape risk but, according to the plaintiffs, gives “disproportionate weight to an individual’s theoretical ability to flee in a vehicle and entirely fails to address community ties.”

The plaintiffs have also filed a motion to certify a class comprising anyone who, since January 20, 2025, has been or will be “arrested in the District of Maryland for alleged immigration violations without a warrant and without a pre-arrest individualized assessment of probable cause that the person poses an escape risk.”

They claim the class comprises thousands of individuals, including people being held in immigration detention facilities.

DHS defended its practices in an emailed response to a request for comment.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the email said. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

DHS said the Supreme Court “has already vindicated us on these practices,” an apparent reference to the high court’s conservative majority’s Sept. 7 move to stay an order from a California federal court that had prohibited ICE agents from questioning and detaining people based solely on their race, ethnicity, language, occupation or location.

The plaintiffs are represented by Crowell & Moring LLP, We Are CASA, Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll LLP, Amica Center for Immigration Rights, the ACLU of Maryland, and National Immigration Project of the National Lawyers Guild.

text:
Trump’s mass deportation agenda is a nightmare. Some people - including me - warned about this when mass deportations were just a gleam in Trump’s eye (and a major feature of Project 2025).

Two years later, the nightmare has come true. We’ve witnessed U.S. citizens and targeted immigrants die at the hands of ICE and Border Patrol - whether on our streets or in ICE custody. We’ve had hundreds of immigration agents deployed at major U.S. cities and airports, stoking fear and often abusing their power. And the Trump administration is drastically expanding ICE detention centers across the country, holding immigrants in inhumane conditions.

What’s making this all possible is the public money - our hard-earned tax dollars - being funneled into the mass deportation and detention machine. Under the Trump administration, Congress and federal agencies have already committed a total of $269 billion in federal funds to immigration enforcement from FY 2025 through FY 2029. This amount comes from two GOP-backed funding bills that redirected enormous funds from public services to mass deportation, plus the annual baseline budgets of ICE and CBP, as well as funding to other federal agencies like the Department of Defense helping to implement this dangerous agenda.

The beacon of hope in the midst of this nightmare is the increase in movement organizing to protect immigrant communities from the administration’s attacks. I remain steadfast and hopeful - despite these terrifying times - because of the deep care and commitment evident among those showing up to protect their neighbors and loved ones. This line of defense consists of ordinary people from all walks of life - parents walking kids to school, healthcare staff, faith leaders, restaurant owners and workers, climate activists, and street bystanders. We’re preventing agents from coming into our places of work and worship and taking to the streets to protest.

Here are three examples of what taking a stand against mass deportations and detention looks like:

1. An Immigrant Rights Coalition Mobilizes to Shut Down Detention Centers

There are more than 200 detention facilities currently in the U.S. - at least 100 more than when Trump took office. Trump’s so-called Big Beautiful Bill allocated $45 billion just to create new detention facilities - about four times ICE’s previous annual budget.

Against this onslaught, Detention Watch Network has launched a new campaign called End the ICE Age. The campaign urges members of the public and members of Congress to support the “Melt ICE Act” that would redirect ICE funding, get ICE agents out of communities, and shut down and prevent the expansion of detention centers. End the ICE Age works in tandem with the Communities Not Cages campaign which uplifts local organizing and provides people the tools to fight against detention centers in their own communities.

We’ve seen wins in places like Pennsylvania, which shut down plans for two detention centers in July due to pressure from local leaders and residents.

2. Nurses Against ICE’s Partnership with Palantir

If you’re a well-known brand or company working with ICE, chances are that people know about it. That’s definitely the case for tech giant Palantir. Palantir provides an app that has helped ICE locate immigrants for arrest and detention, which includes improperly obtained Medicaid data containing patients’ immigration status and address - even encompassing personal information of citizens and legal residents.

The National Nurses United, a labor union of 225,000 members, has been taking a stand against Palantir collaborating with ICE. In late August, hundreds of registered nurses, from Los Angeles, California to Portland, Maine, stopped traffic to proclaim, “Palantir Out!” These nurses displayed dozens of baby shoes on the street, representing the thousands of babies who have been detained since Trump took office. They joined in other protests honoring the lives that we've lost to ICE, including Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, and launched a week of action for Alex Pretti.

3. Climate Advocates Say No to Authoritarianism and ICE Agents

The Sunrise Movement, known for popularizing the Green New Deal, is no stranger to pushing back against harmful leadership and policies. This youth-led movement working to advance climate action has shifted to fight authoritarianism since the beginning of this administration.

This year, Sunrise has been vocal about “ICE Out For Good” with focus on refusing the presence of ICE agents in communities. Sunrise acknowledges that climate activists must oppose ICE because fossil fuel companies, along with ICE, are all part of the same power web threatening American democracy.

Over the last couple of months, the Sunrise hub in Minnesota has been protesting outside hotels hosting ICE agents. And the response? ICE agents have gone undercover and joined Sunrise meetings and online group chats, convincing group members to engage in confrontational tactics - all the while Sunrise stresses its complete nonviolent approach to organizing.

One of my favorite quotes goes, “Hope is a discipline.” To me, hope is a practice that demands moments of calibration to assess what we and others need of ourselves at the moment. I’m inspired by people across issue areas and walks of life prioritizing the need to protect our targeted community members.

We must continue the fight to shut down detention centers, resist partnerships of companies working with ICE, and redirect money from family separation and into family needs. Our democracy is counting on it.

text:
Former heads of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) called for a public safety agency to be established on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

In a joint interview with NBC News on Thursday, former DHS Secretaries Michael Chertoff and Jeh Johnson discussed the current direction of the agency, which they both said “has gotten off track.”

Johnson, who served under former President Obama from 2013 to 2017, said he believes the agency needs “a reset.”

“When I stepped into the job of secretary in 2013, the department was still, I think, viewed primarily as security,” he said. “Now I fear in many communities DHS has become a pariah, radioactive, the department of mass deportations, heartless, locking up kids, and that is one of the reasons why I think we need a reset.”

The Deportation Data Project found that Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which falls under the DHS, had arrested 49,571 people in July, the highest such number during President Trump’s second term.

Chertoff and Johnson asked for any agency that did not fall under the realm of public safety to be spun off, including the Federal Emergency Management Agency, resembling a European model of public safety ministries.

Chertoff, who served under former President George W. Bush from 2005 to 2009, said he believed it “would help the Cabinet secretary deconflict, unify and achieve a common effort of priorities in terms of where to protect the country and how to reduce the most serious threats that we would be facing.”

“We’re spending most of our time worrying about gardeners and home health aides and getting them thrown out of the country, as opposed to focusing on people that actually are doing a lot of damage,” he added.

Their comments come as America mourns the loss of 2,977 lives in the attacks on the World Trade Center in New York City; the Pentagon in Arlington, Va.; and at the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93 in Pennsylvania.

A DHS spokesperson told The Hill, “Counterterrorism and immigration enforcement go hand in hand. Child exploitation, trafficking, terrorism, scams, and smuggling all have a nexus to illegal immigration.”

“Despite multiple Democrat shutdowns of DHS, the Department is more than equipped to keep Americans safe in an ever-changing threat landscape. DHS has been recruiting, reforming, and modernizing at a record pace—including in areas of counterterrorism,” the spokesperson continued.

When asked if the modern DHS could handle another attack of this magnitude, Johnson said he believes it could because “we are better at tracking who enters the country.”

“The problem, however, is the terrorist threat morphed, and the DHS that Secretary Chertoff and I led years ago is not equipped to deal with that form of domestic terrorism,” he said.

text:
PHOENIX— A federal judge has granted preliminary approval of a class-action settlement between OneAZ Credit Union and recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) and other immigrants who allege they were denied loans and financial services based on their immigration status rather than their ability to repay.

MALDEF (Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund) and Arizona attorney Daniel Ortega of Ortega Law Firm filed the suit on behalf of Deyra Pamela Carranza Aguilar, of Phoenix, a DACA recipient, and other immigrants who comprise the settlement class.

“Non-discrimination is an essential aspect of any thriving economy,” said Thomas A. Saenz, MALDEF president and general counsel. “This agreement helps to ensure that immigrants do not face discrimination in accessing credit and other financial tools in the future.”

As part of the settlement agreement, which received preliminary approval on September 9, OneAZ Credit Union has agreed to establish a $100,000 settlement fund. The settlement includes compensation for the plaintiff, attorneys' fees and costs, and a $63,500.16 fund to compensate the class of immigrants affected by the challenged practice. OneAZ has also ended the challenged practice and agreed that it will not deny financial products to, or discourage applications from, otherwise qualified applicants solely on the basis of alienage.

“We are pleased to have reached a settlement that recognizes the limitations of considering immigration status or closely related proxies in assessing credit-worthiness,” said Eduardo Casas, MALDEF staff attorney. “Immigrants are an integral part of our economy, and parity in access to financial institutions will enable their continued pursuit of America’s promise.”

In October 2022, Aguilar visited a Flagstaff branch of OneAZ to ask about applying to refinance a $17,000 car loan. Aguilar told a representative there that she had previously been turned down for refinancing because she is a DACA recipient. According to the lawsuit, Aguilar wanted to find out whether OneAZ gave loans to DACA holders. After checking with a manager, the representative told Aguilar that she would “probably be denied” since DACA required renewal every two years. Hoping the representative would reconsider, Aguilar explained that she was employed – DACA recipients can lawfully work in the United States – and had a good income and credit rating. Instead, the representative reiterated that he expected her application to be denied because of her status and took no further action on her request.

The suit challenged OneAZ’s denial of a loan as a violation of Section 1981 of the federal Civil Rights Act of 1866, which prohibits discrimination in contracting based on race, color, ethnicity, or alienage. ​

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court, District of Arizona.

OneAZ is a member-owned credit union with $3.4 billion in assets. It serves over 200,000 members across Arizona and offers savings and checking accounts as well as credit cards, mortgages, consumer loans, and other financial services.

The settlement is one of more than a dozen MALDEF has reached with financial institutions that deny services to DACA recipients and other immigrants because of their immigration status rather than their creditworthiness.

name: Litigation
title: Ordinary Origins: How 9/11 Built Today's Immigration Enforcement Machine | Lawfare
description:
Very little of the sharing was built for immigration enforcement, and none of it was built for what it now does.
Sept. 11, 2001 recast immigration as a national security problem, and a national security problem invites an intelligence solution: more data, more sources, fewer barriers between them.
It moved the courts toward deference, because immigration was now national security, where deference to the political branches runs deepest.
The failed effort to make government data speak a common public language paved the way for the rise of private vendor involvement in immigration enforcement.
The technology still cannot deliver true end-to-end immigration enforcement, but the infrastructure to house such a biometric capability already exists.
text:
Editor's note: This piece is part of Lawfare's collection "9/11 at 25: The Legal Architecture of the War on Terror, Twenty-Five Years On," examining how 9/11 remains—or doesn't—embedded in current legal and policy frameworks, a quarter century after the attacks. Read the full collection here.

***

The Department of Homeland Security’s fingerprint repository holds more than 290 million distinct identities and answers nearly 350,000 biometric queries a day from state and local law enforcement, the intelligence community, and foreign governments. The State Department says it now monitors and re-evaluates more than 55 million people who hold a U.S. visa, continuously, against information that comes to light after issuance. None of this was built in the past two years. Very little of the sharing was built for immigration enforcement, and none of it was built for what it now does.

Sept. 11, 2001 recast immigration as a national security problem, and a national security problem invites an intelligence solution: more data, more sources, fewer barriers between them. That reframing did four things at once. It changed how the public and the political class talked about immigrants. It produced a new agency, then statutes and executive orders that expanded what the executive could do without asking permission from Congress. It moved the courts toward deference, because immigration was now national security, where deference to the political branches runs deepest. And it built the technical capacity to execute. Enforcement then became a political mission measured in volume; volume demanded efficiency, and efficiency demanded automation. None of it was built for end-to-end automated enforcement. That ambition arrived around 2018. By then the capacity was standing, the law authorized it, the doctrine would not review it, and the public had been taught to call it security. What made today’s system possible was a seemingly ordinary response to an extraordinary tragedy.

From Immigration To National Security

Two thousand nine hundred seventy-seven people were killed on 9/11; 343 of them were New York City firefighters. Within weeks, letters carrying anthrax began arriving on the doorsteps of major media outlets and members of Congress; five people died. At that moment, no one in government had reason to think the calamities would end. And the facts about the hijackers pointed toward immigration systems: They had entered on visas the government issued, most were in lawful status on the day of the attacks, and the ones who were not had gone unnoticed. The lesson drawn was not that immigration law had failed. It was that the government had not been looking hard enough at what it already knew.

The 9/11 Commission supplied the organizing principle for the response: The problem was the government’s “resistance to sharing information.” Valuable information sat in databases not usually treated as intelligence, including customs and immigration records. Border security, the commission’s staff concluded, had not been understood as a counterterrorism tool; now it had to be. The diagnosis was brutally simple: The information that could have prevented 9/11 had been there, but “someone had to ask for it.” A cataclysmic national security event turned on access to immigration data; the prescription to the diagnosis was to build a system that made asking unnecessary.

The country had connected immigration and terrorism before. After the first World Trade Center bombing in 1993, Congress required cities to permit employees to share immigration-status information with federal authorities. But the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) had fewer than 2,000 immigration agents, and identifying someone in a local jail for federal enforcement still depended on a local official choosing to ask and a federal official choosing to answer. Six weeks after 9/11, then-Attorney General John Ashcroft made the new theory explicit: Mundane visa overstays would be used as counterterrorism tools, and criticism of the administration’s tactics was cast as assistance to terrorists. The narrative born of 9/11 remains with us today: Immigration is a national security concern.

Building The Information-Sharing State

The institutional response mirrored the prevailing narrative: Immigration and national security were inextricably tied. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 pulled 22 agencies and roughly 180,000 employees into a new Department of Homeland Security, the largest federal reorganization since the creation of the Department of Defense. DHS was given an “overriding and urgent mission” centered on counterterrorism: prevent attacks, reduce the country’s vulnerability to them, and minimize the damage when they occurred.

Immigration appeared later in the statutory list, almost as an afterthought, as a function inherited from the now-dissolved INS. The ordering captured the change. Immigration administration had been moved inside an institution whose organizing purpose was security. The statute also embedded the architecture that matters here: DHS was to ensure information sharing among border-management, law-enforcement, and intelligence databases, backed by the data-mining and analytical tools needed to use what those systems produced. Immigration and national security were not merely placed in the same department. Their information systems were supposed to speak to one another.

Congress made that command concrete the same year. The Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act ordered an “interoperable electronic data system” giving immigration officials current and immediate access to federal law-enforcement and intelligence databases. Two years later, the intelligence-reform statute created an information sharing environment built around “direct and continuous online electronic access” and access to data rather than merely to particular systems or networks. By 2007, Congress envisioned the “full range of analytic and operational activities” occurring without centralizing the underlying information. That distinction was consequential. A single warehouse is expensive, visible, and bounded. Interoperability lets separate systems remain where they are while making their contents available across institutional lines—and lets new systems plug in later.

The category of information eligible for sharing was correspondingly broad: information that could improve identifying or investigating a suspected terrorist—a definition that appeared boundless. Congress imported that definition into the Information Sharing Environment in 2007, while executive orders pushed agencies toward ever broader information-sharing—including information that might seem wholly unrelated to counterterrorism—within the executive branch and with state, local, tribal, and private-sector partners. The point was not to build one database. It was to build a standing capacity to reach across as many of them as possible.

The legal architecture was already unusually deferential. Immigration doctrine had long committed questions of admission and removal largely to the political branches, with courts applying only narrow review to decisions by Congress or the president. Enforcement doctrine gave the executive more room still to decide whom to pursue and whom to remove. Recasting immigration as national security layered one deferential domain onto another.

The biometric border shows how 9/11 changed the political price of that project. Congress had ordered an automated entry-exit system in 1996, but resistance from border states, Canada, and industry stalled it; Detroit’s mayor warned the system could turn downtown into a “virtual parking lot.” In 2000, Congress expressly promised no new documentary or data-collection requirements. Six weeks after 9/11, however, the PATRIOT Act ordered the system built “with all deliberate speed” and directed particular attention to biometric technology.

Biometric entry was fully operational at every port by December 2006. Biometric exit is taking far longer and remains incomplete; as of 2025, it is only operational in commercial airports, even after 17 years and eight statutes. Even now, part of the system is funded by the “9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee,” a surcharge on employers sponsoring certain H-1B and L-1 workers. A Customs and Border Protection (CBP) rule taking effect Sept. 9 extends that fee to extension petitions as well, substantially expanding the share of sponsored petitions subject to it. Twenty-five years on, a fee named for the attacks still helps pay for the machinery built in their name.

Interoperability Moves Inward

The same architecture extended beyond the border through fusion centers. Fusion centers are state owned and operated intelligence hubs—roughly 80 nationwide—that gather, analyze, and share threat-related information among federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies. They made the post-9/11 information-sharing project physically present inside state and local government. Rather than combine federal and local databases into one warehouse, the governing guidelines embraced access to “a variety of disparate databases.” Counterintuitively, and somewhat ironically, privacy objections to immigration surveillance justified the shift to an interoperable apparatus rather than an integrated one. Instead of forging a single, centralized database, the government intentionally kept systems separate but interconnected, therefore ensuring the apparatus remained nimble and extensible.

Congress then put on paper the deepening marriage of immigration enforcement and counterterrorism. In 2007, lawmakers required DHS officers and analysts assigned to fusion centers to receive appropriate access to all relevant federal databases and information systems, and they prioritized the deployment of CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel to centers located near borders. By 2017, ICE officials were detailed to 11 centers. The immigration function arrived through personnel and access even though immigration was not the centers’ stated purpose.

Their reach was also enormous and their mission, malleable. A bipartisan Senate investigation in 2012 found that it could not identify a fusion-center report that uncovered a terrorist threat; much of the reporting concerned ordinary crime, and federal spending could be estimated only within a range of $289 million to $1.4 billion. DHS nevertheless continued to fund their maturation and enhancement. Fusion centers are thus a useful miniature of the larger story: Counterterrorism supplied the rationale; interoperability supplied the design; and the resulting capacity traveled well beyond terrorism.

Secure Communities carried the same logic into local jails. The underlying fingerprint systems predated 9/11: After the Border Patrol released a serial-murder suspect because INS and FBI systems could not communicate, Congress pressed to link them. Post-9/11 funding and mandates produced the bridge between DHS’s IDENT system and the FBI’s fingerprint system. Secure Communities, launched in 2008, then made fingerprints that local jails already sent to the FBI automatically run against immigration records as well. The local decision whether to notify ICE—a phone call that local politics could reach—was engineered out of the process. Interoperability is no longer a passive feature; it is an active trigger. The commission’s failure had been a request no one made. The remedy obviated the need for one.

Section 287(g) moved people and data through the same channels. The 1996 statute authorizing federal deputization of state and local officers as immigration agents went unused for six years. The first agreement came in Florida in 2002 and trained officers serving on post-9/11 domestic-security task forces. From one agreement, the program grew to 67 by 2008, much of that growth occurring in Southern jurisdictions responding to new immigrant populations rather than terrorist threats. It fell to 35 by the end of the Obama administration, passed 1,000 agreements in September 2025, and now exceeds 2,000. Beyond deputizing officers, 287(g) added new data flows: ICE supplied participating agencies with secure connections, workstations, and fingerprint equipment linking them directly to federal immigration databases, and trained deputized officers to search and enter information into those systems. The legal authority was old. The national security reframing reinvigorated it, and the infrastructure made it scalable.

The failed effort to make government data speak a common public language paved the way for the rise of private vendor involvement in immigration enforcement. The National Information Exchange Model, launched in 2005 as a common data standard, never achieved universal adoption; by 2010, six of 26 surveyed agencies did not use it at all, and only its two founding agencies used it at enterprise scale. Vendors increasingly supplied the interoperability that ultimately mattered: Proprietary data models and platforms could connect systems the government had not standardized itself.

And where government systems did not contain enough information, agencies bought it. The Privacy Act governs systems of records operated by or on behalf of an agency, but federal officials treated commercial data resellers’ databases as outside that rule because the vendors served multiple customers. By 2006, 91 percent of reported federal reseller use was for law enforcement or counterterrorism, and ICE was already DHS’s largest customer; agencies commonly bought address and vehicle information—where people were. The scale advantage was dramatic: in one 2005 test, a TSA contractor sent roughly 240,000 passenger names to three commercial providers and received more than 100 million records back. Interoperability could connect government silos; the commercial market could fill the gaps between them.

Programs Change; The Pipes Remain

This architecture survived precisely because the most visible programs did not have to. Congress defunded Total Information Awareness in 2003, but the prohibition itself contained an exception for certain counterterrorism intelligence processing and collaboration tools described in a classified annex. The Pentagon’s own advisory committee warned that tools of this kind, used against people without an adequate predicate, risked becoming the 21st century equivalent of general searches. Seven months after the ban, the Government Accountability Office counted 199 data-mining efforts across 52 agencies, 77 of them drawing on other agencies’ data and only 14 classified as counterterrorism. The cross-agency plumbing had already spread beyond the program Congress killed.

The National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS) is the sharper example. The post-9/11 special-registration program fingerprinted, photographed, and interviewed 83,519 nonimmigrant men from 25 designated countries and placed 13,799 of them in removal proceedings during its nine years in operation. The system was suspended in 2011 and repealed in 2016. But the government’s explanation for repeal was that the information was already captured through “more comprehensive and efficient systems”: CBP now fingerprinted and photographed nearly all nonimmigrants, regardless of nationality. A notorious program aimed at 25 countries disappeared because universal biometric collection had made it redundant.

Secure Communities likewise demonstrated how little policy reversal required infrastructure reversal. DHS “discontinued” the program in 2014 but replaced it with one that continued relying on the same booking fingerprints sent by local law enforcement to the FBI. A January 2017 order revived Secure Communities; a January 2021 order revoked that order in a sentence and said nothing about the fingerprint pipeline. Three administrations changed policy at the surface. None dismantled the pipes. The executive order that had directed an interoperable terrorism-information-sharing environment in 2005—and made sharing with state, local, tribal, and private-sector entities a priority—remains in force today.

From Capacity To Automation

By 2018, the ambition had a name. A presidential memorandum described the “national vetting enterprise” not as a new program but as the coordinated work agencies were already doing. It claimed no new authority. Instead, where authorized and appropriate, agencies were to process information on a recurrent basis using relevant federal intelligence and law-enforcement information—the same categories Congress had ordered connected in 2002—and a National Vetting Center would coordinate the work.

When I wrote about the National Vetting Enterprise in 2019, the ambition still surpassed the technology. A 2017 executive order demanded a process to assess whether an applicant was likely to become a “positively contributing member of society,” and ICE asked industry for a system that could make that determination continuously. Fifty-four technical researchers responded that no computational method could reliably or objectively measure the traits ICE wanted. ICE ultimately shifted the project from a technology contract to a labor contract, and the National Vetting Center later said it did not use automated analysis to discover predictive patterns or anomalies.

But automation’s siren song could only be resisted for so long. The enforcement mission itself was growing in scale—first a little, then a lot. Interior enforcement staffing had grown from fewer than 2,000 agents in the INS era to roughly 21,800 positions in fiscal 2024, with ICE appropriations above $10 billion. After 2024, though, the expectations and the resources to fund them grew outlandishly. The July 2025 reconciliation act then appropriated $191 billion for DHS through fiscal 2029, nearly three-quarters directed to ICE and CBP; a second reconciliation act in June 2026 added another $69.5 billion. One ICE officer testified that a team of nine to 12 officers had been directed to target eight arrests a day. A mission funded and measured this way cannot depend on humans making one individualized decision at a time. Volume demands efficiency; efficiency demands automation. And doctrine developed in a world that already granted exceptional deference over immigration and national security gives the executive unusual room to use the machinery Congress built.

The legal ambition has now caught up. In January 2025, Executive Order 14161 directed agencies to vet and screen “to the maximum degree possible” noncitizens seeking admission and those already inside the United States, including for “hostile attitudes” toward American citizens, culture, government, institutions, or founding principles—a standard no more computable than the one vendors could not build in 2017.

In November 2025, DHS proposed continuous immigration vetting under which lawful residents could be required to submit biometrics at any time until citizenship. The technology still cannot deliver true end-to-end immigration enforcement, but the infrastructure to house such a biometric capability already exists. The databases are connected, the access rules are in place, the biometrics are already collected, state and local systems feed federal ones, commercial vendors supply what the government lacks, and the policy layer can be changed by signature.

The people who laid this groundwork were not designing for what it does today. The Commission’s diagnosis was not irrational. The pre-9/11 objections to automated entry-exit focused on commerce and federalism. Fusion-center guidelines were written in part to protect privacy. Secure Communities solved a real interoperability problem. But together these choices produced a standing immigration enforcement capacity for which no administration has had to claim full accountability, insulated by a narrative that calls it security, statutes that authorize it, and doctrine that reserves its deepest deference for those magic words.

That is the harder problem. No single scandal, lawsuit, program, or administration is the cause, so no single one is the cure. But it is also an opportunity. Every pipe was laid by a statute, a rule, a memorandum, or a contract, and each remains reachable through ordinary law. Reversal is still available through ordinary democratic processes. How that software Pangea actually works, and why the remedies aimed at it keep missing, is the subject of a companion piece.

text:
National Nurses United (NNU), the largest union of registered nurses in the U.S., is demanding that hospitals cut ties with Palantir, with nurses citing the firm’s role in developing technology used to surveil immigrants in the U.S. and target civilians in Gaza.

The union – which represents more than 225,000 nurses in all 50 U.S. states — has announced a global week of action against Palantir, set to begin on September 28.

Palantir’s “AI-powered tools for large-scale data collection and mass surveillance… threaten human rights globally,” the union said in a press release announcing the campaign.

The global week of action is aimed at pushing all public institutions — including hospitals and other health care providers — to end contracts and partnerships with Palantir, and to divest from the company, the union said.

The global week of action builds on a national day of action, also led by the union, which saw demonstrations in eight cities across the U.S. on August 27, including in Portland, Maine; Washington, D.C.; Chicago; Austin; and Los Angeles.

The global week of action is also coordinated with health care workers in the U.K., where National Health Service (NHS) workers and activists will protest Palantir’s use in health care on October 1. Other organizations, like Amnesty International and the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) Movement, are also part of the global week of action.

“Palantir has no place in patient care, no place in our communities, and no place in our society,” a NNU nurse said in a video from the August 27 day of action.

The nurses have outlined Palantir’s complicity in human rights violations both nationally and internationally, from detentions of immigrants by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to the genocide in Gaza.

“We think that a company that specializes in mass surveillance, kidnappings and killings, has no place in patient care,” one nurse explained in a video posted by the California Nurses Association.

During the August day of action, nurses placed 50 pairs of baby shoes in the street in each city – to represent the 500 babies and toddlers who have been detained in immigrant jails since President Donald Trump started his second term. The nurses also brought letters written by children in ICE detention.

“Palantir, we know, helps ICE identify people to kidnap off of our streets,” another nurse said during the day of action.

The company also has “their hands in the genocide and murders of civilians in Gaza,” another nurse present at the protests said. “They’ve [helped with the targeting of] hospitals, schools, mission workers taking food and aid….”

In a statement shared with Truthout and read at the August 27 day of action, Chicago-based nurse and NNU member Elizabeth Lalasz said that “nurses, health care workers, our patients, immigrants, and allies from every walk of life stand united here in Chicago and all across the country to demand an immediate end to the violence inflicted by Palantir technologies and the Trump administration.”

“As we speak, Palantir’s AI is enabling atrocities and human rights abuses: ICE killings, mass deportation, and concentration camps with no access to health care – even the imprisonment of more than 500 babies and 6,200 children – and Palantir is providing the technology for Israel’s U.S.-funded genocide in Gaza, the cruel and illegal war in Iran, and mass surveillance at home and abroad,” she went on.

Lalasz also noted that Palantir has partnered with the world’s largest health care corporations “to suck more and more profit from our broken health care system, causing untold suffering in our hospitals.”

“This country could fund health care for 12 million children with the money spent on ICE detention alone,” she said.

text:
DAYSI GONZÁLEZ HAS WORKED WITH some of the biggest names in Democratic politics—Senate candidate James Talarico, Sen. Ruben Gallego, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and more. She’s done so as a partner at the consulting firm Solidarity Strategies and as a constituency mail vendor for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, where she’s working on every competitive race with a Latino engagement program ahead of the November midterms. These include top Democratic opportunities in Texas, California, Nevada, and New Mexico.

If Democrats take back the House in a blue wave, some of that success will be owed to the work Daysi has done. When the time comes, though, she will be trading whatever comfort she takes in professional success for the cold hard reality of Trump’s deportation zealotry.

That’s because Temporary Protected Status for Salvadorans is in serious limbo. It was set to expire on September 9—this past Wednesday—but is now extended for some undefined period. Daysi, knowing that her time in the United States is running out, is planning to self-deport to a country she barely remembers.

“It’s so sad that she will have done so much with a team of people to elect ten new Democrats . . . and could be fearing for her life,” Daysi’s boss, Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha, told me. “One of the most powerful Latina operatives in this country, because we lost an election, now has to self-deport to protect her and her sister.”

Like many immigrants who “pass” as native-born Americans, Daysi lives a compartmentalized life. On work calls, her peers and colleagues all tell her the same thing: I can’t believe this is happening to you. There’s not much Daysi can say to that, so she just does her job.

“I’m terrified all the time, but I still need to work,” she told me in a video interview. “I have people depending on me.”

Share

Daysi was 5 years old when she came to the United States in 2000. Shortly after she arrived, a 7.7-magnitude earthquake off the coast of El Salvador led the Bush administration to grant Temporary Protected Status to Salvadorans in the United States. The order affected some 150,000 to 200,000 people.

Congress established the category of Temporary Protected Status in the Immigration Act of 1990. It is a tool the government can use to allow people from countries experiencing extraordinary crises to legally remain in the United States; it can be applied in increments of six, twelve, or eighteen months. Importantly, TPS does not provide a pathway to citizenship. Ongoing insecurity and civic instability in El Salvador, including gang violence, made the Central American state the country with the longest-running TPS designation.

For Daysi, TPS was a fairly mundane administrative reality; to keep her status up to date, she had to occasionally take long trips to update her biometrics. In exchange for doing that, she received stability and security for the first part of her life.

That all changed when Donald Trump was elected. Not in 2024 but in 2016. After his first win, Daysi sobbed for an hour in the shower. Her fears proved well founded. The first Trump administration terminated TPS for El Salvador, among others, in 2018. That termination wound its way through court challenges and injunctions. In 2021, Sanchez v. Mayorkas affirmed that TPS could not be the basis for a green card application. The Biden administration rescinded the TPS termination in 2023, but Salvadorans with TPS—who by this point had lived in the United States for over two decades—were on shaky ground.

“One of the last things Biden did was redesignate El Salvador for TPS. That’s what bought me these last eighteen months,” Daysi told me.

The very day Trump took office for a second time, he issued an executive order “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” It called on TPS programs to be curbed, making it clear where his second administration stood. Eventually, those TPS terminations were sanctioned by the Supreme Court.

I asked Daysi how she has coped with the uncertainty.

“I . . . shut down for all of last year when my TPS was in process,” she replied. “It technically wasn’t expired; I could still keep my job. But I couldn’t renew my license, I couldn’t get a REAL ID. I was landlocked and couldn’t travel.”

Share

THOUGH DAYSI WAS LARGELY RESIGNED to her fate—and her plans for self-deportation—the nearing of the end of her TPS status instilled some fresh new emotions. There was the now-familiar stress and anxiety. But there were also green shoots of hope.

A USCIS posting this week came right at the September 9 deadline for TPS to end. It read that “an announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection including work authorization.”

Daysi believes that period could potentially buy TPS holders like herself an additional six months in the country. Guidance from the counsel for the National TPS Alliance says it is legally at least sixty days. She still plans to self-deport, she told me. But she now believes she will do so after this November’s election.

“My license is still expired, a bunch of stuff was contingent on TPS. My sister lost her job, I don’t know if I can cover the mortgage by myself for more than six months, so I’m taking this week to figure things out,” she told me. But she made clear that a life in limbo takes a serious toll, which is why she is still considering self-deportation.

“I don’t know if I can continue living like this,” she said after the announcement. “The emotional and physical damage of the last few months, I don’t know how bad it is.”

That her hopes have been lifted at the eleventh hour is another illustration of the mental anguish that the Trump administration has placed on immigrant communities.

For months, Daysi had been trying to dull her optimism and get into a headspace where she could leave the United States on her own terms.

She created a public record on Instagram, keeping a countdown of the days until her TPS expires. In a video exactly a month out, the unfairness of having an American life dangled before her for two and a half decades got to her.

“It just threw my life into this ten-year limbo,” she said in the video. “It’s irreparably damaged my mental health. It’s ruined plans, relationships—any sense of stability. . . . All I’ll say for now is that this really fucking sucks. It’s unfair, and I’ll probably crash out.”

The cleancut Daysi, who doesn’t smoke or drink, received a talking-to from her father for cursing in the video. Meanwhile, her mother worried that she was sharing her story too publicly.

But Daysi saw virtue in being public—the videos, she reasoned, offered a window into what hundreds of thousands are dealing with privately: the sudden demand to uproot their lives and leave almost the only country they have known.

Daysi also shared everyday moments that caused her heartache. In another video, she discussed losing her familiar health care provider. “If my favorite doctor doesn’t have availability before I have to leave, that’s going to break me,” she said.

Share

FOR THOSE WHO KNOW DAYSI, her story seems inherently cruel.

“She’s the living embodiment of what’s wrong with our broken immigration system,” Rocha told me. “She’s doing mail pieces on ICE overreach while she’s hiding at home with the National Guard outside, communicating the anxiety that Latino voters and immigrants are feeling with the Republican party while in real time dealing with it on her own.”

But Daysi seems determined to live out her final days in the United States (whenever they come) making sure others feel less alone. She has spoken to other former and current TPS holders, including a young Haitian woman considering trying to wait out deportation, and two Venezuelans who have already left. Daysi knew one of the Venezuelans from college: When he was forced to leave, he took his two children, both U.S. citizens, with him.

“I know my situation is terrible, but it could be a lot worse,” Daysi said.

I was struck by her decision to leave of her own accord and on her own terms. Daysi will be going with her sister. She is confident she will make it work. But she doesn’t know where they will live in El Salvador, beyond a hotel when they first arrive. She is hopeful that El Salvador is safer now than it has been—a product of Trump friend President Nayib Bukele’s brutal crackdown on gangs—and she isn’t afraid. But, she insists, having to leave her home for the place of her birth won’t make the United States any safer.

“I have savings. I’m going to figure it out. But no one would choose to leave the country and life they love arbitrarily to move, and that’s what this is,” she said. “Me leaving the country is not going to change anything.”

The Fight to Help Other Daysis in the Future

Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) recognizes Daysi’s hustle. She’s one of the reasons he was elected and then re-elected in New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District. In 2022, Daysi worked as part of a pro-Vasquez PAC. Then in 2024, Daysi worked on a multimillion-dollar bilingual mail, digital, and radio program on his behalf. Vasquez beat a Republican by 4 points; Trump won the district that year by nearly 2.

Vasquez told me that Daysi’s experiences highlight how both parties have failed Americans and immigrants. One lesson he draws from this failure is that future immigration-reform efforts shouldn’t chase the elusive and failed comprehensive reform packages of the past.

“We find ourselves in a moment of reckoning for this nation about the future of immigration reform and what it looks like. We’ve clearly seen what the Trump administration idea of immigration enforcement looks like,” Vasquez said. “But people like Daysi . . . she worked incredibly hard to get where she is and shouldn’t have to suffer because of both parties’ lack of making immigration a priority.”

He mentions a piece of legislation he developed, the Careworker Visa Act, as an example of the sort of meaningful, incremental progress that could draw bipartisan support. Designed to address the childcare and eldercare shortage, the bill would create a new visa category that would allow careworkers to stay and work in the United States for three years if they care for children, seniors, or the disabled, which some with TPS would qualify for.

Vasquez emphasized that there should be bipartisan compromises to protect people like Daysi from deportation: “Nothing about her experience with TPS separates her from Dreamers who should benefit from the Dream Act.”

Still, he put the onus on his own party.

“The Democrats have to wake up in this next Congress and make immigration reform one of the cornerstone policy issues,” he said. “Daysi has worked to help elect Democrats her entire professional career—helped to protect democracy, and voting rights, and candidates like us that should be focusing on helping people like her.”

title: Appeals court slams migrant mandatory detention policy | The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
description:
Circuit Court of Appeals became the ninth federal appeals court to reject the administration's mandatory detention policy -- a key part of its mass deportation campaign.
Mandatory detention was generally reserved for people arrested at the border.
Last July, immigration officials issued guidance expanding mandatory detention to immigrants in the U.S. interior.
President Donald Trump's administration has argued that Congress changed immigration law in 1996 to allow mandatory detention beyond the border, but previous administrations didn't enforce that provision.
In a 2-1 decision, 4th Circuit Judges Barbara Keenan and Nicole Berner said Congress in 1996 would have provided greater clarity if it intended to allow the mandatory detention of millions of people.
text:
The Trump administration's policy of holding immigrants without a chance for release on bail is illegal and "hearkens back to some of the darkest moments in our country's history," including the mass detention of Japanese Americans during World War II, a divided federal appeals court ruled Thursday.

The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals became the ninth federal appeals court to reject the administration's mandatory detention policy -- a key part of its mass deportation campaign. Two other appeals courts have upheld it, creating a split that greatly increases the odds that the U.S. Supreme Court will take up the issue.

The split also means immigrants in some parts of the country are getting bail hearings while those in other places, including Texas and Louisiana, face additional hurdles to seek release.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement it was "confident in its legal position regarding mandatory detention," noting it had recently asked the Supreme Court to take up the issue.

Under previous administrations, most non-citizens without a criminal record who were arrested inside the U.S. were allowed to seek a bail hearing while their immigration cases were pending. Mandatory detention was generally reserved for people arrested at the border.

Last July, immigration officials issued guidance expanding mandatory detention to immigrants in the U.S. interior. President Donald Trump's administration has argued that Congress changed immigration law in 1996 to allow mandatory detention beyond the border, but previous administrations didn't enforce that provision.

"President Trump and Secretary Mullin are now enforcing the law as it was actually written to keep America safe," Homeland Security said, referring to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

The 4th Circuit and most other federal appeals courts have rejected that interpretation.

"The government's track record speaks for itself at this point," said Michael K.T. Tan, deputy director of the ACLU's Immigrants' Rights Project and lead attorney on the lawsuit before the 4th Circuit.

In a 2-1 decision, 4th Circuit Judges Barbara Keenan and Nicole Berner said Congress in 1996 would have provided greater clarity if it intended to allow the mandatory detention of millions of people. Keenan was nominated by President Barack Obama; Berner by President Joe Biden. Judge Allison Rushing, who was nominated by President Donald Trump, dissented.

Writing for the majority, Berner said the administration's policy would "implicate the constitutional due process rights of millions of noncitizens in our country, many of whom have lived, worked, and become integral parts of their communities, for years."

"Mass detention of marginalized individuals without due process hearkens back to some of the darkest moments in our country's history," she wrote.

She cited Japanese internment and the mass detention of Chinese immigrants in the late 1800s and said the Trump administration's policy was even more expansive than "those shameful and abhorrent past detentions."

text:
The Trump administration is proposing a dramatic overhaul of the once-a-decade U.S. Census head count that could leave out millions of immigrants based on status and key racial and ethnic data, jeopardizing the allocation of resources and the country’s voting map.

The potential changes, announced Wednesday, would exclude undocumented immigrants, asylum seekers and anyone without permanent status. Certain demographic questions from the traditional questionnaire would also be eliminated.

It echoes Trump’s previous idea to add a citizenship question to the 2030 census.

The U.S. Census Bureau, in a post on the Federal Register website, argued “illegal aliens (among others) should not be included in the apportionment count, as they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a ‘usual residence’ in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States.”

The census also “should be colorblind and should not be distorted in any way by questions about immaterial personal characteristics, such as race,” the agency said. It also is considering nixing questions related to people who identify as part of the LGBTQ+ community.

These changes would harm the quality of the data, said Beth Jarosz, a data researcher and vice president of the Association of Public Data Users. She called the proposals “unprecedented.”

“Not counting all of the people who reside here is actually where the real threat is,” Jarosz said. “If you think about all of the ways that census data are used.”

Census figures are traditionally used for an “apportionment count” to determine how many seats each state will have in the U.S. House of Representatives. That count also determines the number of votes in the Electoral College.

“You can imagine if we have undercounts or if we have people counted in the wrong place,” Jarosz said. “Then their political power or their political representation gets diluted.”

Immigrants of every status have historically been counted

Historically, the decennial census has not sought to conduct a full count of people by citizenship status, she added. It may come up in the Census’ periodic American Community Survey.

Getting an accurate count of immigrants of various statuses is useful when assigning resources for public health emergencies or natural or human-made disasters.

“If you don’t have a count of everyone who’s there, you’re not going to have the resources you need,” Jarosz said. “And that puts everybody at risk.”

Why race and ethnicity census data matters

Race-related questions have been on the once-a-decade census since 1790. Starting in 2000, the U.S. census began allowing people to identify by more than one race. A 2015 Pew Research Center study found that multiracial people in the U.S. were growing at a rate three times faster than the general population. By 2020, 33.8 million people in the U.S. identified as being more than one race, according to the census.

Race and ethnicity data is essential for researchers who gauge discrimination, crime rates and wealth gaps in communities of color.

Manjusha Kulkarni is co-founder of Stop AAPI Hate and executive director of AAPI Equity Alliance, two advocacy groups that rely on census counts of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. The proposed changes would have tremendous impact on the populations they serve, she said.

“It also seeks to exclude important demographic data from millions that enables lawmakers, health care providers, public safety officials and community advocates — really anyone who cares about the health, safety and well-being of all Americans — from having the necessary data to keep us safe and healthy,” Kulkarni said via text message.

Dropping race and ethnicity data as well as some immigrants sends a message that these communities don’t matter, she added.

Collecting data for the 2030 Census with all these missing elements would be detrimental, Jarosz said.

“These changes are like trying to land an airplane when you are in thick fog and someone has thrown paint across the front window and your instruments are also not working,” she said.
