title: It's Been 25 Years Since 9/11. What Has DHS Become? - POLITICO
description:
He hoped to build a homeland security structure akin to the National Security Council, which coordinates interagency work among cabinet departments, and saw a presidential-level office with strong budget responsibilities as the best way to focus disparate agencies and functions.
Yet as evidence mounted about the myriad warning signs that U.S. law enforcement and intelligence had missed leading up to the attacks, congressional pressure for a major reorganization became politically inescapable by 2002.
At the time, there was a widespread push to split the bureau into a British-style domestic law enforcement agency, like Scotland Yard, and a domestic intelligence agency, like MI5.
But in a careful, quiet personal lobbying campaign, Mueller made the case that having the bureau’s intelligence and law enforcement capabilities under one roof made the nation safer.
Instead, DHS possessed very narrow domestic criminal investigative authorities, mostly focused on customs smuggling and human trafficking (Homeland Security Investigations) and counterfeiting and financial crimes (Secret Service).
text:
The Sept. 11 attacks, though, raised terrorism from background noise to an existential dread. It was clear to the officials leading government at the time that living up to Bush’s mantra would require a new approach. “I don’t think that anybody of my generation — and even older generations — had ever experienced anything like this kind of successful attack, killing over 3,000 Americans. It was worse than Pearl Harbor in numbers and in terms of the fact that the victims were civilians and not even military,” Michael Chertoff, who at the time was head of the criminal division at the Department of Justice and who later became the second secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, told me this summer, when we spoke as part of my podcast, Long Shadow. “It was a real revolution in what the threats were. We needed to re-orchestrate how we secure our people and our property against this kind of attack.”

Bush resisted the push for the new Cabinet department for months, believing that he could best coordinate existing departments from a newly created White House Office of Homeland Security, which was created 11 days after 9/11 and first headed by former Pennsylvania governor Tom Ridge. He hoped to build a homeland security structure akin to the National Security Council, which coordinates interagency work among cabinet departments, and saw a presidential-level office with strong budget responsibilities as the best way to focus disparate agencies and functions.

Yet as evidence mounted about the myriad warning signs that U.S. law enforcement and intelligence had missed leading up to the attacks, congressional pressure for a major reorganization became politically inescapable by 2002.

“There was a recognition that we were too fragmented and that there were a lot of silos and that we needed to find a way to bring together all of the sources of information and all of the expertise to build a capability to prevent acts of terrorism,” Chertoff said.

Exactly what that new structure would look like, though, was very much an open debate. Amid fierce turf battles and lobbying by Cabinet officials and congressional leaders, the very agencies that failed to “connect the dots” ahead of 9/11 — the FBI and the CIA — remained apart from the new Cabinet department. Instead of a sweeping “homeland security” mandate, the new department that emerged from legislative and presidential wrangling and horse-trading in late 2002 might have been better termed the “Department of Border and Transportation Security.”

Jeh Johnson, who served as DHS secretary in the second term of the Obama administration, says the focus at the time the department was founded was more about securing borders than the more nuanced work of preventing terrorism.

“The thinking was that terrorism was an extraterritorial threat, so let’s consolidate the regulation of all the different ways somebody can enter the country into one Cabinet-level department — land, border patrol, courts, customs, aviation security, air and water, Coast Guard — and throw in a few additional ones in there with it, like the Secret Service and FEMA,” Johnson told me in an interview.

Nevertheless, at the time of its creation, DHS was the largest reorganization of government since the creation of the Department of Defense after World War II and brought together all or parts of 22 separate government agencies, from the U.S. Coast Guard, housed in the Transportation Department, and Treasury’s Secret Service to the Immigration and Naturalization Service at the Justice Department to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service and Plum Island Animal Disease Center, as well as FEMA, which had been an independent agency reporting to directly to the president.

The result became the nation’s third-largest Cabinet department, with an amalgamation of organizational cultures that ranged from the U.S. Customs Service and Coast Guard, which date to the first years of the U.S. government in the late 1700s, to the fiercely independent Border Patrol — whose leaders lobbied to keep its traditional green uniform rather than unite under a common CBP blue uniform — to then-entirely new creations like the Transportation Security Administration.

Given that complexity, it’s perhaps not surprising that DHS has struggled ever since to coalesce into one organization with a shared mission and culture — and it shows. DHS’s own workforce has borne the brunt of the mission mismatch; it has consistently ranked at or near the bottom of federal government morale surveys. In the 18 surveys of the U.S. government’s “Best Places to Work” conducted by the non-partisan Partnership for Public Service between 2005 and 2024, DHS ranked last or second-to-last an astounding 13 times among the roughly 20 large government departments.

Many of the agencies reflect deeply troubled internal cultures: Using CBP’s own discipline reports, I calculated earlier this year that 4,913 CBP officers and Border Patrol agents have been arrested for crime, corruption and misconduct from 2005 to 2024 — a total that works out to be one agent or officer arrested every 36 hours for more than two decades, and a number that itself would represent the nation’s fourth-largest civilian police department, equal roughly to the entire size of the Philadelphia police force. While exact statistics are difficult to calculate, it appears that CBP has a misconduct rate five times greater than other federal law enforcement agencies — and that perhaps CBP officers and Border Patrol agents even are arrested at a higher rate per capita than that of the unauthorized immigrant population.

While DHS leadership under previous presidents has been largely steady, it has proven a damaging revolving door in both Trump presidencies; the department lacked a Senate-confirmed leader through nearly the entire final two years of Trump’s first term and the administration even struggled to prove in court who was legally in charge of the department. In his second term, DHS secretary Kristi Noem lasted just 14 months before being forced out.

But if DHS has proven itself ill-suited to focus on foreign terrorism, it has become a useful catch-all presidential “Praetorian Guard” across both of Trump’s presidential terms. In his first term, amid the nationwide protests that followed the murder of George Floyd, Trump turned to a dubious legal interpretation to deploy Border Patrol agents and other DHS officers to do battle with protesters in cities like Portland, Oregon. “I don’t need invitations by the state, state mayors or state governors to do our job,” then-acting DHS secretary Chad Wolf told reporters amid the 2020 unrest. “We’re going to do that whether they like us there or not.” In recent days, Trump has launched a nationwide “surge” of ICE agents to investigate voter fraud, a vanishingly rare crime with no clear nexus to ICE’s normal investigative responsibilities.

Altogether the ranks of DHS have swelled greatly since its creation and fundamentally altered the balance of federal law enforcement; recent government figures show that roughly half of all federal law enforcement officers are now housed inside DHS, while just a third of federal agents and officers are housed in the Department of Justice, which includes the FBI, DEA, and ATF. Today, again, while it’s hard to calculate exact figures given the recent hiring surge by ICE and CBP, DHS may in fact employ as much as 55% to 60% of all federal law enforcement personnel. Last summer’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act funneled billions of fresh dollars into DHS, ICE and CBP, turbocharging their budgets even further. As I calculated earlier this year, the $53 billion procurement and construction budget for CBP alone is equal to the entire 2024 defense expenditures of 10 European countries — Hungary, Austria, the Czech Republic, Switzerland, Finland, Greece, Belgium, Romania, Denmark and Norway.

Today, 25 years after 9/11, DHS’s core original mission of combating and responding to terrorism seems all-but forgotten in the public eye — and it seems particularly ill-poised to respond to the modern terrorism or national security threats as they currently exist.

While al Qaeda certainly remained dangerous for years after 9/11 — including executing the 2004 Madrid train bombings and the 2005 bus and train bombings in London, remembered as the 7/7 attacks — Osama bin Laden never successfully directed another attack at the U.S. homeland before he was killed in 2011 by a SEAL Team Six raid after intelligence located his secret hideout in Pakistan. (The only al Qaeda-directed attack to hit the U.S. homeland since 2001 was a December 2019 shooting by a Royal Saudi Air Force aviation student at Naval Air Station Pensacola that investigators later determined was directed by al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, an affiliate group known as AQAP; the shooter killed three U.S. sailors before being killed by responding sheriff deputies.)

The U.S. did weather a wave of attacks across the mid-2010s by individuals inspired by ISIS, an Islamic extremist group that grew out of the chaos caused by the U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, but in the last decade, the primary terrorism threat has become domestic actors — especially far-right white supremacists and mass shooters. DHS has specifically struggled to even name that threat: Then-DHS secretary Janet Napolitano backpedaled after a 2009 intelligence report cited the rising threat of far-right actors and former military veterans.

Elizabeth Neumann, then-DHS assistant secretary for counterterrorism, told me that in Trump’s first term she was startled to realize that there was no one paying attention to the rise of domestic extremists and white supremacists. As she said, “In the analysis field, it takes years for you to gain an understanding of an enemy and their tactics, their techniques, so that you can look at an event and say, this matters or this doesn’t matter. It just turns out there had been nobody working the domestic terrorism beat…. We really felt like we were in the dark.”

It’s a threat that has grown even more serious in the years since — and yet still remains largely off the radar of DHS. “Most acts of terrorism now — by any objective measure — in this country are from within,” Johnson told me. “There are not a whole lot of DHS cops running around the interior looking for terrorists. That task has always been with the FBI.”

Looking back, there were three decisions that hobbled DHS’s mission and responsibilities from the start.

The first was FBI director Robert Mueller’s successful argument that the FBI should remain intact. At the time, there was a widespread push to split the bureau into a British-style domestic law enforcement agency, like Scotland Yard, and a domestic intelligence agency, like MI5. The U.S., in fact, is one of the few Western countries that unites its domestic intelligence capabilities along with its equivalent of a national police force. (Canada, for instance, has both the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.) Immediately after the 9/11 attacks, and as evidence mounted of the failures of the FBI and the CIA to communicate successfully and “connect the dots,” many on Capitol Hill called to break the bureau apart. But in a careful, quiet personal lobbying campaign, Mueller made the case that having the bureau’s intelligence and law enforcement capabilities under one roof made the nation safer. Ultimately, congressional leaders acquiesced — largely as a personal endorsement of Mueller, who had taken over the bureau just a week before 9/11 and who had committed to a top-to-bottom reorganization of the bureau.

Second, despite its new labeling as “homeland security” — a phrase all-but born into official Washington lingo in the wake of the 9/11 attacks — the newly formed DHS actually had shockingly little responsibility for combatting terrorism, which mostly remained firmly the purview domestically of the Department of Justice, with its FBI and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Instead, DHS possessed very narrow domestic criminal investigative authorities, mostly focused on customs smuggling and human trafficking (Homeland Security Investigations) and counterfeiting and financial crimes (Secret Service). In fact, despite its name, many of HSI’s most legendary and important investigations and prosecutions have come in cases overseas, focused on cybercrime, transnational organized crime and the smuggling of weapons of mass destruction. As early as 2005, a Washington Post investigation concluded, “To some extent, the department was set up to fail. It was assigned the awesome responsibility of defending the homeland without the investigative, intelligence and military powers of the FBI, CIA and the Pentagon; it was also repeatedly undermined by the White House that initially opposed its creation.”

Third, there was a challenge more visible in retrospect: The new department inherited what would become one of the nation’s most divisive issues — immigration and border security — alongside a whole host of what were traditionally more nonpartisan responsibilities, from FEMA’s disaster relief to the search-and-rescue efforts and navigation aid maintenance of the Coast Guard to the airport security checkpoints of the newly-created TSA, as well as the protection of the nation’s critical civilian infrastructure, from water utilities to government IT networks, of what is now called the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. In many countries, these functions are housed in something more like a national civil defense agency. The shortcomings of this model became evident in multiple subsequent crises, including famously during Hurricane Katrina in 2005 when FEMA — which traditionally had reported directly to the White House — struggled to mobilize relief efforts across the government.

The result of this organizational mismatch has become an all-too-obvious mission creep — as a department ill-poised to do the thing it was created to do instead became a politically useful and opportunistic cudgel for a president with authoritarian impulses. Across his two terms, Trump has seized political openings and turbocharged DHS’s funding to target not foreign terrorists like al Qaeda or ISIS, but political dissidents and protesters here at home — people Trump himself has repeatedly labeled “terrorists.”

“I have seen firsthand how law enforcement agencies compete for space,” Johnson says. “Their jurisdiction does tend to overlap in ways the public does not understand — one agency is always nipping at the heels of the other, and very often who has the case depends on who got there first. A consolidation is in order.”

Johnson’s proposed model suggests also separating the government’s investigators from the prosecutors at the Justice Department — in the same way many states separate district attorneys from police departments at the local level. To him, that split would also limit the possibility of the weaponization of federal prosecution, requiring the assent of not just the attorney general but a second Cabinet leader before cases could be pursued against perceived political enemies.

Calls to undo the mistake of DHS’s creation aren’t exactly new — a one-time DHS official at the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute think tank was calling for the department’s end even before its 10th birthday, as did the libertarian CATO Institute. Ahead of the 20th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the ACLU joined in the call for its dismantling, and that was well before Trump sent ICE and CBP en masse into U.S. cities. Yet there are few examples in modern history of a former Cabinet official like Johnson calling for his own former department’s dissolution. Indeed, across Washington, most one-time Cabinet leaders spend the rest of their careers dining out on their prestigious presidential appointments; Johnson, however, tries his hardest now to avoid being publicly recognized as a former DHS official.

“The immigration mission has overwhelmed the department,” Johnson said. “If I have a DHS gym bag or a DHS hat, I don’t wear it in public anymore because the immigration mission has become so politically volatile.”

But DHS isn’t shying away from controversy or its combative stance domestically — in fact, this week, as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approached, current Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced that he was redoing the department’s official seal to reflect that DHS was “at war every single day.”

It’s a striking admission that with the wind-down of the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, the longest-running of the “9/11 forever wars” appears to be the one we launched here at home, against ourselves.

text:
A federal judge has dismissed a petition by a Nashville Spanish-language news reporter that alleged her detention by federal immigration agents this year was an unconstitutional retaliation for her critical reporting on immigration raids.

Estefany Rodriguez, a reporter for Nashville Noticias, was the subject of a targeted arrest on March 4 by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who surveilled her leaving her home with her husband and 7-year-old daughter in a car displaying the news outlet’s logo before pulling the couple over to make the arrest after the child had been dropped off at school.

Rodriguez was held for two weeks in federal facilities in Alabama and Louisiana before her release was secured by attorneys. She has alleged mistreatment during her detention.

In court filings, Rodriguez’ attorneys alleged her arrest, initial denial of bond and swift transfer to out-of-state facilities “indicated retaliation against Rodríguez in violation of the First Amendment due to her work as a journalist, including reporting on ICE.” They also alleged other constitutional violations in her apprehension and detention and sought an injunction preventing “any enforcement action against (Rodriguez) to retaliate against her for past speech or to chill future speech.”

Nashville journalist released from ICE detention details retaliation claims

U.S. District Judge Eli Richardson dismissed those claims largely on procedural grounds Wednesday, ruling it was improper to include them as part of a so-called habeas corpus petition. Habeas corpus petitions challenge the lawfulness of an individual’s detention.

“What [Rodriguez] seeks here is a wide-ranging injunction against all sorts of potential unlawful behavior in the future that is separate and apart from any specific challenge made (in her habeas corpus petition) to her March 4, 2026 arrest and subsequent detention.”

Richardson also ruled the petition, originally filed before Rodriguez was released from physical custody, is now moot. Rodriguez was released from a detention center on March 19, 15 days after she was initially detained. She remains free on a $10,000 bond.

Federal prosecutors alleged Rodríguez is illegally residing in the country after overstaying a tourist visa. Rodriguez subsequently filed for asylum based on threats she received reporting on government corruption in Colombia. She is now married to a U.S. citizen and is seeking permanent status through her husband, according to court filings.

text:
The city of Denver, along with several groups, sued the Trump administration Thursday, seeking to block U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers who are armed from polling sites during the upcoming midterm elections.

In fact, there are no official orders from the federal government to station or deploy armed immigration officers at polling places, although a Homeland Security official recently suggested they could do so under special circumstances — but not to verify voters’ identification.

Additionally, federal laws already prohibit stationing “troops or armed men” by military or federal officials at voting places except when needed “to repel armed enemies of the United States.” Federal laws also bar military members from interfering “in any manner with an election officer’s discharge of his duties.”

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., leans heavily on those prohibitions, though it does not cite specific cases where armed federal agents entered or visited polling centers.

The plaintiffs state that ICE officers’ presence could intimidate and deter voters, thereby interfering with local officials’ ability to administer elections.

“The specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election,” the complaint says. “It places voters in fear that they will be confronted by armed federal immigration enforcement officers if they choose to cast a ballot.”

“The right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy and to being an American,” said Denver Mayor Mike Johnston in a statement provided by Democracy Forward, a national legal organization working with the plaintiffs. “Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes. We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it.”

Speaking to reporters during a Manhattan news event on Sept. 1, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin had suggested that, while ICE agents would not be at polling sites to check voter identification, they could enter polling places under special circumstances.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” he said, adding, “ICE’S job is immigration, customs enforcement.”

“That’s their job,” he also added, “if we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be.”

The plaintiffs assert that with that statement, “Mullin confirmed and clarified the administration’s policy of authorizing armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to go to polling places — not to repel armed enemies of the United States, but to conduct civil immigration and customs enforcement operations, including serving warrants and detaining individuals suspected of being unlawfully present in the United States.”

Mullin, along with the Department of Homeland Security, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and David Venturella, in his official capacity as acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has been named as defendants.

Federal law prohibits non-citizens from voting in federal elections.

There had been recent cases of noncitizens being registered to vote or voting. In New Jersey, about 6,600 noncitizens were registered, the result of a software glitch in that state’s automatic voter registration system. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said about 400 of those noncitizens had cast ballots.

And in Colorado, Secretary of State Jena Griswold, the state’s top election official, mistakenly sent 20,000 voter registration mailers to noncitizens in 2022.

The lawsuit follows efforts by the Trump administration to restrict the mailing of ballots to only American citizens on an eligible voters list.

Trump’s order mandates the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to create those lists — to be given to states — and bars the U.S. Postal Service from mailing ballots to people who are not on the lists of “enrolled” voters.

On Sept.4, a federal judge extended the prohibition against the U.S. Postal Service implementing Trump’s order, just as the first states begin sending out mail ballots.

The decision from U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani in Boston to issue a preliminary injunction replaces a temporary order she had granted blocking the Postal Service’s plan until Sept. 10.

The Trump administration already appealed Talwani’s restraining order, and it will likely appeal the latest order as well.

The administration is running out of time to make big changes in voting procedures. North Carolina began sending out its first mail ballots Friday and more states will swiftly follow.

Denver Clerk and Recorder Paul López told The Denver Gazette he’s not surprised by any of the recent court challenges and that the lawsuit just “underscores what’s already illegal.”

“To be quite honest, it’s been a slow pitch softball that we’ve been watching, and we’re ready to send over the bleachers,” López said. “It is already illegal for any federal agents, or armed agents, to interfere with any election or to intimidate voters from participating in an election.”

López insisted that every executive order or any attempt to interfere with elections is intended to cast doubt on American democracy.

“All these things that they’re trying to do are, simply, to erode faith in American democracy,” he said. “It’s an attack on democracy itself, and it is designed to discourage voters from participating in this election.”

The lawsuit case number is 26-CV-03157. The Associated Press contributed to this story.

The lawsuit, filed by the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), follows Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stating ICE officers can go to polling places across the United States. Mullin said ICE officers will go to polling places in response to "specific threats" or to serve a warrant.

Critics say Mullin's policy is aimed at intimidating voters, will upend longstanding American norms, and violate a law keeping armed forces out of polling places that dates back to the end of the Civil War.

"This policy does its damage before a single officer walks through the door," said Juan Proaño, LULAC's CEO. "When a grandmother who has voted for 40 years, a naturalized citizen casting her first ballot, or a young man whose parents lack status hears that ICE may be waiting at the polls, many of them will stay home."

He added: "That is the chilling effect, and it falls hardest on Latino families in mixed-status households."

DHS on Sept. 10 confirmed Mullin's comments earlier this month that officers will only go to polls as part of "targeted enforcement actions."

"ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations," a DHS spokesperson said. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action."

Website shows who profits from ICE. Why Feds call it a 'threat'

Mullin's move to allow ICE into polling places comes as the agency has faced scrutiny and criticism under President Donald Trump. ICE has also faced criticism over officers wearing masks that conceal their identities, as well as fatal shootings involving Renee Good in Minneapolis, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Silverio Villegas Gonzalez outside Chicago. Dozens of people have also died in detention centers.

LULAC filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on Sept. 10. The city and county of Denver, Latino civil rights group UnidosUS and liberal-leaning watchdog group Common Cause joined in LULAC's lawsuit against DHS, ICE, Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella.

"The right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy and to being an American," Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said in a statement. "Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes. We'll fight tooth and nail to prevent it."

text:
Nearly 300 Canadian civil society groups are calling on the Government of Canada and the Government of Alberta to launch an independent investigation into an immigration raid that took place at a peaceful international student protest in Calgary in August.

On August 12, Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) raided an international student protest in Calgary, asking students for ID and providing them with “exclusion orders,” a process starting their removal from Canada.

At the time, students were protesting a mass refusal of work permits following quiet changes to post-graduation work permit rules. These changes came despite students receiving reassurance from their college and the government that they would not be affected

The groups who have penned the open letter, which include Amnesty International Canada and Migrant Workers Alliance for Change, have said that immigration enforcement at peaceful protests creates a “chilling effect” amid “already growing fear in immigrant communities.”

The groups have four demands of the federal government and government of Alberta, including:

Clear public policies ensuring that participation in peaceful protests, picket lines and other protected political activity does not result in immigration enforcement

An independent investigation into Calgary Police and CBSA’s actions on August 12, with public findings and accountability for any wrongdoing.

Immediate suspension of the exclusion orders and any removal action arising from the August 12 enforcement while these events are investigated.

Resolution to the fundamental injustice that brought these students into the streets by exempting them from the retroactive application of the new PGWP eligibility rules and assessing them under the rules in place when they enrolled.

Following the CBSA enforcement action, Julia Sande, Amnesty International Canada Strategic Litigation, Refugee and Migrant Rights Campaigner, says that the action by the CBSA is “appalling,” and has broad implications for other Canadians.

“Any attack on the right to expression, to assembly, to protest, I think everyone in Canada should be concerned,” Sande told PressProgress.

“People have the right to freedom of assembly, free expression, and your immigration status really has no bearing on that. Regardless of your status, everyone in Canada, both under domestic and international human rights law, have the right to peaceful assembly, to peaceful protest, and so it’s really concerning.”

Sande adds that the raid comes amid the increased scapegoating of migrants and refugees, but the response of hundreds of Canadian organizations pushing back against this, shows that “enough is enough.”

“The fact that so many groups are concerned should really be a signal to everyone in Canada that this is not okay. It’s not acceptable,” Sande said.

“We see the scapegoating, the blaming of refugees and migrants for things that are government policy failures. So it’s a way to say enough’s enough. We’re not standing for this anymore, and we won’t watch as you know, governments slowly, or in this case, very quickly erode at really fundamental rights that we all have and all all rely on for life as we know it.”

Syed Hussan, Executive Director of the Migrant Workers Alliance for Change said that the CBSA’s actions are both immoral and illegal.

“We’re also calling for the federal government to quickly and immediately clarify its position on whether they do go into protest or not, and whether this is part of the approach of the Canadian Border Services,” Hussan told PressProgress.

“It is the first known incident of CBSA going into a protest. Regardless of whether the police call them or not, this does not in any way explain or clarify or justify the actions of Canada Border Services Agency, which effectively targeted a charter-protected right, which is freedom of expression and assembly, for the purposes of immigration enforcement.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Minister of Public Safety said that the CBSA operates at “arms length” from the government.

“Individuals who are found to be inadmissible or who no longer have legal status in Canada are subject to the same legislative framework and due process protections available under Canadian law,” spokesperson Simon LaFortune, told PressProgress.

“Maintaining the integrity of our immigration system requires that immigration laws and decisions be respected and enforced consistently.Canadians expect an immigration system that is fair, orderly, and rules-based, and the CBSA plays an essential role in supporting that objective.”

Hussan added that the climate in Alberta has contributed to the sentiments around immigration and migrants.

“This coming, of course, within a climate of intense racism and xenophobia, particularly in Alberta, where Premier Danielle Smith–what she calls a separation referendum, and what the mainstream media calls a separation referendum–is actually a referendum on immigration. Five out of the 10 questions are on immigration; only one question is on separation,” Hussan said. “That’s part of the political climate in Alberta that we have.

In a statement, Alberta’s Minister of Jobs, Economy, Trade and Immigration, Joseph Schow told PressProgress that the Alberta government “supports the CBSA.”

“Anyone who comes to Canada on a temporary status needs to return home once their permit is expired.” Schow said. “That is the position of our government, and it’s not going to change. We support police services and the CBSA in enforcing the law.”

The groups are planning country-wide demonstrations on September 20 to call for action and condemn the immigration enforcement action.

“It is the task of every progressive person in this country, every thoughtful person in this country, to remember that migrants are the places where all of this begins,” Hussan said.

He added that government policies and the rolling back of basic rights often begin with migrants–from the privatization of healthcare, rising costs of education, labour laws and more.

“People have to understand that this is not about just immigration enforcement targeting a single protest, but rather this is the Canadian state under Prime Minister Carney that is moving towards a very specific form of response to the ability for people to speak up and take action.”

In a response to PressProgress, a spokesperson for CBSA acknowledged that they have received the letter issued by civil society organizations last week.

“We fully agree that the freedom of peaceful assembly is a Charter-protected right. We are aware of and reviewing the letter issued on September 2 by civil society organizations,” Luke Reimer, spokesperson for CBSA said in a statement to PressProgress.

CBSA also noted that they are “committed to the fair and equitable application of Canada’s immigration laws.”

“It is important to note that persons who have been ordered removed from Canada are afforded due process provided for by legislation, including access to appeals and judicial reviews, and can only be removed after all legal avenues of recourse that constitute a stay of removal are exhausted,” Reimer added.

However, Hussan noted that students who were issued deportation orders were within their 90-day restoration period.

The 90-day restoration period is a window in which to apply to regain status. Students must stay in Canada and are unable to work or study until they regain status.

“These people were within the 90-day restoration period. Now, why does Canada have a 90-day restoration period in immigration law if you can also be deported within the same time period?”

description:

The grace period also covers H-1B1 visas for nationals of Chile or Singapore working in a specialty occupation, and E-3 visas for Australian citizens working in a specialized professional occupation.
Eliminating the grace period would favor American laborers, the DHS argued.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security has proposed scrapping the policy allowing certain foreign workers—including H-1B visa holders—to remain in the U.S. for up to 60 days after losing their jobs to find a new sponsor, according to a government notice published Friday.

The White House-approved proposal is the latest disruption to the H-1B visa, which sits at the intersection of the Trump Administration’s priorities to restrict legal immigration, put an “America First” policy to work in the labor sector, and increase oversight of tech companies that rely on workers under this category.

Under the new proposal, some foreign workers would be considered immediately removable from the U.S. if they no longer work for an employer linked to their visa status.

The proposal “restores a direct relationship between an alien’s nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden,” according to the notice in the Federal Register.

Public comments on the proposal are accepted for 60 days. If adopted, the policy would mark one of the biggest changes to immigration policy, almost a decade after the grace period was created.

Cracking down on legal immigration

In early 2017, during the final days of the Obama Administration, a rule took effect stating that foreign citizens with legal immigration status under the H-1B visa, as well as several other visa categories, would have a 60-day grace period after they lose their job. That leeway allowed these workers to look for a new job or to change their immigration status.

The other visas covered by the grace period are E-1 treaty trader visas and E-2 treaty investor visas; L-1 visas allowing short-term work for executives and managers with international firms; O-1 ⁠visas for ​individuals with “extraordinary ability” in science, sports, or the arts; and TN visas for qualified Canadian and Mexican professionals. The grace period also covers H-1B1 visas for nationals of Chile or Singapore working in a specialty occupation, and E-3 visas for Australian citizens working in a specialized professional occupation.

According to DHS’s calculations, nearly 4,000 workers a year utilize the grace period to submit a new nonimmigrant worker petition after a layoff or resignation. More than 99% of them are H-1B visa holders.

Eliminating the grace period would favor American laborers, the DHS argued. “DHS assumes that almost all these entities would offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers, go through the I-129 petition process to sponsor nonimmigrant workers, or reassign the work to other current employees,” the document read.

Its removal would also reduce administrative work, as the existing rule states the DHS could skip or shorten the grace period at its discretion. According to the document, from Oct. 1, 2017, through May 20, 2026, the DHS calculated 1.9 million petitions or applications on which USCIS had to assess whether the 60-day period could have potentially applied.

A ripple effect

The DHS acknowledges that the policy changes would not only affect prospective employers but also families of the workers who may be forced to leave the U.S.

The proposal could also affect the immigration status of dependents of H-1B visa holders. Immigration advocacy group FWD.us estimates about 730,000 H-1B visa holders living in the U.S., plus 550,000 dependents, including spouses and children.

But according to the proposal, the department says it believes “the harm of the up to 60-day discretionary grace period outweighs the potential benefit it provides to the impacted aliens and employers, the alien’s dependents, and the community at large.”

Remaking the H-1B visa

Since 1990, hundreds of thousands of skilled foreign workers have entered the U.S. through the H-1B visa system. Citizens from India make up the bulk of H-1B visa holders, according to an April U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services report, with China a distant second. Tech industry titans like Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and even SpaceX’s Elon Musk have stayed in the U.S. with the help of H-1B visas.

Congress has set the current annual cap for new H-1B visas at 65,000, though an additional 20,000 is allotted for those with advanced degrees. Demand for H-1B visas often outpaces the cap.

But the Trump Administration has subjected the H-1B visa to various changes, as Trump claims skilled foreign workers have taken away jobs from Americans.

It has since replaced the traditional H-1B lottery with a weighted system favoring higher-skilled, higher-paid workers. And while a court blocked an attempt to impose a $100,000 fee on certain H-1B employers, the Administration in August proposed a new $103,265 fee for certain H-1B petitions and expanded a $4,000 biometric and security fee to cover extension applications from employers with a large foreign workforce.

text:
Your browser does not support the audio element.

An Arkansas law that provides in-state tuition and financial assistance to some immigrants is being challenged by the U.S. Department of Justice, which says the statute discriminates against U.S. citizens not given the same benefits.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Little Rock, the Justice Department asked a federal judge to declare invalid and issue a permanent injunction prohibiting the state from enforcing Act 844 of 2019, which created the program.

“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

The suit against Arkansas came as the department also sued Utah, Hawaii and the District of Columbia on Thursday. The Justice Department has now sued 25 states across the country over similar issues.

A message left for the Arkansas Division of Higher Education was not immediately returned late Thursday afternoon. The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge D.P. Marshall.

Jeff LeMaster, a spokesman for the Arkansas attorney general’s office, said the department is reviewing the complaint before deciding what the next step is.

“We agree with the U.S. Department of Justice that federal law preempts state law in this case, and the state law should not be enforced,” LeMaster said.

Act 844 allows state-supported colleges and universities in Arkansas to charge in-state tuition and fees to what the law describes as some “nontraditional documented immigrant students.”

The law requires the student to have lived in Arkansas for at least three years, to have earned a high school diploma and to have an approved, unexpired or renewed Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, exemption.

The DACA program, created under the Obama administration, applies to certain unauthorized immigrants who were brought to the U.S. as children. The program does not provide official legal immigration status, but it does protect its recipients from deportation and allows them to access work permits.

The suit seeks to invalidate the Arkansas law under the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act and the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, which sought to limit public assistance for undocumented immigrants.

The Justice Department also cites Executive Order 14218, signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025, directing federal departments and agencies to “ensure to the maximum extent permitted by law, that no taxpayer-funded benefits go to unqualified aliens.”

The Arkansas law grants in-state status for the purposes of tuition to the holder of an Employment Authorization Document, commonly known as a “work permit,” which allows an undocumented person to legally work for any employer.

The law also covers people legally present in the country who immigrated from the Marshall Islands, which has agreements with the United States to provide military defense, subsidies and access to the U.S. Postal Service.

Neither the work permit, nor DACA status, confer legal immigration status upon someone, but the Arkansas law treats them as legal, in-state residents for the purposes of tuition, the Justice Department said.

“At the same time, Arkansas explicitly denies eligibility for resident tuition rates to U.S. citizens who are not Arkansas residents,” the Justice Department said.

Arkansas, like most states, has in-state tuition rates for residents and out-of-state tuition rates for nonresidents. In-state tuition at the University of Arkansas is about $33,988 for one year and $56,256 for an out-of-state resident.

The Justice Department cites a web page aimed at DACA students for the University of Arkansas Community College at Morrilton, which states “UACCM welcomes all students regardless of immigration status.” The school charges in-state residents $140 per credit hour and out-of-state students $190 per credit hour.

The law providing for in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants violates the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, by contradicting federal laws, the Justice Department said.

The federal ban on providing benefits to undocumented immigrants supersedes the Arkansas law, the Justice Department said.

The federal government reached a consent decrees with Nebraska and Kansas earlier this year. Those agreements enjoined the states from providing in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants.

And a federal judge appointed by Trump struck down a similar law earlier this month in Illinois.

A federal judge in Minnesota in March rejected a similar lawsuit brought by the Justice Department.

In that case, United States District Judge Katherine Menendez said the federal government couldn’t show that programs offering in-state tuition for immigrants without legal status discriminated against U.S. citizens.

Menendez said the Justice Department misinterpreted the 1996 federal law, passed by Democratic former President Bill Clinton, because anyone who attended a Minnesota high school for at least three years is granted the same public benefits, regardless of whether they have U.S. residency or immigration status.

text:
The Connecticut chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union, or ACLU-CT, filed a federal lawsuit on Wednesday alleging that the Hartford immigration court is withholding access to “basic immigration court records.”

The lawsuit names U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and the chief immigration judge for the Hartford court, Angela Munson.

According to the suit, ACLU-CT requested all docket numbers and case captions — a line at the top of a court document that identifies basic information like the names of the parties involved — for May 2026 through July 2026. It also requested all “in absentia” removal orders, which are the orders of deportation made when people with pending immigration cases do not show up for court. The organization said it requested the information twice and did not receive a response.

The ACLU-CT claims in the legal complaint that such information should be available under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and should not require going through the Freedom of Information Act process to obtain.

The FOIA request process gives the government the right to withhold certain information for a variety of reasons. It can take a state or federal department months to comply with a request. Part of the purpose of the lawsuit, according to ACLU-CT, is to get such information contemporaneously to see what is happening inside the courts in close to real time, rather than waiting for months.

Dan Barrett, legal director for the ACLU-CT, said that while the public can attend court hearings and see the day’s docket, that is not a practical way for people to access that information and get a broad picture of what’s going on. For example, when people are being removed in absentia or to a third country, what are the details of their cases and why are they being removed?

The lawsuit seeks a declaration from the United States District Court that “the Immigration Court is bound by the First Amendment right of public access,” and seeks to prohibit Blanche and Munson from blocking the ACLU’s records requests.

Information such as full names is not normally provided via FOIA, according to Barrett. Such information is usually denied on the grounds of privacy.

A request for comment from the Department of Justice was not immediately returned.

The case has the potential to set legal precedent, which could have an impact elsewhere in the country, Barrett said.

The request, had it been satisfied, might have provided the ACLU with a comprehensive look at who is going through the immigration court system at a time when caseloads are growing astronomically.

But release of the data could also raise a number of questions about privacy and safety, issues that have been top of mind for Connecticut officials. Late last year, state lawmakers passed a bill that prevents public agencies, including schools, from sharing an individual’s address, hours of work, public agency appointments or “any other information that provides the date, time or place where such individual may be located.” The bill was in response to federal officials’ requests for state-level data related to programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the potential for its use for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement action.

Also, some immigration cases involve people seeking asylum because they are being persecuted by a foreign government and releasing a person’s full name could be considered sensitive or even dangerous.

Barrett said the group isn’t seeking for information about individuals in immigration court to be proactively published in a database, the way information for criminal cases can be accessed via online databases. He said rather that the ACLU-CT is arguing Americans should have the right to request and quickly receive such information without a FOIA request.

He said that, as in a judicial court, anyone with concerns about their safety could move to seal relevant information. “Even better, a court rule could presumptively seal certain things automatically. Both the state and federal trial courts have such rules — for example, names of minors, and birthdates or SSNs of anyone. Those rules would be just fine from the First Amendment’s perspective.”

Barrett said that he expected that should a ruling allow for access to such information, the immigration court will adopt a practice of automatically sealing the names of asylum applicants and other sensitive information.

U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on Tuesday tried to drive attention to the issue of in absentia orders by speaking with media after attending immigration court in Hartford. Blumenthal said he attended court to get a “snapshot of what seems to be purposeful chaos in the immigration court.”

Blumenthal said many people failed to appear for court on Monday, in some cases likely because they were not given adequate notice. If they fail to appear in court they can be ordered removed from the country “in absentia.”

“It is purposeful because it is due to lack of staff, reduction in numbers of judges, a system that is running amok and doing injustice,” he said. “And it is intentional injustice designed to deport as many people as possible as quickly as the system is able to do it, regardless of the merits of these cases.”

Currently, case-level immigration court information is available through the Executive Office for Immigration Review, a division of the Department of Justice that releases data regularly. While the releases do not include identifying information like the respondent’s name, the information released on the case itself is robust. These datasets include, among dozens of other fields, case outcome, respondent birth year, nationality and primary language, relief applied for, and if the most recent proceeding was an in absentia hearing.

This year, more than 99.8% of cases decided in Hartford with in absentia rulings have resulted in a removal order, according to immigration court data requested by the Deportation Data Project.

A CT Mirror analysis of Hartford immigration court data found that both this year and especially this summer, a higher percentage of cases were closed in absentia, where the respondent did not show up to their final court date. This almost always end in a removal order, according to the analysis.

In May alone, respondents in more than 90% of cases closed that month did not show up to their court date.

On the whole, fewer people are showing up to Hartford’s immigration court this year. From January to August 1, more than 79% of cases out of the court were marked in absentia at a final hearing. And 2025 saw the next-highest in absentia rate in at least 10 years, second to 2026, with 41% of respondents not showing up to their last court date in Hartford.

“All too often, we have focused on the detention of people, the seizure of people, which needs attention,” Blumenthal said, “but there’s also a kind of behind-the-scenes set of procedures here that also deserves attention. The basic infrastructure of the justice system is failing, and it is intentional and purposeful, designed to simply achieve deportations as quickly as possible, regardless of what evidence there may be to support people staying here.”

Laura Tillman and Sasha Allen are reporters for the Connecticut Mirror. Copyright 2026 @ CT Mirror (ctmirror.org).

title: REGULATION SHOULD NOT MEAN DISCRIMINATION - Amnesty Kenya
description:
Such narratives have, at times, contributed to xenophobic hostility and violence against African migrants and traders.
As a member of the East African Community and the African Union, Kenya has obligations to uphold equality, non-discrimination and the rights of migrants and refugees.
r. There is also a harder question the directive conveniently avoids, how did we arrive at a point where undocumented foreign traders are such a visible presence in Kenya’s informal economy?
Economic hardship should not be used to justify discrimination or hostility against people based on their nationality.
The government should suspend enforcement of the directive and undertake a lawful, transparent and inclusive process to determine how economic regulation can protect Kenyan livelihoods while respecting the rights of foreign nationals.
text:
There has been simmering tension among foreign nationals living and operating small businesses in Kenya following a Presidential directive on 2 September 2026, ordering foreign nationals operating small businesses, particularly hawking and small retail shops, to close their operations from 7 September 2026. The announcement has raised serious questions about the rights of thousands of foreigners who are legitimately in the country and have lived here for years.

While the concerns raised by Kenyan traders and small business operators about increased competition and its impact on the value of labour, services and goods are legitimate, regulation must remain within a legal framework that protects the dignity and freedoms of those affected. Questions therefore arise about the legal basis for enforcing such a blanket directive, particularly where the legislation cited as providing a framework for local-content measures has not yet been enacted.

It is worth acknowledging that the Kenyan government should, in fact, regulate economic activity and support citizens in the informal sector, many of whom face real and difficult competition for scarce livelihoods, but that legitimate interest should not be pursued through blanket measures that distinguish between people primarily on the basis of nationality, enforced ahead of any law authorising it and without distinguishing between refugees and asylum seekers, EAC nationals, foreign nationals with valid work or business permits, long-term residents and people who may be undocumented.

The announcement has also sparked a public debate increasingly framing African migrants and refugees living away from home in other African countries as enemies of citizens, particularly against the backdrop of unemployment and the rising cost of living. Such a directive raises serious questions under Article 27 of the Constitution guarantees equality and non-discrimination, particularly if people are subjected to different treatment solely because of their nationality. It prohibits the State from discriminating, directly or indirectly, against any person. A directive ordering an entire category of people to cease their livelihoods, identified by nationality rather than individual wrongdoing, therefore sits in direct tension with this constitutional guarantee. Article 2(5) and 2(6) of the Constitution further bind Kenya to the general rules of international law and treaties it has ratified. The 1951 UN Refugee Convention, its 1967 Protocol and the 1969 OAU Refugee Convention protect refugees’ access to wage-earning employment and self-employment. Kenya’s Refugees Act, 2021, goes further by expressly granting refugees and asylum seekers the right to engage in gainful employment and run businesses. An administrative directive cannot simply override a right Parliament enacted only a few years ago. The East African Community Common Market Protocol also provides for rights relating to the movement of workers, establishment and provision of services among nationals of partner states, subject to the Protocol and applicable implementing measures. Measures that affect EAC nationals therefore need to be assessed against Kenya’s regional obligations as well as domestic law.

Kenya’s standing as a haven for people fleeing conflict in Somalia, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia and beyond has been built over decades of Kenyans living, trading and building families alongside refugees and migrants. Some of those affected may have lived in Kenya for many years, established families and communities here, and may have limited or no meaningful ties to another country. Rhetoric that frames economic hardship in terms of nationality carries risks far beyond the traders directly affected. South Africa’s experience demonstrates the risks of political and public narratives that blame migrants for economic hardship and portray them as competitors for scarce opportunities. Such narratives have, at times, contributed to xenophobic hostility and violence against African migrants and traders. As a member of the East African Community and the African Union, Kenya has obligations to uphold equality, non-discrimination and the rights of migrants and refugees. r.

There is also a harder question the directive conveniently avoids, how did we arrive at a point where undocumented foreign traders are such a visible presence in Kenya’s informal economy? This has very little to do with the vulnerable traders themselves than with the institutions meant to regulate entry, work permits and residency. Kenya has previously documented cases of corruption and irregularities in immigration and work-permit processes.

If the government is serious about restoring order to who enters and trades in Kenya, accountability must begin at the border posts and within the institutions responsible for immigration and permits, not on the pavement where the people affected by those institutional failures are now standing.. Punishing the beneficiaries of institutional failure while leaving the institution itself untouched does not fix the system. It simply finds a more vulnerable target to blame.

What has been encouraging, though, since the announcement is that many ordinary Kenyans, commentators and civil society voices have refused to simply cheer the directive along. Across social media, opinion pages and public commentary, a real strand of resistance has emerged questioning both its rationale and legality. This signals something important about where the country’s conscience sits. Public concern about the directive also demonstrates that there is an important space for public debate about how Kenya regulates economic activity while respecting the rights of migrants, refugees and other foreign nationals. Economic hardship should not be used to justify discrimination or hostility against people based on their nationality.

The government should suspend enforcement of the directive and undertake a lawful, transparent and inclusive process to determine how economic regulation can protect Kenyan livelihoods while respecting the rights of foreign nationals. Protecting Kenyan traders and treating foreign residents with dignity are not competing goals. Kenya can regulate its economy, protect local livelihoods and still uphold the constitutional promise in Article 27 that equality before the law belongs to everyone within its borders.

title: Trump administration allows TPS to continue for Salvadorans – for now
description:
The Trump administration declined this week to terminate TPS for Salvadorans, even though it has done so for people from other countries like Haiti and Syria.
In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said it will make an announcement on Salvadoran TPS, "at the appropriate time."
Groups like the National TPS Alliance are advocating for Congress to step in.
"There are legislations in Congress that would provide a pathway for permanent residency," said Jose Palma, a TPS recipient and the national coordinator for the National TPS Alliance.
The National Salvadoran American Association is trying to convince Republicans to pass a more short term solution that would extend TPS for another 18 months.
text:
Roughly 170,000 immigrants from El Salvador covered by Temporary Protected Status can still legally work and live in the U.S. – for now.

The Trump administration declined this week to terminate TPS for Salvadorans, even though it has done so for people from other countries like Haiti and Syria. But it also hasn't said whether it will extend the protection in the future.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said it will make an announcement on Salvadoran TPS, "at the appropriate time."

The lack of action means that TPS recipients still have legal status, but their lives remain in limbo.

'I feel numb'

"I feel numb … the physical and emotional damage of the last month, it's so frustrating that it feels like we suffered that all for nothing," TPS recipient Daysi Gonzalez said in an Instagram post.

Gonzalez has been chronicling on social media what it has been like to live under the weight of uncertainty.

Gonzalez, who is now 31, arrived in the U.S. with her parents and older sister when she was six years old. They were visiting family in California and she was promised a trip to Disneyland. But a month and a day into their six month tourist visa, a 7.7 magnitude earthquake devastated El Salvador, and TPS was extended to Salvadorans who were in the country at that time.

She's never been back to El Salvador. She's now a partner at the political consulting firm where she started off as an intern. She and her older sister own a home together. Those accomplishments have turned into a painful checklist of things she has to figure out how to dismantle, if her TPS is ultimately revoked and she has to leave the country.

"I've tried to adjust status in different ways, but there are very limited legal options to adjust your status and there is no pathway to citizenship for TPS," she told NPR.

The start of TPS

Congress created TPS in 1990 to allow eligible migrants to live and work legally in the U.S. if they can't return safely to their home countries because of things like natural disasters and armed conflicts.

It was granted to Salvadorans in 2001, after earthquakes devastated the country. Since then, more than 150,000 Salvadoran TPS holders contribute an estimated $5.4 billion to the U.S. economy each year as part of the work force, paying about $1.5 billion in federal and state taxes, according to immigrant advocacy group fwd.us. And over the last 25 years, they've given birth to approximately 150,000 American children.

A legislative solution

In his second term, Trump has ended TPS for more than 10 countries. And in June, the Supreme Court ruled the president has virtually unrestrained power to end the program.

Groups like the National TPS Alliance are advocating for Congress to step in.

"There are legislations in Congress that would provide a pathway for permanent residency," said Jose Palma, a TPS recipient and the national coordinator for the National TPS Alliance.

Palma said one of those bills is one Republican vote away from reaching the House floor.

The National Salvadoran American Association is trying to convince Republicans to pass a more short term solution that would extend TPS for another 18 months.

"Let's not think about this as solving an immigration issue as make this like the next humanitarian extension for people that just can't all of a sudden be told, you can't be here anymore and you only have 60 days or 6 months to leave," said Francisco Semiao, chairman of the association. "But people need more time than that if they need to sell their homes, sell their businesses, other arrangements."

That would at least give Salvadoran families more time to make plans on how to proceed.

description:
