text:
[Editor's note: This piece is part of Lawfare's collection "9/11 at 25: The Legal Architecture of the War on Terror, Twenty-Five Years On," examining how 9/11 remains—or doesn't—embedded in current legal and policy frameworks, a quarter century after the attacks. Read the full collection here.]

***

For my generation of Americans, Sept. 11, 2001, is the date that lives in infamy.

It was a Tuesday. I was in Manhattan that day, my 44th birthday. The stark contrast of the black smoke billowing off the north tower of the World Trade Center against the crystal-clear blue sky is forever burned in my memory. When the south tower collapsed into a cloud of dust, my brain refused to register what my eyes were seeing. By the time I drove home to New Jersey that afternoon, the world had changed. A fighter jet patrolled the skies over Manhattan. The National Guard was posted on the George Washington Bridge. In just a few hours, New York City had become a war zone.

I had worked at the Pentagon just nine months before as general counsel of the Air Force in the Clinton Administration. The Pentagon was also hit that day. On Sept. 11, 2001, I was a private citizen again, a mere observer of cataclysmic events. A feeling of helplessness enveloped me.

Twelve years later, I found myself in the Rose Garden, standing between President Obama and then-Vice President Biden as the president announced he was nominating me to become the fourth secretary of homeland security. I had served as general counsel of the Defense Department in Obama’s first term, steeped in national security but from a legal viewpoint. By 2013, like 2001, I had returned to private law practice. In a surprise move to almost everyone, the president asked me to return to duty running a Cabinet department of 250,000 people and 24 components. Privately, I wondered whether I was qualified for the job, but I could not refuse it.

Congress created the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 2002 in direct response to the events of 9/11. Up until then, our nation, unlike others we know well, did not have any kind of national ministry of the interior or public safety. We indulged ourselves in the belief that we were separated by two oceans from most of the rest of the world and all the terrorists who populated it. Sept. 11 shook us to a new reality. The 9/11 hijackers were all from the Middle East and had entered this country legally by way of tourist, student, or business visas.

In the aftermath of 9/11, our nation’s leaders therefore saw terrorism as an extraterritorial threat: Do a better job of securing our borders at the ports, on land, at sea and in the air and we can keep the terrorists out. Thus, DHS was created as one vast Cabinet-level department with oversight of the agencies that regulate all the different ways someone can enter this country by land (Border Patrol), sea (Coast Guard), air (TSA), and at the land, sea, and air ports of entry (Customs). To enforce our immigration laws in the interior, Congress added Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to the mix. Congress also added to the mix the Secret Service, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). In some respects, Congress went too far and in other respects not far enough.

From the start, DHS has never been able to function as the U.S. government’s leader in the counterterrorism space. Then and now, the FBI is the well-earned dominant player in the area. Though our government is smarter and better at monitoring and regulating who enters our country today, terrorism has evolved from an extraterritorial threat to one that is also domestic based and domestic inspired. Increasing levels of mass shootings and gun violence by domestic perpetrators with a political motive can properly be classified as “terrorism,” but DHS has little role in this space.

The politically volatile immigration (or, as some would say, anti-immigration) mission has overwhelmed DHS. The component of our government originally intended to “keep us safe” is viewed in many communities primarily as a pariah, an enemy of the people, a heartless deportation machine to be reviled for family separation, masked men snatching people off the streets at night, and the killing of innocent civilians for which there has been no apparent accountability. Mayors and city councils in blue cities don’t want to work with DHS at all, to the detriment of public safety.

Twenty-five years after 9/11, it’s time to rethink homeland security.

In the United Kingdom, France, and other nations, there is a Cabinet-level ministry for public safety, distinct from the justice ministry, which oversees national law enforcement, security, and immigration. Congress should consider a similar model to address our domestic security in an enduring way, in the face of an ever-evolving threat picture.

Law Enforcement and Counterterrorism

At present, federal law enforcement is scattered largely, but not entirely, across the Justice, Treasury, and Homeland Security Departments. Still other federal departments and agencies, such as the Postal Service and certain IRS components, engage in law enforcement. Shuffled and reshuffled over the course of history, Americans should rightly question the configuration. Law enforcement across the federal government lacks clear dividing lines and overlaps; investigations and arrests often depend simply on who discovered the crime first. Meanwhile, a holy grail among federal agency heads is to never cede ground or resources to another agency; we all cling to our existing prerogatives.

Congress should consider eliminating DHS as we know it and creating one new Cabinet-level department with a greater consolidation of federal law enforcement agencies—including the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, ICE, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Coast Guard, the Secret Service, the Marshals Service, the Federal Protective Service, and the Federal Air Marshal Service—led by a secretary empowered to deconflict and streamline their law enforcement missions. Certain law enforcement entities with highly specialized missions, such as the U.S. Postal Service Inspectors or criminal investigations division of the IRS, should remain where they are.

In all, domestic law enforcement and domestic security in this country should be the responsibility of one Cabinet-level official, supported by competent, apolitical agency heads, as it is in other nations. We can and should allow each law enforcement agency to retain its culture, its heritage, and its brand, but with common oversight. There is virtue in multiple law enforcement agencies at the table together, reporting to one individual. The lack of common oversight invariably leads to duplicity, competition, a waste of government resources, and vital matters falling between the cracks.

Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity should be included in this newly created department. Security is closely aligned with law enforcement. The same is true of cybersecurity and cybercrime. Previously, cybersecurity was part of a directorate of DHS with a cumbersome name, the National Protection and Programs Directorate (NPPD). In 2018, NPPD was officially renamed and transformed by Congress into an agency within DHS, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Given the growing and evolving cyber threat to the country, this was a step in the right direction. Though it has had some capable leaders since its creation, CISA has had difficulty getting off the ground. It has yet to win wide public credibility, and the Trump administration has hobbled it with massive budget cuts and layoffs. Meanwhile, multiple other federal agencies—domestic, financial, and military—have also taken on a cybersecurity mission. The public is rightly confused about who to look to as the federal government’s primary watchdog for cybersecurity. CISA should be retained, strengthened, and included within the newly created Cabinet-level department.

Aviation Security

TSA is not a law enforcement agency, but like CISA and the Secret Service, it has a closely aligned security mission. Aviation security—preventing bad people from doing bad things on aircraft—is distinct from aviation safety, the province of the FAA. Despite its vital mission, TSA has been crippled by low morale, departures, and government shutdowns. When it comes to aviation security, we should never be lulled into complacency. The risks are too high. TSA benefits as an agency part of a larger security department of the government. It should remain so. Local airport authorities should be aware that aviation security can be privatized at airports, so long as it is subject to TSA oversight.

Intelligence

In a larger, newly created Cabinet department with most federal law enforcement agencies under its umbrella, a centralized intelligence directorate to support the mission is critical. DHS currently has an Intelligence and Analysis (I&A) directorate to support its missions, led by an under secretary. Administratively, I&A is housed in DHS, but is part of the U.S. government’s overall intelligence community, subject to the oversight and budgeting of the director of national intelligence. Under the capable leadership of a seasoned professional, an intelligence directorate can consolidate and deconflict information and capabilities, and the directorate can ensure that the right law enforcement agencies receive the right intelligence at the right time.

The Lawyers

The Department of Justice must be retained, but limited to the legal function. Across many foreign governments, and state and local governments in this country, the separation of the prosecutors from the police force is the norm, not the exception. In New York City, for example, the New York Police Department is separate and distinct from the district attorneys in the five boroughs and the city’s corporation counsel. There is virtue in placing some distance between government lawyers and the agency clients they represent, including law enforcement. While government lawyers are bound like other attorneys to zealously represent their clients, some degree of independent judgment by the lawyers who appear in court in criminal and civil cases is warranted. And, under such an arrangement, “weaponization” of the law to go after perceived political enemies would require the buy-in of two Cabinet-level officials, not one. (There is a separate debate ongoing about the degree to which the Department of Justice should be free of political pressure from the White House, which is not addressed here.)

OPLA

Within ICE is the Office of Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA), a group of about 1700 attorneys charged with representing ICE in prosecuting removal cases before immigration judges. OPLA is therefore part of DHS. Like other federal civilian prosecutors, these attorneys who represent the U.S. government in court should be part of the Department of Justice, not ICE and DHS, and trained like assistant U.S. attorneys in the ethical, independent, and lawful exercise of prosecutorial discretion.

Immigration Judges

Immigration judges are employees of the Department of Justice and therefore under the attorney general’s supervision. In other words, a court system under the control of the nation’s top prosecutor. The flaws in such a system should be self-evident. The attorney general can fire immigration judges en masse (and has, as recently as 2026). Under the current system, immigration judges are also bound to follow the politically-appointed attorney general’s legal interpretations of immigration law, which can (and have) shifted from administration to administration. The American Bar Association and other organizations have long called for shifting the immigration courts to an independent Article I court system similar to the U.S. Tax Court. Legislation has been pending in Congress to achieve this.

FEMA

Given its vital and unique disaster mission in times of global warming and increasingly severe weather events, FEMA should be elevated to an independent agency of the U.S. government, not subordinate within a security or law enforcement department.

USCIS

USCIS is an agency within DHS. Though there are security aspects to its mission, it is best known for naturalizations, managing visa and asylum applications, refugee resettlement, and administration of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. I have observed that USCIS’s culture is more like that of the State Department, which issues passports, and not of a law enforcement or security agency. For the sake of efficiency and symmetry, USCIS should be part of the State Department.

Privacy and Civil Liberties

Finally, a large and powerful Cabinet department that includes most, if not all, federal law enforcement is bound to raise privacy and civil liberties concerns. DHS currently has an Office for Privacy and an Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. These offices are currently understaffed and lack real authority and stature. To bolster public confidence in a large, newly created national public safety arm of the U.S. government, these functions should be transformed into a semi-independent directorate overseen at the under secretary level, with independent reporting obligations to Congress.

* * *

Government policymakers, with the best of intentions, too often respond to the circumstances of the moment. Twenty-five years after 9/11, the homeland security threat environment and capabilities have changed significantly. The DHS constructed in 2002 is now outdated, reviled by many, and was imperfect from the start. The task now is to rebuild a national public safety apparatus responsive to the present day, agile enough to respond to an evolving future, which will inspire confidence and not scorn.

This set of recommendations should not be read as an “abolish ICE” or “abolish DHS” rallying cry. Each of the missions DHS pursues—to one degree or another—is essential to a civilized society. But through realignment, the government can perform these missions more efficiently and effectively to meet present day and future challenges.

text:
The city of Denver—along with multiple Latino civil rights groups—on Thursday sued Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and the Trump administration to stop them from allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to serve immigration warrants at polling sites.

While Mullin has denied that ICE would be monitoring voting booths this election, he was concrete about agents having the right to be there if there was a “threat to that polling place” or “we’re serving a warrant.” Denver argues that even that violates 18 U.S. Code § 592, a Civil War-era law which blocks armed forces from patrolling polling locations.

“The right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy and to being an American,” Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said in a press release. “Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes. We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it.”

Federal agents have already been reported at polling places in New York, California, and Texas, as Trump continues his attempt to use baseless claims of widespread voter fraud as a means of fully controlling—or postponing—the midterm elections.

“The presence of federal force at the polls interferes with the smooth administration of elections at the local level,” the lawsuit reads. “It disrupts voting and makes it more difficult for state and local election officials and law enforcement to do their jobs by making polling places spaces of confrontation.”

Other parties in the lawsuit noted that the presence of federal agents would have a chilling effect on Latino voters, potentially stopping many from showing up at all.

“Sending armed ICE officers to polling places is not immigration enforcement — it is voter suppression, plain and simple,” UnidosUS President & CEO Janet Murguía said. “All Americans—including Latino voters—have a constitutional right to cast their ballot without fear of interrogation, detention, or family separation. This case is about protecting voters, preserving confidence in our elections, and ensuring that every eligible voter can participate free from intimidation.”

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins relented on the state’s congressional maps Thursday, ending weeks of election season chaos sparked by a scheme to eke out another Republican seat in the House.

“Following the United States Supreme Court’s stay, the only governing court order in effect is from the Missouri Supreme Court. In accordance with that order, my Office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map,” Hoskins said in a statement.

The order came hours after a contentious hearing before the Missouri Supreme Court that weighed whether Hoskins should be held in contempt of court. By Thursday afternoon, the court found that Hoskins “was in CONTEMPT” of their decision, but he would avoid punishment because his decision to use the 2022 map had purged the civil contempt.

Last week, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the state needed to use its original maps drawn up in 2022, and could not use maps that were created in 2025 at Donald Trump’s behest (also known as the H1 B map)—even though state officials had used the new map during the August primary. The court held that the 2022 map was the only legally viable legislative map, since the 2025 map was still pending due to a referendum petition filed in December.

Yet Hoskins did not comply with the court order. Instead, he sought emergency relief from the U.S. Supreme Court, though Justice Brett Kavanaugh chose to reject the request on Tuesday.

Then matters got even more complicated. That same day, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark—a Trump appointee—issued a temporary restraining order in a separate federal case, directing Missouri to use the 2025 maps while prohibiting state officials from using the 2022 map.

The U.S. Supreme Court chimed in on the matter for a second time on Thursday, overriding Clark’s decision by ordering the state to rely on Missouri’s prior ruling.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway issued her own statement Thursday afternoon in support of Hoskins’s decision to walk back the 2025 map effort ahead of the midterms.

“We affirm the Secretary of State of Denny Hoskins’s position and decision to advise local election authorities that the 2022 map is in effect,” Hanaway said. “We respect and will continue to comply with all court decisions, including orders issued by the Supreme Court of Missouri. We appreciate Secretary Hoskins’s continued commitment to upholding the law and working diligently to fulfill his duties on behalf of Missouri.”

Republicans are reportedly leaning toward Vice President JD Vance as their pick for 2028.

While attending a closed-door breakfast at the Republican midterm convention Thursday, Vance was met with cheers of “forty-eight” from the crowd of delegates from key battleground states, four people who were in the room told Politico.

Ahead of Vance’s scheduled address Thursday night, the breakfast served as reassurance that the vice president is favored by party members to eventually replace Donald Trump. Vance is currently leading the most recent Republican presidential primary polls, ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Even Trump seems to have settled on Vance as his successor—though he still jokes about running for a third term.

Things weren’t always so peachy for Vance. Earlier this summer, the vice president was the target of online attacks from within the GOP after his involvement in a now-collapsed ceasefire agreement with Iran. Vance’s allies tried to spin the criticism, claiming that coordinated opposition from “establishment” and “neoconservative” Republicans could actually help him in 2028.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao reportedly admitted that the Iranian military “blew the hell” out of the U.S. naval base in Bahrain—a shocking claim that contradicts the Trump administration’s narrative of total destruction of Iran’s attack capabilities.

While the damage to the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters at Naval Support Activity Bahrain in a February 28 drone attack has been well documented, Cao’s Thursday comment to a reporter at the conservative outlet TheEpoch Times is perhaps the most vivid, sober analysis of the situation from an individual of his ranking.

Cao also told The Epoch Times’ Ryan Morgan that Iran’s attack left American forces unable to “pull in” the USS Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier that was at sea for months and ravaged by reports of poor conditions and low morale.

“This is a pretty stunning admission by the Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, whose nomination is hung up in Congress, about how Iranian forces ‘blew the hell out of (U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet base in) Bahrain,’” Fox News’s Jennifer Griffin wrote. “Haven’t heard a senior U.S. official admit this on the record until now.”

Others noted the Iranian military capacity does not seem to be as depleted as Trump claims.

“A clear and particularly stark pattern we see in the war with Iran is that the Iranians are inflicting tremendous STRATEGIC damage with their missiles, but that the USG denies this at first and only admits it weeks, if not months, later. This creates a PROLONGED false impression that the war is going much better than it actually is and that strategic setbacks are not taking place at all,” wrote Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute. “The media narrative was that Tehran was utterly failing. In reality, Tehran was showcasing capabilities that the official Western narrative ensured were underestimated.”

When asked about any plans to return to the U.S. base in Bahrain, Cao told the Times, “I have a task force that’s looking at that.” That’s not what you want to hear in an expensive war that’s going very poorly.

“Why not just give the money now? If you have the money, why not give it now?” Ingraham asked.

“Because they can’t. I’ll tell you what, because the Democrats can’t do it, because with them it’s negative growth,” Trump said. “With us, it’s so positive.”

In reality, Republicans are simply not on board. Even Fox News hosts balked at the hypothetical handouts’ estimated $1.3 trillion total price tag. If Republicans were the least bit interested in moving forward with these checks, then they already control Congress. They could just make it happen.

Trump also claimed Thursday that he’d give $500 rebate checks to about one million people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act in 30 states, claiming they were overcharged by the Biden administration.

It’s increasingly clear that Trump is hoping he can pay Republicans’ way through the midterm elections by dangling cash in front of voters. But the president has promised to deliver cash payments multiple times, including $2,000 stimulus checks of tariff revenue and $5,000 stimulus checks for the bygone “DOGE dividend.”

text:
A former San Francisco immigration judge is suing the Trump administration, alleging she was fired just days after raising alarms about what she described as unlawful and unconstitutional treatment of a detained child.

Chloe Dillon, who served as an immigration judge in San Francisco, filed suit Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The complaint alleges she was terminated in August 2025 in retaliation for whistleblowing, about 48 hours after she emailed a supervisor about what she described as potential statutory-law and due-process violations involving ICE’s detention of an unaccompanied minor after a court hearing.

According to the complaint, Dillon said the detained minor could not be placed in expedited removal proceedings and had the right to have his already-filed asylum application considered first.

The lawsuit alleges violations of the Whistleblower Protection Act, the First and Fifth Amendments, the Appointments Clause and Article II.

Dillon also alleges she had previously objected to a 2025 directive requiring immigration judges to grant all ICE motions to move cases to different court venues. Her supervisor allegedly told her that “the White House” was watching the issue and warned her against resisting the directive.

The White House and Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges work for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review and are part of the executive branch, not the federal judiciary.

The lawsuit comes amid a wave of firings. The Trump administration has fired more than 100 immigration judges since January 2025, according to Bloomberg Law. MS NOW reported at least 135 had been fired since Trump returned to office. Other fired immigration judges have separately sued, alleging discrimination based on gender, age, ethnicity or prior advocacy for immigrants.

In a separate case, a Merit Systems Protection Board decision found the attorney general may remove immigration judges at will, though that decision is under appeal.

San Francisco’s immigration court, where Dillon worked, permanently closed Sept. 4.

text:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.

Ohio officials and candidates alike have reacted to the death of a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant who died by apparent suicide after being bullied because of his immigration status and the ankle monitor he was required to have.

Pierre Damas Bel was a Springfield High School graduate and Wright State University student at the time of his death, when he walked into Interstate 70 traffic on Aug. 31. Social media posts from Damas Bel’s account talked about his desire to pursue his education in the U.S., to build a future and play college-level soccer while working toward medical school.

“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” Damas Bel wrote.

His father said Damas Bel had told him earlier in the day on Aug. 31 that he hadn’t been “feeling okay mentally because of the bullying” he was receiving due to the ankle monitor.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement required the tracking anklet after the Trump administration eliminated Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants living in Springfield and across the country.

At a vigil for Damas Bel on Sept. 2 at Columbus City Hall, state Rep. Munira Abdullahi, D-Columbus, related to Damas Bel’s story of hoping to better the country with his presence. She decried the process that brought with it an ankle monitor and discouragement for the young student.

“We can not accept an immigration system that loses sight of people over paperwork and political dogma,” Abdullahi said. “Pierre deserved better. His family deserves better.”

She demanded the end of “cruelties,” the release of those in ICE detention, and “for my colleagues across the aisle and our Congress members to stand up and do something about this and end it.”

More than 40 Haitians living in Springfield had already been detained by ICE at the time of Damas Bel’s death.

Abdullahi’s fellow state Rep. Latyna Humphrey, also a Democrat representing Columbus, released a statement honoring Damas Bel and talking about the “devastating toll” the immigration process had had on him.

“There are real human beings behind every immigration policy and every government action,” Humphrey said. “…Whatever our political disagreements about immigration may be, our government should never lose sight of the dignity and humanity of the people affected by its decisions.”

The Ohio Senate Democratic Caucus released a joint statement calling Damas Bel’s death “a direct result of this administration’s inhumane and racist immigration policies.”

Democratic Ohio U.S. Rep. Greg Landsman said his office has “reached out directly to the Department of Homeland Security to end the use of ankle monitors on our Haitian neighbors who have done nothing wrong.”

According to the letter dated Sept. 3, Landsman mentioned Damas Bel by name in pushing for the Department of Homeland Security to “reconsider the policy of requiring former TPS holders with no criminal history to wear ankle monitors while going through the legal immigration process.”

“Our country needs border security and immigration enforcement, but the manner in which we prioritize deportations and allocate resources is skewed,” the letter read. “We are wasting time, money, and lives targeting good, law-abiding people rather than clearly prioritizing threats to public safety.”

In a separate statement, Landsman said the U.S. House has passed legislation to extend temporary protections for Haitians for three years, but the U.S. Senate has not taken up the measure.

Federal immigration officials have encouraged Haitians to “self-deport,” despite the fact that the U.S. Department of State still lists Haiti at a Level Four “Do Not Travel” advisory because of the risk of “crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare.”

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has made previous comments disagreeing with the decision to end the Temporary Protected Status for Haitians in Springfield, believing that “it will hurt us in the long run.”

“You’ve heard me talk a lot about what I consider to be a very misguided and wrong policy in regard to mass deporting people from this country,” DeWine said in comments on Sept. 1.

He said there are consequences to mass deportation, just as there are for other things done by the government. In defending the work of immigrant populations, he said one-third of caregivers in nursing homes and home healthcare workers are immigrants.

“I think we have to ask ourselves: Is it really good, is it what we want done, to see people like this being picked up and facing deportation,” DeWine said. “Do we want that done in our name? And my position has been that it’s a mistake.”

DeWine also said, however, that he felt the Trump administration “has done a very good job with regard to the Southern border, and I think that’s what people wanted.”

Former congressman and Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Sherrod Brown said in a Substack post about Damas Bel that he agreed with DeWine on the issue of immigrants in Springfield, adding that the decision to suspend TPS for the Haitian community “was wrong and has done nothing to make our communities safer.”

The incumbent in the Senate seat for which Brown is campaigning, Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, did not release a statement about Damas Bel. In a Sept. 3 press conference, he said his office plans to help those who have had their Temporary Protected Status taken away “to find out if there are any other methods for them to stay here legally,” but his office plans to maintain “the rule of law,” according to the Springfield News-Sun.

The Democratic candidate for governor, Dr. Amy Acton, released a statement saying she was “devastated by the tragic passing” of Damas Bel.

“Everyone in Ohio deserves to feel safe and to be treated with dignity, and we can uphold the rule of law without creating chaos and fear in our communities,” Acton said in a statement. “Ohio, this is a moment where we are all being asked to stand up for our common humanity. We must build a better way forward.”

In terms of immigration enforcement, Acton has made comments that conflict with Ohio Democratic Party stances, saying she wouldn’t prevent local law enforcement from working with federal law enforcement.

Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy didn’t release comments on Damas Bel, but has previously made comments that the Trump administration’s general mass deportation policy was “pragmatic.”

Back in 2024, Ramaswamy attended a town hall in Springfield, in which residents expressed concerns about the number of Haitians in the community. Ramaswamy said he didn’t blame the Haitian migrants who were brought here “by unconscionable means,” instead blaming “federal policies,” according to coverage of the meeting by WSYX.

At the time, Ramaswamy also said he supported mass deportation, but “if you’re going to pick a limited number, you may as well pick the ones who are most likely able to assimilate, most likely to participate in economic action, and those who are able to actually integrate their kids into the schools.”

text:
San Diego, CA — Today, Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) released the following statement after San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD) and San Diego City College both informed the Congressman's office of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest activity outside their schools within the past week:

"I am deeply troubled by reports that students and parents were detained without warning while trying to attend classes or bring kids to school. Schools are supposed to be a safe place for young people to learn. Yet this Administration exploits the places we trust most—schools, childcare facilities, hospitals, courthouses, and places of worship. President Trump has turned these places into hunting grounds.

“ICE isn’t going after the 'worst of the worst,' as President Trump promised. We saw this at Buona Forchetta, when ICE agents threw the owner against a wall, handcuffed employees, and used flash-bang grenades on bystanders. These people weren't drug lords or violent criminals; they were workers trying to make a living.

“Parents and children should not have to worry about ICE agents waiting outside a classroom or a doctor's office. That's why I led introduction of the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, which would bar immigration enforcement within 1,000 feet of schools, hospitals, and churches except in true emergencies. I will also continue working with SDUSD and City College to make sure San Diegans have the resources they need to stay informed and protected.

"Until ICE operates responsibly and reasonably to target dangerous criminals instead of hardworking families, I will push for real reforms from ICE and hold them accountable for the fear they have inflicted on my constituents and communities across the country. I urge all state and local elected officials to express their support for the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act and my Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act so we can deliver commonsense reforms that keep our communities safe."

Background:

Last year, Rep. Peters led the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, a bill to make our communities safer by establishing a stronger standard for Federal immigration agents' use of force. The bill would also restrict use of crowd munitions like tear gas and create greater transparency in enforcement by requiring the use of body cameras and strictly limiting the use of masks. Rep. Peters has pushed Congress to pass these common sense reforms, but they have been blocked by the Republican majority.

text:
A former San Francisco immigration judge fired by the Trump administration last year filed a federal whistleblower lawsuit Thursday accusing the Department of Justice of terminating her for raising due process concerns over new policy directives and ICE enforcement tactics.

Judge Chloe Dillon is among 14 San Francisco judges fired since President Trump’s return to office and is the first of the group to sue over her removal.

Her lawsuit opens with a quote from George Orwell: “If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.”

Dillon, like dozens of other immigration judges fired since last year, was originally appointed by the Biden administration. She first took the bench in 2022 after serving for nearly a decade as a federal public defender in San Diego.

“I was really excited,” Dillon told NBC Bay Area. “I felt like it was an excellent fit for me. I felt it was something that I cared about – ensuring justice in immigration court.”

Over the next three years working as a judge at one of the country’s busiest immigration courts, Dillon said she resolved thousands of cases, earning excellent performance reviews along the way. According to Dillon’s lawsuit, her “decisions were almost never appealed.”

“It was really interesting work,” Dillon said. “I felt like it was really important that people were heard and that their cases were decided carefully and based on all the evidence.”

But Dillon said the job began to change almost immediately following President Trump’s inauguration, as new appointees took over the senior levels of the country’s immigration court system.

In the spring of 2025, Dillon’s suit alleges that San Francisco Assistant Chief Immigration Judge Loi McCleskey directed the court’s judges “to grant any and all motions to change venue” filed by ICE attorneys. That meant immigrants’ cases would be transferred out of San Francisco to another court – potentially far away from their attorneys and witnesses.

“I think my first reaction was confusion because I felt that the policy was not in accordance with what the law was,” Dillon said. “It was certainly part of a larger project to detain people and bring their cases to conclusion, likely resulting in deportation, as quickly as possible. Because these cases were being moved to detained courts and being moved to locations that were more remote.”

Dillon’s suit alleges she expressed concern over the new directive in an email to McCleskey and later met with her supervisor in person.

“ACIJ McCleskey expressed empathy with Plaintiff’s point of view but warned her that the 'White House’ was paying attention to this and to be careful about pushing the issue further,” the lawsuit alleges.

McCleskey did not immediately respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment.

In one case, according to the suit, Dillon denied an ICE motion to change venue, but learned the case was transferred anyway.

Later that summer, Dillon described being alarmed by another new ICE tactic as the agency filed thousands of boilerplate motions to re-calendar cases in immigration court that had previously been administratively closed. Many of the cases had been administratively closed – essentially pausing removal proceedings – because USCIS, rather than the Immigration Court, had initial jurisdiction over the pending asylum applications.

Some of those cases involved unaccompanied minors, according to the lawsuit, and Dillon denied two government motions to reopen such cases.

“For unaccompanied minors, they have a statutory right under the law to have their asylum case decided in the first instance by the asylum office,” Dillon said.

The situation came to a head in August of last year. According to the lawsuit, ICE agents arrested a young man who came to the U.S. as an unaccompanied minor after a hearing in Dillon’s courtroom, telling the judge he would be placed in expedited removal.

“I had concerns because, first of all, people who are in that position cannot be put into expedited removal,” Dillon said.

Protestors clashed with federal agents as they took the young man from the courthouse and Dillon said she could hear the commotion from her chambers.

That afternoon, Dillon’s lawsuit alleges she emailed her supervisor warning of possible legal and due process violations, adding that courthouse ICE arrests – which had become common by then – were disrupting “the orderly administration of justice.”

Dillon said she was fired by email two days later by the acting director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

Dillon described being terminated as “really scary” – especially since it would leave her family of four without health insurance. But she said she has no regrets about sending the email.

“I don’t,” Dillon said. “Like, not at all. I felt that it was my duty to bring forward something that I felt was a violation of the law.”

Nearly a year after her firing, Dillon sued the DOJ, EOIR and Attorney General Todd Blanche, alleging a host of civil violations, including retaliation and violations of the Whistleblower Protection Act.

“I felt it was important for people like Judge Dillon to know that they had legal recourse and they had support,” said Melanie Proctor, Dillon’s attorney. “Federal employees have a right and a responsibility to raise suspected violations of the law to the appropriate authorities within their agencies.”

In an emailed statement, a DOJ spokesperson said the agency doesn't usually comment on pending litigation or personnel matters but described the allegations in the lawsuit as "patently false."

"After four years of the Biden Administration forcing Immigration Courts to implement a de facto amnesty for hundreds of thousands of aliens, this Department of Justice is restoring integrity to our immigration system," the agency added.

San Francisco’s immigration court was officially closed earlier this month following a wave of firings and retirements involving the court’s judges. Most of the court’s cases were reassigned to the immigration court in Concord.

“I think if you go back and you look at Project 2025, that’s essentially a plan that you can see happening in real time right now,” Dillon said. “They consider the immigration courts to be sort of an obstruction to a project to detain and deport as many people as possible.”

For the immigrants with pending cases in immigration court, Dillon said the stakes are high.

“For people who are seeking asylum, it's about making a decision as to whether they should be returned to a country that they're saying that they face persecution and potentially even death in that country,” Dillon said. “I think that we all have an interest in seeing that those cases are heard and decided fairly because these are people that we know and that we interact with on a daily basis.”

text:
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Elected officials and Haitian community leaders are demanding answers after ICE arrested two parents near John Marshall Elementary School in San Diego's City Heights neighborhood Wednesday morning.

On Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed the arrests of James Mervil and Josselene Polidor were part of a targeted enforcement operation. The agency said the couple entered the country lawfully in 2022 but overstayed their welcome, though officials did not specify how.

DHS said the pair ran when agents initiated a traffic stop, and that Polidor ignored commands to stop and bit an officer while resisting arrest.

People who know the couple said they had Temporary Protected Status until late July, when the Trump administration ended TPS for all Haitians in the country. They also said the couple has a pending asylum case.

DHS said the children's father was released late Wednesday night with an ankle monitor. Polidor will remain in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.

Witnesses say the couple's 2- and 5-year-old children had just been dropped off at John Marshall Elementary when the arrests took place. With no one immediately available to care for them, the school stepped in.

"So terrible, there was nobody else to pick up the kids; it was the school who organized to drop the kids to a stand-in guardian," Wister Gaetan said.

San Diego Unified board trustee Cody Petterson became emotional after watching video of the arrest.

"It's hard to watch," Petterson said.

He also addressed the presence of ICE near school campuses.

"We obviously, we've made it very clear we don't want ICE at drop-off or nearby or pick-up," Petterson said.

The arrests took place in City Councilman Sean Elo-Rivera's district, which includes the City Heights and Chollas Creek neighborhoods. He also became emotional watching the video.

"It makes me think, what are we doing? Like what are we doing?" Elo-Rivera said.

On Thursday morning, Elo-Rivera and other community leaders were at John Marshall Elementary for school drop-off.

"To stand with other community members who are trying to make sure that the kids got to school safe," Elo-Rivera said.

Also Thursday, Haitian community leaders condemned the arrests at a weekly ICE protest outside the federal building downtown, saying that since TPS expired, those who came to the country legally are now being targeted.

"That's just one snip example of what is happening in our community," one community leader said.

text:
One private company is benefiting financially from ICE increasingly using GPS ankle monitors to track immigrants awaiting legal proceedings instead of a less expensive smartphone app.

B.I. Incorporated won a contract in September 2025 initially valued at $1.02 billion to provide ankle monitors and other non-detention supervision services for ICE. The agency has so far obligated $228.5 million to the company under the contract.

B.I. Incorporated is part of the GEO Group, a business already profiting from immigration enforcement as the nation’s largest private operator of ICE detention centers.

RELATED STORY | DHS is placing ankle monitors on Haitians who were in the US under Temporary Protected Status

The ankle monitors have become a significant source of revenue, GEO Group Chairman and CEO George Zoley told investors during an August 2026 earnings conference call.

“The app is far less expensive than the ankle monitors,” Zoley said.

On the call, the GEO chief also said the number of immigrants on ankle tracking devices had more than tripled from 17,000 in 2025 to 54,000 so far this year. He predicted more monitors and money from the ICE contract yet to come, particularly from scores of Haitians who recently lost Temporary Protected Status under the Trump administration.

"Most of them we believe would be placed under the ankle monitoring supervision technique,” Zoley said.

Pierre Damas Bel, 20, was one of the Haitian immigrants required by ICE to wear a GPS ankle monitor.

He posted a photo on Instagram saying the device caused "a feeling of shame and humiliation.”

Weeks later, he died after stepping out into traffic in what his family says was suicide, blaming the ankle monitor for some of his despair.

A class action lawsuit challenging the use of ankle monitors says they can cause “pain, swelling and scarring.” A declaration in the lawsuit says the stigma makes it difficult to keep a job.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Corporate owners of ICE detention centers report another revenue surge

The electronic clasps are both intrusive and expensive, said Sarah Decker, senior staff attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center.

“These devices come at enormous taxpayer expense," Decker said. “It drives up profits directly into the hands of the private prison company that is manufacturing these devices. It's not an unintended side effect. It's really the reason why this rule is implemented in our view.”

DHS disputes that money has anything to do with the increasing reliance on ankle monitors, saying they allow officers to more accurately track immigrants in supervision compared to the app.

“Illegal aliens--just like U.S. citizens--are subject to the legal system and may be subject to release conditions that include ankle or wrist-worn GPS technology,” an unnamed DHS spokesman said in an email responding to a Scripps News inquiry. "Any illegal alien who is worried about having to wear an ankle monitor or any other GPS devices should accept the $3,000 stipend from the U.S. government and free flight home by self-deporting through the CBP Home App.”

description:

“No more placing illegal aliens over American citizens on this Department of Justice’s watch,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said in a statement.
“We have now sued every state across our nation that has a state law or regulation granting illegal aliens in-state tuition.

text:
(CN) — The Department of Justice sued three states and the District of Columbia on Thursday over what it calls preferential treatment toward student immigrants living in the country illegally and discrimination against U.S. citizens.

The lawsuits filed in federal court against Hawaii, Arkansas, Utah and D.C. are the the latest in a series brought by the Trump administration challenging state laws providing university financial assistance to immigrant students without legal status.

The DOJ claims these state laws are unconstitutional violations of the supremacy clause and discriminate against U.S. citizens who do not receive the same reduced tuition rates, scholarships, incentives or rewards, the DOJ said in a press release.

“No more placing illegal aliens over American citizens on this Department of Justice’s watch,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said in a statement. “We have now sued every state across our nation that has a state law or regulation granting illegal aliens in-state tuition. We look forward to favorable court rulings and will continue to deliver on President Trump’s promise: illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to American citizens.”

There are now 25 such lawsuits across the country, the DOJ says.

The DOJ seek to block enforcement of laws in the states and D.C. that provide colleges and universities the ability to offer in-state tuition rates for students, regardless of their legal status.

“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the DOJ’s Civil Division. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

The department also seeks to block Hawaii, D.C., Arkansas and Utah from enforcing their state laws and regulations that afford financial assistance and scholarships to students without permanent legal status.

“Federal law prohibits illegal aliens from receiving postsecondary education benefits based on residence within a state if such benefits are denied to U.S. citizens residing in other states,” the DOJ says in its complaints. “There are no exceptions.”

In response, the Arkansas Attorney General’s Office seemed likely to comply with the Trump administration.

“We agree with the U.S. Department of Justice that federal law preempts state law in this case, and that this state law should not be enforced,” Arkansas Attorney General’s Office spokesman Jeff LeMaster told Courthouse News. “We are reviewing the complaint to determine our next steps.”

The offices of the attorneys general for D.C., Hawaii and Utah did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This most recent round of lawsuits comes after the Trump administration scored a victory in Kansas, where a federal judge found state law there is preempted by the federal government.
